title: Automating the Observer OPTION-5 measure of shared decision making: Assessing validity by comparing large language models to human ratings
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study tackles the labor-intensive nature of observer-based shared decision-making assessment by testing whether large language models can score breast cancer surgery consultations using Observer OPTION-5. The goal was to compare LLM-generated scores from anonymized consultation transcripts against two trained human raters in women deciding on surgery for early-stage breast cancer. Its novelty lies in using a prompt-optimized, segment-based, inference-only pipeline that scores all five OPTION-5 items and benchmarks performance against the ceiling set by human-human agreement, rather than introducing a newly trained model. The main takeaway is that GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro-002 achieved substantial agreement with human ratings and could distinguish high- from low-shared-decision-making encounters, supporting scalable automated assessment of pre-operative breast surgery decision conversations, although the work is not a direct surgical-planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: What Matters Most randomized controlled trial breast cancer surgery consultation transcript corpus (private); 287 anonymized English transcripts from 4 cancer centers and 12 surgeons (private); internal validation split n=40 (private); held-out test split n=247 (private); no external validation dataset reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Key models: GPT-4o; Gemini-1.5-Pro-002. Additional comparators: Llama 405B; Llama 70B; Gemini-1.5-Flash-001; GPT-4o-mini. Reference standard/comparator: two trained human raters using Observer OPTION-5 (OO5).
Training Approach: Prompt engineering / inference-only; no task-specific fine-tuning reported. Best setup asked the LLM to score all 5 OO5 items simultaneously using detailed item descriptions, score-level examples, output-format constraints, and explanations. Transcripts were split into 120-line segments because of context-length limitations, segment predictions were aggregated to encounter-level scores, and prompts were iteratively optimized on the 40-encounter validation set.
Medical Modality: Audio-recorded breast surgery consultations transcribed to text (clinical dialogue transcript; non-imaging).
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Human-human agreement ceiling: Pearson r overall=0.77; ICC overall=0.77. Best validation prompt on GPT-4o: Pearson r=0.50, p<0.01. Test encounter-level Pearson r: GPT-4o=0.64 (p<0.01), Gemini-1.5-Pro-002=0.59 (p<0.01). Clinician-level Pearson r: Gemini-1.5-Pro-002=0.88 (p<0.01), GPT-4o=0.75 (p<0.01). High-vs-low encounter t-tests: Gemini=9.02 (p<0.01), GPT-4o=10.05 (p=0.039); clinician-level t-tests: Gemini=4.02 (p<0.01), GPT-4o=2.71 (p=0.022). Item-level Pearson r on test set—Gemini: Item1=0.15, Item2=0.23, Item3=0.39, Item4=0.63, Item5=0.52; GPT-4o: Item1=0.17, Item2=0.37, Item3=0.31, Item4=0.63, Item5=0.50. Bland-Altman bias for GPT-4o vs mean raters: +0.25 on the 0-4 scale, p<0.01.

title: LLM-powered breast cancer staging from PET/CT reports: a comparative performance study
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the challenge of deriving standardized breast cancer TNM and UICC stage from unstructured PET/CT reports, a step that is clinically important but manually time-consuming and variable. The main goal was to compare four off-the-shelf LLMs for direct staging from report text according to current UICC/AJCC breast cancer rules. The novelty is that it evaluates LLM-only staging specifically for breast cancer PET/CT reports, using internally authored clinically realistic reports that deliberately included ambiguity, synonym variation, and reporting heterogeneity rather than relying on structured EHR fields or report-generation tasks. The main takeaway is that Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved the strongest performance and suggests potential clinical utility, but the study remains proof-of-concept because the cohort was small and based on physician-authored fictitious reports rather than real multi-center clinical data.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal physician-authored fictitious breast cancer PET/CT report cohort (private; n=111); expert consensus TNM/UICC reference labels from nuclear medicine physicians (private/internal)
Baseline model/architecture: Claude 3.5 Sonnet; ChatGPT-4o; DeepSeek V3; Gemini 2.0 Flash (comparative benchmark of proprietary LLMs; no separate non-LLM baseline)
Training Approach: Zero-shot prompting / inference-only with one standardized prompt; no task-specific fine-tuning or retraining reported; outputs compared against expert-generated ground truth
Medical Modality: PET/CT
Model input modality: text-only (free-text PET/CT report)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary comparison for complete TNM classification accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet=0.901; ChatGPT-4o=0.775; DeepSeek V3=0.730; Gemini 2.0 Flash=0.541. Best model Claude 3.5 Sonnet: T precision/recall/macro-F1/micro-F1/accuracy=0.97/0.96/0.97/0.95/0.95; N=0.89/0.96/0.91/0.95/0.95; M=1.00/1.00/1.00/1.00/1.00; UICC stage=0.93/0.92/0.92/0.92/0.92. Comparator micro-F1 for T/N/M/UICC: ChatGPT-4o=0.93/0.86/0.97/0.90; DeepSeek V3=0.88/0.84/0.98/0.91; Gemini 2.0 Flash=0.75/0.80/0.98/0.82.

title: Bootstrapping BI-RADS classification using large language models and transformers in breast magnetic resonance imaging reports
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses automatic BI-RADS recommendation/classification from Chinese breast MRI free-text reports, aiming to support radiologic decision-making for follow-up versus biopsy. The main goal was to convert unstructured MRI reports into more learnable structured representations while preserving clinically useful information from the original text. Its main novelty is a privacy-preserving, locally deployed LLM pipeline that uses a knowledge-driven prompt based on the BI-RADS MRI lexicon, adds missing category information with default values, and fuses structured reports with the original free-text for classification. The key takeaway is that the full pipeline outperformed conventional text classifiers and few-shot LLM baselines on both internal and external cohorts, and the fine-tuned Qwen model also surpassed GPT-4o for report structuring.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: SYSMHReports (private; Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital breast MRI reports, n=11,884; internal cohort split into train=8,320, val=1,188, test=2,376); SCHReports (private; Shantou Central Hospital breast MRI reports, n=5,043; external test cohort); 50 radiologist-created virtual breast MRI reports with structured reference standards for report-structuring evaluation (private/synthetic expert-created).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed pipeline: Qwen-14B-Chat with knowledge-driven prompting for report structuring, followed by LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen-7B-Chat for improved structuring; transformer-based Chinese text classifier with concatenation fusion over free-text and structured reports (12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768). Key comparators: GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, unfine-tuned Qwen-7B-Chat and Qwen-14B-Chat for structuring; TextCNN, TextRCNN, DPCNN, MacBERT, BERT-wwm, BERT-wwm-ext, RoBERTa-wwm-ext, and Qwen-14B-Chat few-shot for classification.
Training Approach: Two-stage training/inference pipeline: (1) prompt engineering with a knowledge-driven template plus 5 in-context examples using locally deployed Qwen-14B-Chat to extract structured reports from free-text MRI reports; (2) parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen-7B-Chat on 10,000 physician-screened structured reports to improve information extraction. For classification, a supervised transformer was trained on the internal 70/10/20 split using free-text reports, LLM-generated structured reports with default-filled missing category information, and a fusion strategy that concatenated both representations; external validation was performed on SCHReports.
Medical Phase (pre/post): pre (diagnostic/pre-biopsy BI-RADS recommendation; some reports contain prior personal history and post-surgical follow-up information)
Medical Modality: Breast MRI radiology reports (text derived from breast MRI examinations)
Model input modality: Text-only; dual-text input in the final classifier (original free-text report plus LLM-generated structured report)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Report structuring: BERTScore Precision=0.9381, Recall=0.9217, F1=0.9298 for fine-tuned Qwen-7B-Chat (best; GPT-4o F1=0.8963). BI-RADS classification, internal SYSMH test: Precision=0.9003, Recall=0.9024, F1=0.9000, AUC=0.9542. External SCH test: Precision=0.8759, Recall=0.8665, F1=0.8694, AUC=0.9295.

title: Structured Report Generation for Breast Cancer Imaging Based on Large Language Modeling: A Comparative Analysis of GPT-4 and DeepSeek
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective two-institution study examined whether large language models can convert multiple free-text breast cancer imaging reports into one structured report covering primary lesion findings, metastatic lesions, and TNM staging. The main goal was to compare GPT-4 and DeepSeek for multimodal report synthesis across mammography, ultrasound, MRI, and 18F-FDG PET/CT in pretreatment breast cancer patients. The key novelty is cross-modality integration of text-only radiology reports into a unified markdown-style report with explicit TNM reasoning, rather than single-modality extraction or simple reformatting. The authors also designed a task-specific prompting and workflow framework and evaluated physician satisfaction, descriptive accuracy, and staging correctness. The main takeaway is that both models achieved similarly high performance overall; GPT-4 produced slightly more concise outputs, DeepSeek offers a local-deployment advantage, and ambiguous lesion descriptions still need human review.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Institution 1 internal pretreatment breast cancer cohort (private); Institution 2 internal pretreatment breast cancer cohort (private); combined dataset: 1358 free-text reports from 501 patients across two institutions, including 501 PET/CT, 275 mammography, 404 ultrasound, and 178 MRI reports; no public dataset used
Baseline model/architecture: GPT-4 custom GPT (GPTs) versus DeepSeek LLM; no conventional non-LLM baseline reported
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt-engineered comparison on proprietary LLMs; no model fine-tuning/weight training reported. A 20-patient Institution 1 development subset was used to optimize the input instructions and output framework. The workflow fused text-derived findings by averaging lesion sizes across modalities, using PET/CT SUV values, taking the union of metastatic sites, and applying NCCN-based TNM rules; physical-exam text was optionally added for N-stage
Medical Modality: Multi-modal imaging: 18F-FDG PET/CT, mammography, ultrasound, MRI
Model input modality: text-only (free-text radiology reports plus exam metadata/instructions and physical-exam text)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Physician satisfaction: Institution 1 correlation coefficient=0.665, ICC=0.664, P<0.001; Institution 2 correlation coefficient=0.558, ICC=0.554, P<0.001. Primary lesion feature extraction mean accuracy: GPT-4=91.7%, DeepSeek=92.1%. Combined feature synthesis mean accuracy: GPT-4=93.4%, DeepSeek=93.9%. Overall metastatic lesion identification accuracy: GPT-4=93.5%, DeepSeek=94.4%; notable institution-level differences: pleural lesion accuracy GPT-4=94.9% vs DeepSeek=79.5% (P=0.04), mesentery accuracy GPT-4=43.8% vs DeepSeek=87.5% (P=0.02); metastasis size/SUV extraction accuracy >93% for both. TNM staging for all patients: T-stage GPT-4=92.9%, DeepSeek=93.1%; N-stage without physical exam GPT-4=79.8%, DeepSeek=79.6%; N-stage with physical exam GPT-4=92.7%, DeepSeek=91.7%; M-stage GPT-4 accuracy/sensitivity/specificity=0.94/0.94/0.95 and DeepSeek=0.94/0.94/0.93

title: Interpreting BI-RADS-Free Breast MRI Reports Using a Large Language Model: Automated BI-RADS Classification From Narrative Reports Using ChatGPT
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective single-center study tested whether ChatGPT (GPT-4o) could infer BI-RADS categories and next-step management from de-identified free-text breast MRI reports after the original BI-RADS labels and recommendations were removed. The goal was to assess whether a general-purpose large language model can function as a decision-support aid for standardizing unstructured breast MRI reporting. The main novelty is a zero-shot evaluation on real-world narrative MRI reports, manually translated from Turkish to English, with performance judged against consensus from two expert breast radiologists rather than image re-interpretation or a fine-tuned task-specific model. ChatGPT showed moderate performance for detailed BI-RADS subcategorization but much stronger performance for benign-versus-suspicious discrimination, and its management suggestions were perfectly aligned with its own assigned BI-RADS class. Overall, the paper suggests LLMs may help structure and triage narrative breast MRI reports, but expert oversight remains necessary for nuanced category-level decisions.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Gaziantep University institutional breast MRI narrative report cohort (private; single-center; n=352 reports from Jan 2024 to Jun 2025; de-identified reports with at least one lesion; originally Turkish and manually translated to English); institutional biopsy/histopathology subset from the same cohort (private; n=278, descriptive only and not used as the reference standard); no external validation dataset
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT GPT-4o (transformer-based large language model); no separate ML baseline/comparator model reported; outputs compared against consensus of 2 expert breast radiologists
Training Approach: Zero-shot, inference-only prompt engineering; no fine-tuning or retraining on the study dataset; each report was manually de-identified, manually translated to English, and queried with 2 standardized prompts for BI-RADS category and recommended next clinical step
Medical Modality: MRI (contrast-enhanced breast MRI; report-based radiology data)
Model input modality: text-only (narrative breast MRI report)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: BI-RADS agreement: Cohen kappa=0.510, p<0.001. Class-wise correct classification: BI-RADS 2=66.6% (46/69), BI-RADS 3=52.4% (33/63), BI-RADS 4A=60.0% (27/45), BI-RADS 4B=29.4% (5/17), BI-RADS 4C=11.1% (2/18), BI-RADS 5=77.9% (109/140). Binary benign vs suspicious/malignant agreement: Cohen kappa=0.843, p<0.001; benign correctly identified=91.7% (121/132); suspicious/malignant correctly identified=93.2% (205/220). Management recommendations were 100% concordant with the model's own assigned BI-RADS categories.

title: Using Open-Source Large Language Models to Identify Access to Germline Genetic Testing in Veterans With Breast Cancer From Unstructured Text
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study examined whether locally deployable open-source large language models can identify access to germline genetic testing for Veterans with breast cancer from unstructured VA clinical notes. The goal was to automate a labor-intensive chart review workflow used to monitor access to hereditary cancer testing across the VA while keeping sensitive data inside the health system. Its main novelty is a privacy-preserving hybrid pipeline that combines rule-based triage of note snippets with prompt-engineered Llama models, without task-specific fine-tuning or reliance on external API-based LLMs. Among the evaluated models, Llama 3 70B performed best and achieved expert-comparable results. The main takeaway is that open-source generative AI can accurately extract clinically important genetic-testing access information from routine notes using limited labeled data.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: VA Cancer Registry System (private); VA Corporate Data Warehouse/CDW and VistA Computerized Patient Record System-derived clinical/consult notes (private); nationwide VA breast cancer cohort with available notes, n=1,201 (private); manually reviewed 200-patient labeled subset used for development/testing (private)
Baseline model/architecture: Key model: Llama 3 70B; comparators: Llama 3 8B and Llama 2 70B (baseline); preliminary rule-based NLP approach mentioned as an early comparator
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt engineering on locally deployed open-source transformer LLMs; no task-specific fine-tuning; 50/50 stratified development/test split on 200 subject-matter-expert-labeled cases; zero-shot and few-shot prompt experiments across prefix, template, and cloze styles; final system used a zero-shot template prompt with instruction refinement; hybrid production pipeline added rule-based preclassification for no-snippet cases as No and excessive-snippet cases as Yes; temperature=0.75; top_p=0.9
Medical Modality: Unstructured EHR text from clinical notes and consult notes
Model input modality: Text-only (keyword-centered note snippets merged into one patient-level document; some patients auto-classified by rule before LLM inference)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Best standalone LLM, Llama 3 70B on 60-case LLM test set: Accuracy=0.875 (95% CI 0.800-0.950); F1=0.912 (0.853-0.971); Precision=0.898 (0.816-0.979); Recall=0.921 (0.842-1.000); Execution time=251.95 s. Final production pipeline on 100-case test set: Accuracy=0.930; F1=0.941; Precision=0.933; Recall=0.949. Agreed-case subset: Accuracy=0.965; F1=0.972; Precision=1.000; Recall=0.946. Mean reviewer accuracy=0.960; chi-square P=0.188 versus pipeline.

title: Natural language processing for local, regional, and distant breast cancer relapse identification in pathology reports
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addressed the difficulty of tracking breast cancer relapse because manual review of pathology reports is labor-intensive and many registries do not routinely capture relapse outcomes. The main goal was to automatically identify local, regional, distant, and any relapse from unstructured pathology report text. The novelty is that it fine-tuned a transformer-based biomedical language model on pathology reports, rather than broader clinical notes or imaging reports, to distinguish relapse subtypes; the authors describe it as the first pathology-report NLP approach for these four relapse outcomes. The paper also uses targeted text segmentation to isolate diagnostically relevant report sections and shows that useful classifiers can be built from a relatively small labeled corpus. The main takeaway is that the approach achieved strong performance, especially for local relapse, supporting pathology-report NLP for automated outcome surveillance while still requiring external validation and broader data integration.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Fine-tuning/evaluation dataset: BC Cancer Breast Cancer Outcomes Unit pathology report cohort, British Columbia, Canada (private; 1,888 pathology reports from 993 breast cancer patients diagnosed 2005-2014 who later relapsed, sampled within 120 days before/after relapse dates). No external validation dataset reported. Backbone pretraining source: PubMed abstracts (public) + MIMIC-III clinical notes (public) via BlueBERT.
Baseline model/architecture: BlueBERT (biomedical BERT transformer encoder) fine-tuned as four separate binary classifiers for local, regional, distant, and any relapse; no explicit non-BERT comparator baseline reported in this study.
Training Approach: Supervised fine-tuning on manually annotated pathology reports; labels were created by four trained annotators with 95% agreement on 200 double-annotated reports; 70/30 train-test split; 5-fold cross-validation plus random grid search on the training set; regular-expression extraction/segmentation of Diagnosis and Diagnosis Comments sections plus metastasis-keyword context extraction to fit the model token limit; task-specific oversampling/undersampling used to address class imbalance.
Medical Modality: Pathology / histopathology reports (free-text pathology from FNA/cytology, core biopsy, and surgical biopsy specimens).
Model input modality: text-only (segmented unstructured pathology-report text, mainly Diagnosis and Diagnosis Comments, plus extracted metastasis-context phrases).
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Local: Accuracy=95.2%, Sensitivity=97.6%, Specificity=93.9%, AUC=0.98; Regional: Accuracy=92.8%, Sensitivity=73.3%, Specificity=97.0%, AUC=0.95; Distant: Accuracy=91.4%, Sensitivity=88.8%, Specificity=92.6%, AUC=0.97; Any relapse: Accuracy=93.7%, Sensitivity=97.8%, Specificity=76.2%, AUC=0.97

title: Validation of large language models for detecting pathologic complete response in breast cancer using population-based pathology reports
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study tackled automatic detection of pathologic complete response (pCR) from unstructured breast cancer surgical pathology reports after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, where pCR is often implicit and not stored in structured EMR fields. The main goal was to validate whether locally deployable LLMs could interpret these narrative reports accurately enough for research, surveillance, and clinical information extraction within a secure health-system environment. Its main novelty is the two-pipeline design: benchmarking embeddings from 15 transformer models with downstream classification, and separately fine-tuning GPT-2 with a lightweight neural head and LoRA for task-specific pCR detection. The key takeaway is that LLM-based approaches outperformed the prior decision-tree method, with the fine-tuned GPT-2 model achieving the strongest overall results, although only internal single-region validation was performed.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Alberta Cancer Registry cohort (private); Sunrise Clinical Manager EMR final surgical pathology reports from 4 tertiary acute care hospitals in Calgary, Alberta (private); manually chart-reviewed pCR reference labels from the same internal cohort (private). Final analytic cohort: 351 female patients treated between 2010 and 2017; no external validation dataset.
Baseline model/architecture: Pipeline B main model: GPT-2 + mean pooling + feed-forward neural network classification head with sigmoid. Pipeline A models/comparators: BERT base uncased; BERT base cased; DistilBERT; BioClinicalBERT; TinyBERT; BERT multilingual base cased; GatorTronS; BART base; BART large; BART-large-mnli; FLAN-T5 small; T5-large; T5-small; GPT-2; GPT-2 Large; each paired with a downstream logistic regression classifier. Traditional comparator: decision tree-based method.
Training Approach: Pipeline A used pretrained transformer embeddings without task-specific fine-tuning; long reports were chunked with overlap, segment/document embeddings were mean-pooled, and a Bayesian-optimized logistic regression classifier was trained after a stratified 80/20 train-test split, 5-fold cross-validation on the training set, and SMOTE for class imbalance. Pipeline B fine-tuned GPT-2 for binary pCR classification using LoRA plus an added fully connected head, with Adam optimizer and a learning-rate scheduler. Metrics were further summarized with stratified 5-fold cross-validation and 10,000-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.
Medical Modality: Narrative surgical pathology reports / pathology text in EMR after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Best overall model (GPT-2 fine-tuned, Pipeline B): Sensitivity=95.3% (95% CI 84.0-100.0); PPV=90.9% (76.5-100.0); Specificity=96.0% (90.0-100.0); NPV=98.0% (93.3-100.0); Accuracy=95.8% (90.1-100.0); AUC-ROC=95.6% (89.4-100.0); F1=93.0% (83.7-100.0). Best non-fine-tuned models (Pipeline A): GPT-2 Large and BART base each achieved Accuracy=94.4%, AUC-ROC=96.0%, F1=91.3%. Decision-tree baseline: Sensitivity=90.5%; PPV=76.0%; Specificity=87.8%; NPV=93.8%; Accuracy=88.6%; AUC-ROC=87.9%; F1=81.8%.

title: Iterative refinement and goal articulation to optimize large language models for clinical information extraction
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the challenge of converting complex free-text pathology reports into structured data for research and clinical analysis. Its goal was to build an end-to-end LLM pipeline that can identify entities, infer clinically relevant labels, normalize terminology, map relationships such as specimen or block to IHC results, and directly output analysis-ready tables. The key novelty is the combination of a centralized extraction schema, modular multi-step prompt templates with reasoning, and a human-in-the-loop iterative refinement process guided by a detailed error ontology rather than model fine-tuning. The main takeaway is that precise task definition and interdisciplinary refinement were as important as model choice, enabling very high performance on kidney pathology reports and transfer to breast and prostate pathology tasks without retraining.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: UT Southwestern institutional kidney tumor pathology reports plus structured EMR and CAP kidney resection-biopsy and metastatic RCC template data (private; 152-report development set, 3520 internal reports total, 2297 with structured validation data); TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma BRCA pathology reports and clinical data via TCGA-Reports OCR and cBioPortal (public; 757 available reports, 53 used for HER2, ER, and PR extraction); TCGA Prostate Adenocarcinoma PRAD pathology reports and clinical data via TCGA-Reports OCR and cBioPortal (public; 333 available reports, 253 used for Gleason score extraction)
Baseline model/architecture: Primary architecture: schema-guided multi-step prompt-flow LLM pipeline producing JSON and tabular output; main backbone GPT-4o (2024-05-13 for development, 2024-08-06 for finalized internal and external validation); comparators: custom rule-based regex baseline, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen2.5 72B Instruct
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt engineering with no parameter fine-tuning; multi-step prompting with reasoning carried across steps; human-in-the-loop iterative prompt and schema refinement over 6 cycles using a 152-report development set and a formal error ontology; temperature 0
Medical Modality: Unstructured pathology report text from kidney, breast, and prostate pathology reports; external public reports were OCR-processed PDFs, with structured clinical tabular data used for validation only
Model input modality: Text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Development gold-standard set: major LLM error rate=0.99% (14/1413 entities) after 6 iterations. LLM interoperability exact-match accuracy: GPT-4o=84.1%, Qwen2.5=78.1%, Llama 3.3=70.1%; fuzzy-match accuracy: GPT-4o=90.0%, Qwen2.5=86.1%, Llama 3.3=82.0%; GPT-4o inter-model agreement with Qwen2.5=84.8% and with Llama 3.3=82.2%. Internal kidney validation on 2297 reports: macro-F1=0.99 across 6 histologies; metastatic RCC F1=0.97; per-class LLM F1: clear cell RCC=0.99, papillary RCC=0.99, CCPRCT=0.98, chromophobe RCC=0.99, TFE3-rearranged RCC=1.00, TFEB-altered RCC=1.00. Regex baseline F1: clear cell RCC=0.96, papillary RCC=0.89, CCPRCT=0.71, chromophobe RCC=0.91, TFE3-rearranged RCC=0.11, TFEB-altered RCC=0.36. External portability: BRCA agreement=89% after excluding 9 curated values absent from source text; PRAD agreement=98%

title: A comparative study of large language model-based zero-shot inference and task-specific supervised classification of breast cancer pathology reports
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper evaluates whether zero-shot LLMs can extract clinically relevant breast cancer pathology variables from free-text reports as well as task-specific supervised NLP models, thereby reducing the need for labor-intensive annotation. The authors created an expert-annotated corpus of 769 UCSF breast cancer pathology reports covering 12 document-level classification tasks relevant to diagnosis and treatment. Its main novelty is the direct head-to-head benchmark of GPT-4 and other LLMs against supervised Random Forest, LSTM-Att, and UCSF-BERT on the same low-resource clinical dataset, along with detailed annotation and error analyses. The main takeaway is that GPT-4 matched or outperformed the best supervised model across tasks, especially under label imbalance, but errors in complex multi-sample and history-based reasoning plus the single-center design make it more suitable for research cohort development and pathology information extraction than for direct clinical deployment or surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: UCSF breast cancer pathology reports (n=769; private/internal, de-identified; split into 570 train, 99 validation, 100 test; no external validation cohort). Auxiliary private corpora used for model components: about 110 million UCSF clinical notes for fastText embeddings; 75 million UCSF clinical notes for UCSF-BERT pretraining; about 2500 multi-cancer pathology notes for an internal CNN span-highlighting tool. The 769-report dataset was planned for controlled-access release via PhysioNet after publication.
Baseline model/architecture: Primary generative model: GPT-4 zero-shot. Other LLM comparators: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, Starling-7B-beta, ClinicalCamel-70B. Supervised baselines: Random Forest with TF-IDF n-grams, LSTM with attention plus clinical fastText embeddings, and fine-tuned UCSF-BERT base. An internal CNN was used only to pre-highlight selected spans during annotation, not as the main study comparator.
Training Approach: Comparative design across 12 independently modeled classification tasks. Supervised models were trained on 570 notes, tuned on 99, and evaluated on 100 held-out notes; Random Forest used TF-IDF features, minority-class up-sampling for single-label tasks, and random grid search with 3-fold cross-validation; LSTM-Att used 250-dimensional fastText embeddings and attention; UCSF-BERT base was pretrained on UCSF notes and then fine-tuned. Cross-entropy was used for single-label tasks and asymmetric loss for multi-label tasks in LSTM/UCSF-BERT. LLMs were evaluated with prompt-engineered zero-shot inference using one JSON-formatted prompt per report and no task-specific fine-tuning.
Medical Phase (pre/post): both (biopsy/cytology plus surgical pathology such as lumpectomy and mastectomy specimens)
Medical Modality: Pathology and cytology reports from the EHR; free-text breast pathology, non-imaging
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: macro-averaged F1 on the held-out test set, chosen instead of accuracy because of class imbalance. Mean macro F1 across 12 tasks: GPT-4=0.86; LSTM-Att=0.74 (abstract rounds to 0.75); Random Forest=0.59; UCSF-BERT=0.56; GPT-3.5-turbo-16k=0.55; Starling-7B-beta=0.36; ClinicalCamel-70B=0.34. GPT-4 was significantly better than LSTM-Att for margin status only (approximate randomization test, P<0.01); for all other tasks, differences were not significant.

title: Developing prompts from large language model for extracting clinical information from pathology and ultrasound reports in breast cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the labor-intensive problem of extracting breast cancer clinical factors from unstructured preoperative ultrasound and postoperative surgical pathology reports. Its main goal was to test whether a general-purpose LLM could support large-scale clinical data abstraction more efficiently than manual review while preserving acceptable accuracy. The novelty is the workflow rather than a newly trained model: the authors built 12 Extract prompts and 12 Format prompts in GPT for Sheets and Docs using ChatGPT gpt-3.5-turbo, then standardized outputs with Excel functions and Python regular expressions. In a single-institution cohort, the main takeaway was that LLM-based extraction was much faster and cheaper than manual abstraction but still variable by field, so human oversight or a hybrid workflow remained necessary.

title: Evaluating the Concordance Between ChatGPT and Multidisciplinary Teams in Breast Cancer Treatment Planning: A Study from Bosnia and Herzegovina
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective study examined whether ChatGPT-4.0 could produce breast cancer treatment recommendations that align with real multidisciplinary team (MDT) decisions for newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve patients in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The main goal was to quantify concordance, safety, and clinical appropriateness in a resource-limited LMIC setting using 91 real-world cases. Its main novelty is the use of actual MDT cases rather than hypothetical scenarios, together with independent review by four board-certified oncologists from three reference centers and subgroup analysis of where agreement was stronger or weaker. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT showed generally high concordance in standardized, guideline-driven cases, especially receptor-negative disease and standard neoadjuvant regimens, but was less reliable in individualized situations such as low-grade tumors or uncertain surgical/endocrine decisions, so it should be used as decision support rather than a replacement for expert MDT judgment.

title: Large Language Models as Decision-Making Tools in Oncology: Comparing Artificial Intelligence Suggestions and Expert Recommendations
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective single-center study evaluated whether generalist LLMs can recommend appropriate management for women with early breast cancer using anonymized multidisciplinary team meeting records after primary surgery. Its goal was to compare AI-generated recommendations with expert MDT decisions and to judge discordant AI outputs against NCCN and ESMO guidelines. The key novelty is a head-to-head comparison of Claude3-Opus, GPT-4-Turbo, and LLaMa3-70B on real French-language clinical records, with guideline-consistent but non-identical answers counted as acceptable. Claude3-Opus and GPT-4-Turbo achieved high overall appropriateness, but all models struggled with surgery validation, tended to over-recommend radiotherapy to some extent, and were less reliable for genomic test decisions. title: Proof-of-concept study of a small language model chatbot for breast cancer decision support - a transparent, source-controlled, explainable and data-secure approach
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This proof-of-concept study examines whether a locally hosted small language model can support breast cancer treatment decisions while addressing key barriers of public LLMs, namely opaque source use, limited explainability, and data-security concerns. The main goal was to build a breast-cancer-specific chatbot (BC-SLM) aligned to the German breast cancer guideline and test its agreement with a multidisciplinary tumor board across five treatment domains, including surgical re-excision. Its main novelty is a transparent, source-controlled retrieval-augmented design that restricts generation to machine-readable guideline passages and surfaces the retrieved evidence used for each answer. The main takeaway is that BC-SLM achieved substantial concordance with the tumor board and performance comparable to ChatGPT-3.5/4 in a preclinical simulation, suggesting guideline-constrained SLMs are feasible for breast cancer decision support but still need broader clinical validation.

Training Approach: RAG / prompt-engineered inference-only adaptation to a machine-readable guideline; no end-to-end model training or patient-data fine-tuning reported; five query variants generated, top documents retrieved and reranked, then constrained generation from retrieved guideline passages

title: ChatGPT’s Agreement with the Recommendations from the 18th St. Gallen International Consensus Conference on the Treatment of Early Breast Cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study evaluated whether ChatGPT-4 could align with expert-derived treatment recommendations for early breast cancer by answering the same 127 questions used at the 2023 18th St. Gallen International Breast Cancer Conference. Its goal was to test whether a general-purpose LLM could support development of breast cancer treatment guidelines and scientific discussions. The novelty lies in a direct question-by-question comparison between GPT-4 and public expert panel voting across 17 topics, with each question repeated five times in fresh chat sessions to measure response stability while reducing carryover effects. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT achieved only moderate overall concordance, performing best in genetics, pathology, oligometastatic disease, DCIS, and survivorship, but showing clear weaknesses in BRCA-associated, HER2-positive, endocrine-therapy, local/regional recurrence, and bone-modifying therapy topics. This is better categorized as guideline or treatment-recommendation support than as a patient-specific surgical-planning study.

title: End-to-end breast cancer radiotherapy planning via LMMs with consistency embedding
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the fragmentation of breast cancer radiotherapy planning, where summarizing clinical history, recommending treatment strategy, and contouring target volumes are usually handled as separate steps. Its goal is to build an end-to-end radiation-oncology assistant (RO-LMM) that converts multimodal reports into concise notes, proposes radiotherapy plans, and guides 3D target volume segmentation on CT. The key novelty is a workflow-level LMM framework with separate task experts plus consistency-based training (CEFTune for text and NESEG/CESEG for segmentation) to reduce error accumulation when AI-generated outputs are reused downstream. Across internal and external cohorts, the system outperformed medical LLM baselines on text tasks and improved multimodal target-segmentation robustness, suggesting LMMs can support breast radiotherapy planning after surgery with better generalization.

Baseline model/architecture: Main model: RO-LMM built on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat. Text modules: RO-LMM-S (summary expert), RO-LMM-P / RO-LMM-P+ / RO-LMM-P++ (plan expert with NEFTune/CEFTune). CEFTune adds uniform embedding noise plus consistency regularization between noisy and clean inputs in SentenceBERT/PubMedBERT feature space; NEFTune used as a comparator/variant. title: LLM-driven multimodal target volume contouring in radiation oncology
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper tackles radiotherapy clinical target volume (CTV) contouring, where CT alone is insufficient because target definition depends on clinical context such as stage, laterality, nodal status, and surgery type. Its goal was to build LLMSeg, a 3D multimodal model that combines planning CT with textual clinical information for context-aware target delineation, primarily in breast cancer and secondarily in prostate cancer. The novelty lies in coupling a frozen Llama2-7B-chat model and learnable text prompts with SAM-inspired bidirectional interactive alignment between language features and multi-scale 3D image features. LLMSeg outperformed vision-only and prior multimodal baselines, especially on external validation and in low-data settings, showing that clinical text materially improves robustness and clinical usefulness for radiotherapy planning.

Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Breast CTV, LLMSeg: Internal Dice=0.829, IoU=0.730, HD-95=3.386 cm; External #1 Dice=0.822, IoU=0.709, HD-95=4.256 cm; External #2 Dice=0.844, IoU=0.740, HD-95=3.004 cm. Breast expert total score (/5): Internal=3.973; External #1=3.939; External #2=4.010. Prostate CTV, LLMSeg: Internal Dice=0.754, IoU=0.631, HD-95=3.036 cm; External #1 Dice=0.729, IoU=0.589, HD-95=3.522 cm. Prostate expert total score (/4): Internal=2.162; External #1=1.923.

title: Artificial Intelligence Language Models to Translate Professional Radiology Mammography Reports Into Plain Language - Impact on Interpretability and Perception by Patients
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This observational study examined whether general-purpose LLMs can rewrite breast imaging mammography/sonography reports into plain language that patients understand better. Using 3 fictional BI-RADS 3, 4, and 5 reports, the authors compared ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-4o, and Google Gemini after radiologist vetting, then surveyed 40 women on comprehension, follow-up recommendations, empathy, and added value versus the original report. The novelty is that evaluation was done directly by patients, not only by clinicians or readability scores, and it explicitly measured empathy and perceived utility. The work focuses on patient-facing interpretation of breast imaging reports in the diagnostic/pre-treatment pathway rather than direct image analysis. AI-translated reports were preferred overall, especially GPT-4o and GPT-4, suggesting LLMs may improve patient communication if radiologist oversight is maintained.

Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT-4; ChatGPT-4o; Google Gemini Advanced 1.5 / Gemini; original professional radiology report used as the comparator/reference.

Pairwise comparisons: GPT-4 vs Gemini P<0.001 across all four categories; GPT-4o vs Gemini P<0.001 across all four categories; GPT-4 vs GPT-4o was not significant except empathy P=0.044. title: Probing clarity: AI-generated simplified breast imaging reports for enhanced patient comprehension powered by ChatGPT-4o
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This prospective study evaluated whether ChatGPT-4o can rewrite breast radiology reports into simpler patient-friendly language without losing clinical meaning. The authors used 21 anonymized internal reports spanning mammography, ultrasound, and breast MRI with BI-RADS 0-6 cases, and generated 10 simplified outputs per report. The main novelty is the structured human evaluation pipeline: five breast radiologists rated factual accuracy, completeness, and potential harm, while five non-healthcare readers were tested for comprehension. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT-4o improved accessibility of breast imaging reports and performed best on simpler BI-RADS 0-2 cases, whereas more complex BI-RADS 3-6 findings still required clinician oversight; this is a diagnostic/patient-communication study rather than a surgical-planning paper.

title: Assessing the Accuracy and Readability of Large Language Model Guidance for Patients on Breast Cancer Surgery Preparation and Recovery
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This observational study examined whether ChatGPT-4o can provide accurate and readable perioperative information for patients undergoing breast cancer surgery, addressing patient education rather than technical surgical planning. The authors created 15 standardized patient-style questions on surgical preparation and postoperative recovery, submitted each in fresh chat sessions, and had 29 breast surgeons rate accuracy while readability was measured with Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level. Its novelty is the focused evaluation of breast cancer surgery preparation and recovery using realistic patient prompts and expert review, rather than broader breast cancer Q&A or technical benchmarking. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT-4o was usually accurate but often too difficult for the intended patient audience; the weaker areas were drainage management, psychological wellbeing, hospitalization duration, and postoperative follow-up.

Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT-4o (OpenAI large language model); no comparator baseline model was evaluated.
Training Approach: Inference-only, zero-shot prompt-based evaluation with standardized text prompts; each question began with context that the user needs surgery for breast cancer and was asked once in an independent New Chat session; no fine-tuning or task-specific training.
Medical Modality: non-imaging text-based perioperative patient-education content

title: Generative artificial intelligence as a source of breast cancer information for patients: Proceed with caution

Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study evaluated whether ChatGPT 3.5 can serve as a reliable patient-facing source of breast cancer information by answering 20 advocate-derived questions spanning work-up, surgery, systemic therapy, radiation, supportive care, and clinical trials. The goal was to measure accuracy, clinical concordance with specialist counseling, readability, consistency across repeated prompting, and citation reliability. The main novelty is that the question set was built from breast cancer advocate focus groups and the study explicitly audited whether cited references were real, not just whether answers sounded reasonable. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT 3.5 often produced partially useful answers but was frequently incomplete or partly incorrect, performed poorly for some topics such as lymphedema after axillary surgery and immunotherapy, wrote above recommended patient reading levels, and generated nonexistent references often enough that it should not be treated as a standalone medical information source.

Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT 3.5 (GPT-3.5 large language model via chatbot interface); no formal comparator or alternative baseline model.
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt-based evaluation; no task-specific training or fine-tuning by the authors. A fixed patient-role prompt was used ("I am a patient. Answer the following questions as if you are a breast cancer specialist. With each question provide references for your answers."), each question was repeated 3 times, and outputs were graded independently by multidisciplinary breast oncology specialists.

Medical Modality: text-based breast cancer patient education and clinical Q&A; no imaging or operative-planning data.
Model input modality: Text-only.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Overall accuracy=1.88 on 4-point Likert scale (range 1.0-3.0; 95% CI 1.42-1.94); overall clinical concordance=2.79 on 5-point Likert scale (range 1.0-5.0; 95% CI 1.94-3.64); comprehensive accuracy responses=36.1%; some-correct/some-incorrect responses=24.0%; completely incorrect=0%; completely similar clinical concordance=12.8%; not similar at all=7.8%; average word count=310 (range 146-441); word-count ICC across repeated runs=0.75 (95% CI 0.59-0.91; p<0.001); Flesch-Kincaid readability=37.9 (range 18.0-60.5); readability ICC across repeated runs=0.73 (95% CI 0.57-0.90; p<0.001); readability vs clinical concordance correlation=-0.15 (p=0.025); no significant correlation between readability and accuracy (p=0.079); average references per response=1.97 (range 1-4; total 119); nonexistent website references=41%; worst question-level average accuracy: lymphedema after axillary surgery=2.67; worst question-level average clinical concordance: immunotherapy=3.50.

title: Large language model trained on clinical oncology data predicts cancer progression
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study develops Woollie, an oncology-specific open-source LLM to predict cancer progression from free-text radiology impression notes across lung, breast, prostate, pancreatic, and colorectal cancers. Its goal is to test whether staged domain alignment plus oncology fine-tuning can outperform generic LLMs on real-world oncology tasks while preserving broader reasoning ability. The key novelty is a stacked-alignment pipeline that moves from general instruction tuning to medical alignment and then oncology-specific fine-tuning, plus cross-institution validation on real-world radiology report text. The main takeaway is that Woollie MSK achieved strong internal and external performance for progression prediction from report text, showing that specialized LLMs can extract clinically meaningful disease status signals from oncology narratives.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Alignment and fine-tuning datasets: Alpaca (public); Google Chain-of-Thought instruction dataset or COT (public); InstructionWild (public); OpenAssistant or OASST1 subset (public); PubMedQA (public); MedQuAD (public); MedMCQA (public); MedQA-USMLE (public); MSK radiology impression dataset or MSK-CHORD or AACR Project GENIE BPC subset, 38719 notes from 3402 patients across 5 cancers (private raw notes; labels partly public via cBioPortal and GENIE); UCSF radiology impression validation cohort, 600 notes from 600 patients across breast, lung, and prostate cancers (private). Evaluation benchmarks: COQA (public); LogiQA (public); ARC-Easy (public); ARC-Challenge (public); HellaSWAG (public); MMLU (public); OpenBookQA (public); SciQ (public).
Baseline model/architecture: Llama 1 decoder-only transformer backbone in 7B, 13B, 33B, and 65B sizes; staged variants Woollie Foundation, Woollie Medicine, Woollie, and final oncology models Woollie MSK 7B and 33B. Main comparators: baseline Llama models, non-stacked Woollie All, ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on benchmark comparisons, and Guanaco 65B in discussion.
Training Approach: Supervised stacked alignment and fine-tuning. Pipeline: pretrained Llama to foundation alignment on Alpaca plus COT plus InstructionWild plus OASST1, then medical alignment on PubMedQA plus MedQuAD and later MedMCQA plus MedQA-USMLE, then oncology fine-tuning on de-identified MSK radiology impressions for binary and 5-class progression classification. MSK split was 80 percent train, 10 percent validation, and 10 percent test; prompt-based multiple-choice classification with max 2048 tokens; zero-shot benchmark evaluation; deterministic inference with temperature 0.01 and top_p 1.0; external validation on UCSF.
Medical Modality: Radiology report impression text from oncologic imaging studies; report-text modality derived from mixed radiology exams rather than raw images.
Model input modality: Text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: MSK internal binary progression prediction: Woollie MSK 33B Accuracy=0.90 and AUROC=0.97; Woollie MSK 7B Accuracy=0.86 and AUROC=0.94. MSK pancreatic subgroup: Accuracy=0.92 and AUROC=0.98. MSK 5-class prediction: micro-AUROC=0.97 for 33B and 0.93 for 7B. External UCSF validation: Woollie MSK 33B Accuracy=0.78 and AUROC=0.88; Woollie MSK 7B Accuracy=0.80 and AUROC=0.89. Precision on UCSF: overall=0.95 for 33B vs 0.78 for 7B; lung cancer precision=0.99 for 33B. Benchmark examples: Woollie 65B achieved Accuracy=0.81 on PubMedQA, 0.50 on MedMCQA, and 0.52 on USMLE.

title: In-context learning enables multimodal large language models to classify cancer pathology images
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper asks whether a general-purpose multimodal LLM can classify pathology images without task-specific fine-tuning, which is usually data- and compute-intensive in computational pathology. The goal was to benchmark GPT-4V on three histopathology classification tasks, including breast cancer lymph-node metastasis detection, using zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning plus a kNN strategy that retrieves visually similar labeled exemplars. Its main novelty is extending in-context learning from text to medical image classification and directly comparing GPT-4V against ImageNet-transfer baselines and pathology foundation models under matched low-data settings. Few-shot prompting substantially improved performance over zero-shot, and 10-shot kNN prompting achieved competitive results with specialist models, especially on binary tasks. The main takeaway is that a generalist vision-language model can perform useful out-of-the-box histopathology classification with very few labeled examples, although performance drops on harder multi-class tasks and the workflow still depends on prompt design and external retrieval.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CRC-VAL-HE-7K / NCT-CRC-HE-100K (public; paper refers to the evaluation set as CRC100K); PatchCamelyon/PCam (public); MHIST (public)
Baseline model/architecture: Main model: GPT-4V (OpenAI gpt-4-vision-preview) with zero-shot, random few-shot, and kNN few-shot ICL; kNN retrieval used Phikon ViT-B 40M Pancancer embeddings. Key comparators: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Small (ImageNet-initialized transfer learning), Phikon, and UNI (linear probe and kNN classification)
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt engineering / in-context learning for GPT-4V: zero-shot plus 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-shot prompting with Chain-of-Thought-style prompting, temperature=0.1, and either random exemplar selection or kNN exemplar retrieval by cosine similarity in Phikon embedding space; no parameter updates to GPT-4V. Baselines were trained with supervised transfer learning or linear probing/kNN on pretrained features (Adam, cross-entropy; small-sample and full-dataset settings)
Medical Modality: Histopathology / digital pathology (H&E-stained microscopy image patches from colorectal tissue, colorectal polyps, and breast cancer lymph-node sections)
Model input modality: Image+text (target pathology image + textual prompt; in few-shot setting also labeled support images)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: unweighted accuracy with 95% bootstrap CIs (100,000 bootstrap iterations). CRC100K TUM vs NORM binary task: zero-shot=0.617 (CI 0.500-0.733), 3-shot=0.667 (0.550-0.783), 5-shot=0.783 (0.667-0.883), 10-shot=0.900 (0.817-0.967). MHIST, kNN few-shot: zero-shot=0.567 (0.450-0.683), 3-shot=0.658 (0.553-0.763), 5-shot=0.717 (0.600-0.833), 10-shot=0.834 (0.733-0.917). PatchCamelyon, kNN few-shot: zero-shot=0.600 (0.467-0.717), 3-shot=0.750 (0.633-0.850), 5-shot=0.817 (0.717-0.900), 10-shot=0.883 (0.800-0.950). Under equal-shot comparison, 10-shot GPT-4V exceeded the second-best model (Tiny-ViT) by 3.3% on MHIST and 6.6% on PatchCamelyon.

title: MedCLIP-SAMv2: Towards universal text-driven medical image segmentation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses label-efficient universal medical image segmentation across multiple radiology modalities, where conventional supervised models require dense annotations and often generalize poorly. The main goal is to enable text-driven zero-shot segmentation and then improve those masks with weak supervision by coupling a biomedical vision-language model with an interactive segmentation model. The main novelty is the MedCLIP-SAMv2 pipeline: BiomedCLIP is fine-tuned with a new DHN-NCE contrastive loss, saliency is generated with M2IB, GPT-4 is used to create richer task prompts, and zero-shot masks are further refined with nnUNet checkpoint-ensemble training plus uncertainty estimation. Across ultrasound, MRI, X-ray, and CT, the method clearly outperforms prior zero-/few-shot baselines and the earlier MedCLIP-SAM version, although fully supervised nnUNet variants still achieve the best absolute accuracy and the framework is still mainly limited to 2D binary segmentation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: MedPix (public; BiomedCLIP fine-tuning); ROCO (public; cross-modal retrieval validation); BUSI / Breast Ultrasound Images dataset (public; breast ultrasound training); UDIAT (public; breast ultrasound external validation/test); Brain Tumor dataset, Cheng 2017 (public; MRI train/validation/test); COVID-19 Radiography Database / COVID-QU-Ex (public; chest X-ray train/validation/test); CT lung & heart & trachea segmentation / Konya 2020 (public; lung CT train/validation/test); UniToChest (public; additional challenging CT nodule evaluation)
Baseline model/architecture: Main architecture: MedCLIP-SAMv2 = fine-tuned BiomedCLIP (ViT image encoder + PubMedBERT text encoder) + M2IB saliency attribution + post-processing and connected-component analysis + SAM refinement (tested SAM ViT-B, SAM ViT-H, MedSAM, SAM-Med2D; SAM ViT-H best overall) + weakly supervised nnUNet checkpoint ensemble. Key comparators: MedCLIP-SAM, SaLIP, SAMAug, UniverSeg, ProtoSAM, Self-Prompt-SAM, nnUNet, nnUNet ensemble, CLIP, PMC-CLIP, BiomedCLIP, InfoNCE, DCL, HN-NCE.
Training Approach: Three-stage setup: (1) contrastive fine-tuning of BiomedCLIP on image-text pairs using the proposed DHN-NCE loss; (2) zero-shot text-driven segmentation at inference using GPT-4-generated or engineered prompts, M2IB saliency maps, Otsu thresholding, connected-component filtering, and SAM visual-prompt refinement; (3) weakly supervised nnUNet training on zero-shot pseudo-labels for 600 epochs with 3 cycles, 30 saved checkpoints, checkpoint averaging, and entropy-based uncertainty estimation. No manual segmentation masks are needed for the zero-shot stage.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal radiology: ultrasound, MRI, chest X-ray, CT
Model input modality: image + text prompts for the BiomedCLIP/M2IB/SAM zero-shot pipeline; image-only plus pseudo-masks for weakly supervised nnUNet refinement
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metrics: Dice-Sorensen Coefficient (DSC) and Normalized Surface Distance (NSD). Zero-shot DSC/NSD (%) = Breast US 77.76/81.11, Brain MRI 76.52/82.23, Lung X-ray 75.79/80.88, Lung CT 80.38/82.03, Overall 77.61/81.56. Weakly supervised DSC/NSD (%) = Breast US 78.87/84.58, Brain MRI 80.03/88.25, Lung X-ray 80.77/84.53, Lung CT 88.78/91.95, Overall 82.11/87.33. Additional UniToChest nodule results DSC/NSD (%) = zero-shot big 40.76/46.44, zero-shot small 7.93/10.84, weakly supervised big 60.64/68.79, weakly supervised small 24.73/30.77. Retrieval validation on ROCO: image-to-text Top-1/Top-2 (%) 84.70/94.73; text-to-image Top-1/Top-2 (%) 85.99/95.17.

title: MammoVLM: A generative large vision-language model for mammography-related diagnostic assistance
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses mammography-related diagnostic assistance by aiming to answer patient follow-up questions grounded in screening mammograms rather than generic medical chatbot outputs. The authors propose MammoVLM, a mammography-specific generative vision-language model designed to support multi-round question answering from mammograms. Its main novelty is a density-aware sparse visual mixture-of-experts that routes images to CLIP, DINOv2, or ConvNeXt-Tiny, together with UMiCon, a projection module pretrained with unimodal and multimodal contrastive learning on BI-RADS 3 vs 4 before GLM-4 9B supervised fine-tuning on radiologist-curated Q&A. The main takeaway is that MammoVLM outperformed competing open-source VLMs in radiologist-rated Q&A and showed performance approaching a junior radiologist, while also generalizing well in zero-shot malignancy screening.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal multi-hospital mammogram-report cohort, 33,630 mammogram studies from 30,495 patients collected between 2011 and 2021 (private); radiologist-curated mammography Q&A set, 3,753 patient questions with selected/corrected answers (private); UMiCon BI-RADS 3/4 biopsy-proven sub-dataset, 4,557 patients for training/validation plus a 601-patient temporal test set (private); unseen zero-shot mammographic malignancy test set, 2,402 included mammograms after excluding BI-RADS 0 (private).
Baseline model/architecture: Main architecture: MammoVLM = ResNet-50 density classifier + Visual-MoE with CLIP, DINOv2, and ConvNeXt-Tiny image encoders + UMiCon 6-layer MLP visual-text alignment/projection module + GLM-4 9B LLM; text encoder used in multimodal pretraining: MacBERT-base. Key comparators: LLaVA-1.5, CogVLM, QWen-VL, Mammo-CLIP, BiomedGPT; alternate LLM backbones tested: Llama-3, Mixtral 8x22B, QWen.
Training Approach: Multi-stage training: supervised training of ResNet-50 on breast-density labels for MoE routing; UMiCon pretraining with unimodal contrastive learning on augmented mammograms and multimodal contrastive learning on mammogram-report pairs, followed by supervised BI-RADS 3 vs 4 classification with cross-modal contrastive loss; supervised fine-tuning of GLM-4 9B on radiologist-curated instruction-style Q&A pairs while freezing the visual encoder and UMiCon.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: mammography X-ray (CC and MLO views) + radiology diagnostic reports; biopsy/pathology results used as labels/ground truth for BI-RADS 3 vs 4 and malignancy analyses.
Model input modality: image + text (mammogram(s) + patient question for MammoVLM inference; mammogram + diagnostic report for UMiCon pretraining/classification)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary VQA scores, Table 1: Correctness=91.5; Rationality=82.6; Helpfulness=91.2; Professionalism=94.6; Completeness=96.5. UMiCon BI-RADS 3 vs 4, Table 7: AUC=0.70 [0.65-0.75]; ACC=0.69; SEN=0.81; SPC=0.59; PPV=0.62; NPV=0.79. Zero-shot malignancy screening, Table 10: AUC=0.9270 [0.9264-0.9276]; Specificity at Sensitivity=20%=0.9902 [0.9899-0.9905]. Visual-MoE density selector: ResNet-50 AUC=0.94.

title: Frozen Large-Scale Pretrained Vision-Language Models are the Effective Foundational Backbone for Multimodal Breast Cancer Prediction
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses multimodal breast cancer prediction by classifying biopsy-proven benign versus malignant breast lesions from lesion-cropped mammograms plus EHR-derived clinical and radiographic features. The main goal was to test whether frozen large-scale pretrained vision-language models can serve as stronger multimodal backbones than conventional image-tabular fusion networks. The key novelty is a simple Tab2Text module that converts structured EHR variables into natural-language templates so frozen CLIP-family image and text encoders can be used jointly, with only a lightweight fusion and classification head trained; this also makes cross-dataset training easier when tabular schemas are only partially aligned. Overall, frozen EVA-CLIP and OpenCLIP backbones were more accurate and more stable than conventional baselines, with especially notable gains on CBIS-DDSM and in limited-data BI-RADS 3 evaluation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CBIS-DDSM (public; biopsy-verified lesion-ROI subset with radiographic and EHR features); EMBED (public; biopsy-verified, single-lesion-per-breast linked subset with EHR features); combined CBIS-DDSM plus EMBED training also evaluated (both public).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: frozen CLIP-family dual-encoder multimodal backbone with Tab2Text plus lightweight fusion/classifier; EVA-02-CLIP-B/16, EVA-02-CLIP-L/14, EVA-01-CLIP-g/14+, and OpenCLIP-G/14 with ViT-bigG were tested. Main comparators: conventional image-tabular fusion models using ViT-base, ViT-large, or ViT-giant image encoders plus a shallow ANN/MLP tabular encoder, under frozen-vision and full-finetuning settings. Additional domain-specific baselines: PubMedCLIP and BiomedCLIP.
Training Approach: Supervised transfer learning for benign-versus-malignant classification. In the proposed setting, CLIP image and text encoders were frozen, tabular EHR fields were converted to templated text via Tab2Text, and only the fusion/classification head was trained; conventional baselines used one-hot or multi-hot encoded tabular inputs with a shallow ANN and either frozen or fully fine-tuned vision encoders. Lesion ROIs were augmented by 10 random crops per lesion; training used Adam, early stopping, cosine learning-rate decay, mixed-precision fp16, maximum 20 epochs, and results were averaged over 5 random seeds.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: mammography lesion ROI images (film mammograms in CBIS-DDSM; digital mammograms in EMBED) plus EHR and radiographic clinical metadata.
Model input modality: Image plus text for the main VLM model (lesion crop plus templated text converted from tabular EHR features); comparator models used image plus one-hot tabular.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main reported results from full-text experiments: CBIS-DDSM, EVA-01-CLIP-g/14+ (ViT-giant) - Validation Acc=0.810+-0.014, AUC=0.902+-0.003, AP=0.876+-0.004; Official test Acc=0.723+-0.018, AUC=0.830+-0.002, AP=0.741+-0.002. Best CBIS-DDSM validation overall, OpenCLIP-G/14 (ViT-bigG) - Validation Acc=0.796+-0.028, AUC=0.907+-0.003, AP=0.879+-0.005; Official test Acc=0.727+-0.026, AUC=0.828+-0.002, AP=0.744+-0.003. EMBED: EVA-02-CLIP-L/14 - Validation Acc=0.691+-0.019, AUC=0.806+-0.009, AP=0.611+-0.027; highest EMBED overall with combined CBIS-DDSM plus EMBED training using OpenCLIP-G/14 - Validation Acc=0.717+-0.004, AUC=0.809+-0.008, AP=0.671+-0.004. Limited-data BI-RADS 3 setting: AUC improved from 0.91 to 0.96 on the official test set and from 0.79 to 0.83 on the validation set.

title: A visual-omics foundation model to bridge histopathology with spatial transcriptomics
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper introduces OmiCLIP, a visual-omics foundation model, and Loki, a downstream multimodal analysis platform, to connect H&E histopathology with spatial transcriptomics across many organs and disease contexts. The main goal was to learn a shared latent space that supports cross-modality tissue alignment, tissue annotation, cell-type decomposition, image-to-transcriptomics retrieval, and spatial gene-expression prediction from histology. Its main novelty is representing each spatial transcriptomics spot as a ranked gene-sentence and pretraining a CoCa-style dual encoder on ST-bank, a 2,185,571-pair paired image-transcriptomics dataset curated from 113 public studies across 32 organs, followed by broad downstream evaluation on public and in-house data. The main takeaway is that the platform is robust and versatile across multiple tasks, but the authors explicitly state that OmiCLIP is a contrastive/retrieval model rather than a truly generative model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: ST-bank (public; curated from 113 public 10x Visium studies; 2,185,571 paired H&E-ST patches from 1,007 samples across 32 organs); simulated alignment datasets from 10 public human tissue slices (public); normal human small intestine Visium (public); ovarian carcinosarcoma Visium (public); breast cancer Visium+Xenium (public); TCGA BRCA histology WSIs and paired tumor biopsy RNA-seq (public); GTEx adipose and fibroblast bulk RNA-seq (public); normal human breast histology (public); heart-failure histology (public); CRC7K (public); WSSS4LUAD (public); LC25000 (public); PatchCamelyon (public); colorectal cancer Visium/Visium-HD/scRNA-seq (public); TNBC scRNA-seq (public); mouse brain Visium (public); Allen mouse brain scRNA-seq (public); normal human heart paired ST+H&E, n=39 (public); TNBC Xenium generated in this study (private/in-house); in-house heart-failure, Alzheimer's disease, metaplastic breast cancer, and TNBC tissues for retrieval (private/in-house); retrieval validation/test studies are public but exact accession-level names are deferred by the paper to Supplementary Table 4.
Baseline model/architecture: OmiCLIP/Loki: CoCa-based dual encoder with ViT image encoder (224x224 input) + causal-masking transformer text encoder (76 tokens), producing 768-dim aligned embeddings; Loki Align adds CPD registration; Loki Decompose uses Tangram-style nonconvex optimization on OmiCLIP embeddings; Loki PredEx uses similarity-weighted retrieval/averaging. Key comparators across tasks: OpenAI CLIP, PLIP, UNI, Prov-GigaPath, PASTE, GPSA, CAST, Tangram, RCTD, CARD, Spatial Seurat, CytoSPACE, Cell2location, SpatialDWLS, GeneFormer, scGPT, scFoundation, Hist2ST, HisToGene, BLEEP, mclSTExp, CLAM.
Training Approach: Large-scale contrastive pretraining on paired H&E patch and transcriptomic text pairs; each ST spot was converted into a gene-sentence using the top 50 expressed genes after QC, gene-symbol conversion, and housekeeping-gene removal. OmiCLIP was trained for 20 epochs on ST-bank. Downstream alignment and decomposition typically used contrastive fine-tuning on paired target ST+H&E data, whereas bulk-RNA/marker-gene annotation and retrieval were zero-shot or inference-only. PredEx used 10-fold cross-validation and similarity-weighted averaging of reference ST gene expression rather than sequence generation.
Medical Phase (pre/post): mixed normal and disease tissue analysis
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: H&E histopathology/whole-slide image patches; spatial transcriptomics (10x Visium, Visium-HD, Xenium/pseudo-Visium); bulk RNA-seq; scRNA-seq
Model input modality: Primarily multimodal image+text/omics during pretraining (H&E patch + transcriptomic gene-sentence text); downstream modules use image-only, ST-only, image+ST, bulk-RNA text, or scRNA-seq embeddings depending on task
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Alignment: ovarian carcinosarcoma median PCC=0.88 (ST-to-ST) and 0.86 (image-to-ST); Kendall's tau=0.21 and 0.18; Visium-Xenium mean alignment distance=0.08 mm. Marker-gene annotation weighted F1: CRC7K=0.59, WSSS4LUAD=0.79, PatchCamelyon=0.60, LC25000=0.96; combined Loki+PLIP=0.72, 0.83, 0.62, 0.97 respectively. Decomposition on TNBC: impact score=1.32 (Loki ST) and 1.11 (Loki image) vs Tangram=0.21. Retrieval: Recall@5%=0.125/0.186/0.173/0.140 on brain/heart/kidney/breast validation sets and 0.117 on the independent test set; Recall@10%=0.227/0.291/0.297/0.240 and 0.208 respectively. PredEx: best MSE in 28/39 heart samples and best PCC in 16/39 samples.

title: Aligning knowledge concepts to whole slide images for precise histopathology image analysis
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses weakly supervised whole-slide histopathology analysis, where standard MIL methods usually learn only from slide labels and do not explicitly incorporate pathology expert knowledge. The main goal is to improve prediction accuracy and interpretability by proposing ConcepPath, a concept-based MIL framework that uses GPT-4 to induce traceable disease-specific concepts and class prompts from medical literature, then aligns them with WSI patches through a pathology vision-language model. Its key novelty is the joint use of LLM-induced expert concepts, learnable data-driven concepts, and a two-stage concept-guided hierarchical aggregation with slide adapters, instead of relying only on image embeddings or directly queried language priors. Across public TCGA tasks including breast cancer HER2 scoring, lung cancer subtyping, and gastric immunotherapy-sensitive subtyping, ConcepPath consistently outperformed several MIL baselines, suggesting that concept-grounded multimodal WSI analysis can improve both performance and post-hoc interpretability.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: TCGA-NSCLC (public; LUAD=530, LUSC=512); TCGA-BRCA (public; HER2 positive=164, equivocal=186, negative=583); TCGA-STAD (public; EBV=26, MSI=44, GS/CIN=199, as reported)
Baseline model/architecture: ConcepPath (knowledge concept-based MIL with two-stage concept-guided hierarchical aggregation and slide adapters); default pathology vision-language backbone = QuiltNet (ViT-B/32 image encoder + GPT/77 text encoder); supplementary experiments with CONCH and comparisons using CLIP/PLIP/PathClip; main baselines: ABMIL, DeepAttnMISL, CLAM-SB, GTP, TransMIL, HIPT, TOP
Training Approach: Weakly supervised slide-level MIL with patient-level 5-fold cross-validation; GPT-4 used via prompting/inference-only as a reasoning engine to induce expert concepts and bag-level class prompts from curated medical literature; pathology VLM encoders kept frozen; learnable prompt tokens, complementary data-driven concepts, and slide adapters trained with SGD (LR=1e-4, batch size=2).
Medical Modality: H&E-stained whole-slide histopathology images (digital pathology / RGB WSI)
Model input modality: Image+text (tiled 448x448 WSI patches + textual expert concepts/class prompts)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Mean 5-fold CV AUC: LUAD vs LUSC=96.71; HER2 scoring=78.33; EBV vs Others=92.15; MSI vs Others=84.15; EBV+MSI vs Others=83.91; Average=87.05. Mean 5-fold CV ACC (reported in Fig. 2a): LUAD vs LUSC=92.0; HER2 scoring=65.0; EBV vs Others=92.0; MSI vs Others=88.5; EBV+MSI vs Others=84.0; Average=84.5.

title: PM2: A new prompting multi-modal model paradigm for few-shot medical image classification
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses few-shot medical image classification under severe label scarcity and aims to improve diagnostic performance by combining image features with auxiliary text prompts. It proposes PM2, a CLIP-based multimodal paradigm that evaluates five prompt strategies (classname, vanilla, hand-crafted, GPT-generated, and CoOp-learned) and adds a visual head that fuses first-order class-token features with second-order covariance-pooled visual tokens. A key novelty versus prior CLIP-style linear probing is treating prompts as supplementary samples and enriching visual representations with covariance pooling plus Newton-Schulz normalization instead of relying only on class tokens or average pooled tokens. Across BACH breast histopathology, brain tumor MRI, and diabetic retinopathy fundus datasets, PM2 achieves state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy, showing that domain-aware prompting and second-order feature statistics materially strengthen low-data medical classification. The work is a diagnostic image-classification study rather than a surgical-planning application.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: BACH breast cancer histology dataset (public); Figshare brain tumor MRI dataset (public); APTOS 2019 Blindness Detection / Aravind diabetic retinopathy dataset (public)
Baseline model/architecture: PM2 built on a pretrained CLIP dual-encoder backbone (frozen image encoder plus text encoder); backbones tested: ResNet-50, ResNet-101, ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16; key comparators: CLIP zero-shot, Tip-Adapter, Tip-Adapter-F, CoOp, CoCoOp, MaPLe; pooling comparators: class token only, visual average pooling, bilinear pooling (BP), spatial attention pooling (SAP)
Training Approach: Few-shot supervised learning with a frozen pretrained CLIP backbone and linear probing of task-specific heads; paired image-text training via a shared classifier on image class token and text EOS token; prompt engineering / prompt learning using classname, vanilla, hand-crafted, GPT-3.5-generated, and CoOp learnable prompts; second-order covariance pooling of visual tokens with 1x1 convolution dimensionality reduction and Newton-Schulz matrix square-root normalization; AdamW with warm-up and cosine annealing; 1/2/4/8/16-shot sampling averaged over 3 random seeds
Medical Modality: Multi-modal study across histopathology microscopy images (breast), T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI (brain tumors), and color fundus retinal images (diabetic retinopathy)
Model input modality: Image plus text prompts during training; image-only at inference after the shared classifier absorbs text semantics
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: Accuracy (%). Main PM2 benchmark results - BACH: 1-shot 47.50, 2-shot 55.00, 4-shot 57.78, 8-shot 64.72, 16-shot 76.11; Brain tumor MRI: 1-shot 54.69, 2-shot 55.28, 4-shot 64.99, 8-shot 78.87, 16-shot 84.58; Diabetic retinopathy: 1-shot 66.58, 2-shot 64.38, 4-shot 68.77, 8-shot 68.28, 16-shot 72.17

title: Grounding DINO-US-SAM: Text-Prompted Multi-Organ Segmentation in Ultrasound with LoRA-Tuned Vision-Language Models
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This is a multi-organ ultrasound segmentation paper, not a breast-surgery-specific planning study, although breast ultrasound is one of the included domains. It addresses the lack of fully automated, generalizable ultrasound segmentation across anatomies, where prior methods often need organ-specific retraining or manual point/box prompts. The goal is to enable free-form text-prompted segmentation by combining Grounding DINO for text-guided localization with SAM2 for mask generation; the key novelty is LoRA-based ultrasound adaptation of Grounding DINO while keeping SAM2 frozen and updating only about 1.7% of detector parameters. The main takeaway is that the method achieved strong results across 18 public datasets, generalized well to three unseen datasets without retraining, and ran at about 0.33 s per image.

Unseen test-only datasets: BUSBRA (public); TNSCUI (public); Luminous (public).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: LoRA-tuned Grounding DINO plus frozen SAM2. Grounding DINO is a transformer-based vision-language detector with a frozen image backbone and mostly frozen BERT text encoder, adapted via LoRA; SAM2 is used as the downstream segmentor. Key baselines/comparators: Grounding DINO plus SAM2 without fine-tuning; fine-tuned Grounding DINO plus MedSAM; UniverSeg; BiomedParse; SAMUS; MedCLIP-SAM; MedCLIP-SAMv2.
