Medical Modality: Histopathology / digital pathology (whole-slide images, ROIs, and derived image patches across multiple organs)
Model input modality: Image-only (patches/ROIs for classification; WSI patch-feature embeddings for MIL survival prediction)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Metrics reported: Accuracy, Macro-F1, and C-index. Representative best exact results from the full text tables: PCam Acc=94.24, F1=0.942 (UNI+PEFT); BACH Acc=85.48, F1=0.849 (UNI+PEFT); BRACS Acc=73.30, F1=0.720 (Phikon+PEFT); Kather19 Acc=99.33, F1=0.994 (UNI+PEFT); Kather16 Acc=87.11, F1=0.869 (UNI+PEFT); CRC-TP Acc=80.99, F1=0.728 (UNI+PEFT); KBSMC Colon I Acc=93.32, F1=0.930 (UNI+partial fine-tuning); KBSMC Colon II Acc=91.23, F1=0.900 (CTransPath+PEFT); Chaoyang Acc=77.01, F1=0.768 (CTransPath+PEFT); DigestPath Acc=85.79, F1=0.799 (UNI+PEFT); PANDA Acc=93.95, F1=0.918 (UNI+partial fine-tuning); AGGC22 Acc=78.09, F1=0.629 (Phikon+PEFT); UBC best Acc=80.49 (Phikon+linear probing), best F1=0.625 (Lunit+PEFT). For survival, the same-domain highest exact C-index reported in the text was 0.5577 (Phikon+CLAM-SB on CPTAC-LUAD); average best-method C-index for near-domain CPTAC-LSCC was 0.5695 (DTFD-MIL); average best-method C-index for out-of-domain CPTAC-PDA was 0.6471 (TransMIL).

title: Tissue concepts: Supervised foundation models in computational pathology
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper addresses whether supervised multi-task learning can produce a pathology foundation model without the data and compute burden of large self-supervised pretraining. It proposes Tissue Concepts, a shared histopathology encoder trained jointly on 16 classification, segmentation, and detection tasks from diverse annotated datasets, then evaluates frozen features via multiple-instance learning on breast, prostate, colorectal, and lung whole-slide image classification with cross-center testing. The main novelty is replacing massive unlabeled pretraining with supervised multi-task pretraining on about 912,157 patches while still learning transferable tissue representations. The main takeaway is that Tissue Concepts is broadly comparable to self-supervised pathology encoders such as CTransPath and clearly stronger than ImageNet features, although out-of-domain lung performance remains weaker than models pretrained directly on lung-rich datasets.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Pretraining (all public): NCT-CRC-HE-100K (public); CRAG (public); SemiCOL segmentation subset (public); CoNIC (public); Arvaniti TMA (public); PESO (public); Schoemig-Markiefka prostate dataset (public); PANDA (public); TUH breast subset (public); TIGER (public); BCSS (public); BreakHis (public); MIDOG 2022, excluding lung cases in pretraining (public); HuBMAP large-intestine subset (public). Ablation: BACH (public). Downstream validation: BRACS (public); PANDA (public); SemiCOL WSI set (public); TCGA-NSCLC = TCGA-LUAD + TCGA-LUSC (public).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: Tissue Concepts encoder with Tiny Swin Transformer backbone (TC-Swin; 27.5M params, 768-d latent); also a Tiny ConvNeXt variant (TC-Conv). Pretraining uses a shared U-Net-style decoder for segmentation and an FCOS detection head; downstream whole-slide classification uses a small CNN MIL head over latent WSIs. Main baselines/comparators: CTransPath, ImageNet-pretrained tiny Swin, UMedPT (ablation), plus published external baselines such as HACT-Net for BRACS, Mahdi Behzadi et al. for PANDA, and TransMIL/CTransPath literature baselines for lung.
Training Approach: Supervised multi-task learning across 16 tasks from 14 histopathology data sources, spanning classification, segmentation, and detection; ImageNet-1k initialization; 224x224 patches with standard augmentation. Pretraining used AdamW (lr=1e-4, weight decay=0.01, gradient accumulation=128) for 5 million task-steps, taking about 160 hours on one NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU. Downstream evaluation froze the encoder and trained slide-level multiple-instance learning classifiers on latent whole-slide representations; an ABMIL alternative was tested in the appendix.
Medical Modality: Histopathology / computational pathology; H&E-stained whole-slide images and extracted tissue patches, with some segmentation masks and detection annotations.
Model input modality: Image-only during pretraining (224x224 histopathology patches); downstream MIL head receives image-derived latent whole-slide feature maps only; no text or tabular clinical input.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: BRACS: 2-class wF1=0.951 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.992 +/- 0.001; 4-class wF1=0.545 +/- 0.04, AUC=0.830 +/- 0.01; 7-class wF1=0.405 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.769 +/- 0.02 (TC-Swin). PANDA: 5-fold Acc=0.942 +/- 0.01, F1=0.928 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.983 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin), with best overall 5-fold TC-Conv Acc=0.957 +/- 0.05, F1=0.947 +/- 0.06, AUC=0.990 +/- 0.01; Karolinska to Radboud TC-Swin Acc=0.896 +/- 0.01, F1=0.829 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.914 +/- 0.02; Radboud to Karolinska TC-Swin Acc=0.846 +/- 0.02, F1=0.842 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.926 +/- 0.01. SemiCOL average cross-center: Acc=0.953 +/- 0.02, F1=0.953 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.989 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin). TCGA-NSCLC: 5-fold Acc=0.878 +/- 0.02, F1=0.875 +/- 0.02, AUC=0.949 +/- 0.01; cross-center Acc=0.785 +/- 0.01, F1=0.778 +/- 0.01, AUC=0.863 +/- 0.01 (TC-Swin). Ablation/BACH sample efficiency: mean F1=0.816 for TC-Swin with maximum training images/class vs 0.762 for UMedPT and 0.662 for ImageNet.

title: When multiple instance learning meets foundation models: Advancing histological whole slide image analysis
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This is a full-text benchmark study of weakly supervised computational pathology rather than a generative-AI or surgical-planning paper. It addresses the lack of unbiased evidence on how histology-specific foundation models compare with multiple-instance-learning (MIL) aggregators for whole-slide image classification. The authors systematically benchmark six patch encoders and six slide-level MIL aggregators across seven clinical tasks spanning breast, glioma, liver, and colorectal cancer using 4044 patients from public and private multi-center cohorts. Its main novelty is the broad, controlled comparison across binary, multi-class, and multi-label tasks with both internal cross-validation and external testing. The main takeaway is that domain-specific foundation models, especially UNI and CONCH, generally outperform ImageNet ResNet50 and often other pathology FMs, while online feature re-embedding aggregators such as RRT can further help and stronger encoders also reduce convergence time.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: QHSU breast cohort (private); SHSU breast cohort (private); QCH breast cohort (private); TCGA Glioma (public); SAHDMU Glioma cohort (private); GPPH Liver cohort (private); TCGA-CRC cohort (public)
Baseline model/architecture: Patch encoders compared: UNI (ViT, DINOv2), CONCH (ViT visual-language FM, CoCa), CTransPath (CNN+Swin hybrid), PathoDuet (ViT), PLIP (CLIP-based visual-language model), and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 baseline; slide-level MIL aggregators: ABMIL, CLAM-MB, DTFD, TransMIL, RRT, WiKG
Training Approach: Weakly supervised embedding-based MIL with slide-level labels only; 256x256 non-overlapping 20x H&E patches extracted after CLAM-style tissue detection; pretrained encoders used for offline patch embeddings, with some aggregators performing online feature re-embedding (especially TransMIL, RRT, WiKG); patient-level 5-fold cross-validation plus external cohort testing where available; AdamW, learning rate=1e-4, batch size=1, max 100 epochs, early stopping on validation AUROC; cross-entropy for multi-class tasks and masked multi-label binary cross-entropy for ER/PR/HER2
Medical Modality: Histopathology whole-slide imaging; H&E-stained digital pathology WSIs
Model input modality: image-only (bags of WSI patches / patch embeddings)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Reported as mean ± SD, mainly AUROC and AUPRC. Best task-wise results: Breast grading—QHSU AUROC=86.07±2.47%, AUPRC=70.81±5.45% (UNI+RRT); SHSU AUROC=91.98±1.01% (PathoDuet+DTFD), AUPRC=90.29±0.75% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB); QCH AUROC=92.57±0.53% (UNI+DTFD), AUPRC=85.02±1.70% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB). QHSU biomarkers—ER AUROC=93.09±1.87%, AUPRC=97.47±0.97% (UNI+RRT); PR AUROC=87.01±1.41% (UNI+RRT), AUPRC=93.98±0.65% (UNI+CLAM-MB); HER2 AUROC=90.69±1.02%, AUPRC=80.74±1.77% (UNI+DTFD). SHSU biomarkers—ER AUROC=91.64±0.81% (UNI+ABMIL), AUPRC=97.82±0.26/0.52% tie (UNI+CLAM-MB or UNI+RRT); PR AUROC=86.86±0.86%, AUPRC=96.16±0.29% (UNI+WiKG); HER2 AUROC=85.77±2.75% (PLIP+CLAM-MB), AUPRC=76.07±2.40% (CTransPath+CLAM-MB). Glioma grading—TCGA AUROC=91.77±1.84%, AUPRC=80.74±5.08% (CONCH+CLAM-MB); SAHDMU AUROC=91.51±0.91%, AUPRC=78.17±2.53% (CONCH+CLAM-MB). Liver grading—AUROC=75.96±1.13% (UNI+ABMIL), AUPRC=49.37±3.48% (UNI+DTFD). CRC MSI—AUROC=86.95±4.90% (UNI+RRT), AUPRC=63.15±17.62% (CONCH+ABMIL).

title: Predicting Nottingham grade in breast cancer digital pathology using a foundation model
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses automated prediction of Nottingham histologic grade from H&E whole-slide images in invasive breast cancer, aiming to reduce subjectivity, workload, and inter-observer variability in manual grading. The main goal was to build a unified model that distinguishes grades 1, 2, and 3, including the difficult grade 1 vs 2 boundary, and to test whether AI-predicted grades are clinically meaningful. The key novelty is the combination of a pathology foundation model (UNI, ViT-L/16 pretrained with DINOv2) with multiple-instance learning, especially ACMIL, plus comparison across 14 MIL configurations and external validation on BRACS with pathologist-assigned grades; the authors also linked predictions to survival and RNA-seq/GO signals. The main takeaway is that UNI-based ACMIL outperformed the compared MIL baselines and produced grade predictions that aligned with biologically aggressive pathways and significantly stratified 5-year overall survival.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: TCGA-BRCA H&E WSIs with recorded Nottingham grades (public; 521 slides from 496 patients for model development/internal validation); TCGA-BRCA H&E WSIs without recorded grades (public; 597 slides from 554 patients for clinical utility analyses); TCGA RNA-seq/clinical data via GDC/Firehose/cBioPortal (public; 646 patients for GO/survival analyses); BRACS invasive-carcinoma subset (public; 128 WSIs external validation after expert re-grading).
Baseline model/architecture: Primary model: ACMIL (Attention-Challenging Multiple Instance Learning) using UNI foundation-model features (ViT-L/16, DINOv2 SSL; 1024-d embeddings). Image segmentation/tile extraction: CLAM pipeline. Key comparators/baselines: the same MIL family with ResNet-18 ImageNet features and MIL heads CLAM-SB, CLAM-MB, TransMIL, DSMIL, DTFD-MIL, and ABMIL.
Training Approach: Weakly supervised/supervised slide-level multiclass MIL on whole-slide grade labels; self-supervised pretrained UNI features were extracted from 224x224 H&E patches, then ACMIL was trained with cross-entropy plus semantic/diversity regularization and stochastic top-K instance masking. Stratified internal split 6:2:2 (train/val/test), 100 epochs, AdamW, cosine LR schedule, batch size 1, and random selection of 70-100% patch features for augmentation; hyperparameters were adopted from prior MIL studies without extra tuning. External validation used BRACS slides independently graded by an expert pathologist.
Medical Modality: Digital histopathology (H&E whole-slide images); RNA-seq used only for downstream biological validation.
Model input modality: image-only (bags of H&E whole-slide patch embeddings/features)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Internal TCGA test (best model, ACMIL+UNI): F1-score=0.731; multiclass AUC=0.835. Internal per-grade AUCs: Grade 1=0.83, Grade 2=0.77, Grade 3=0.90. External BRACS per-grade AUCs: Grade 1=0.89, Grade 2=0.70, Grade 3=0.83. Cohen's kappa vs pathologist - TCGA: G1=0.41±0.10, G2=0.51±0.07, G3=0.65±0.05; BRACS: G1=0.46±0.09, G2=0.25±0.09, G3=0.43±0.08. 5-year OS by AI-predicted grade: G1=79.9% (95% CI 74.3-84.4), G2=75.7% (57.4-86.9), G3=59.1% (38.0-75.1), log-rank p=0.0173.

title: Multi-Organ Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Image Segmentation With Task Prompt and Anatomical Prior
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the poor robustness and limited generalizability of single-organ ultrasound segmentation models, which are constrained by small annotated datasets and the narrow field of view of ultrasound images. The goal is to build a universal multi-organ segmentation foundation model that leverages shared information across organs while preserving organ-specific anatomy. Its main novelty is MOFO, a 3-branch architecture that combines a CSWin-based vision branch for organ-invariant features, a CLIP-derived task-prompt branch for organ-specific conditioning, and a multi-organ anatomical-prior branch learned with an auto-encoder. On a 10-organ multi-center dataset of 7039 images, MOFO consistently outperformed individual single-organ models and several SOTA baselines, indicating that cross-organ semantic and anatomical priors can improve ultrasound segmentation, including breast tumor segmentation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Main multi-organ database (7039 US images): breast ultrasound dataset from Al-Dhabyani et al. (public); fetal head ultrasound dataset from van den Heuvel et al. (public); leg muscle ultrasound dataset from Michard et al. (public); Open Access Thyroid Ultrasound Image Database (public); Achilles tendon dataset from Huashan Hospital, Fudan University (private); heart/interventricular septum dataset from East Hospital, Tongji University (private); kidney tumor dataset from Huadong Hospital, Fudan University (private); lymph node dataset from Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (private); median nerve dataset from Huashan Hospital, Fudan University (private); midbrain dataset from Huashan Hospital, Fudan University (private). OOD/external evaluation: open-access breast lesion ultrasound image database, 232 images (public); liver tumor ultrasound dataset from Huashan Hospital, 256 images (private).
Baseline model/architecture: MOFO: 3-branch universal ultrasound segmentation model with a U-shaped image segmenter (CSWin Transformer encoder pretrained on ImageNet + CNN decoder), prompt encoder + dynamic decoder, CLIP text encoder backbone ViT-B/32 for task prompts, and a multi-organ U-shaped auto-encoder/anatomical prior encoder. Key comparators: individual single-organ model, U-Net, UNet++, nnU-Net, TransUNet, Swin-Unet, SAM, MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, AdaptiveSAM, SAMUS, and UniverSeg.
Training Approach: Supervised joint multi-organ segmentation; person-level training/validation/test split of 7:1:2; ImageNet-pretrained CSWin encoder; fixed pretrained CLIP text encoder with learnable MLP prompt refinement; multi-organ auto-encoder trained first to learn anatomical priors using mask reconstruction plus multi-scale consistency loss, then frozen and used as a prior regularizer during MOFO training; hybrid loss = mask Dice + cross-entropy + weighted auxiliary classification loss + anatomical prior consistency loss.
Medical Modality: 2D ultrasound (multi-organ B-mode US; multi-center, multiple probe types)
Model input modality: Image-only at inference; internally conditioned by preset CLIP-derived text task prompts; ground-truth masks used only during training for the prior branch
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary test-set result, average across 10 organs: DSC=88.25±6.49%; HD95=11.87±7.33 pixels; ASSD=3.97±2.57 pixels. Breast tumor test result: DSC=88.18%; HD95=13.64 pixels; ASSD=4.01 pixels. Compared with individual single-organ models on average: DSC=84.65%; HD95=16.89 pixels; ASSD=5.18 pixels; overall improvement significant at p<0.001.

title: Cross Prompting Consistency with Segment Anything Model for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles semi-supervised medical image segmentation when labeled data are scarce, focusing on breast ultrasound lesion segmentation and cardiac MRI structure segmentation. Its goal is to make Segment Anything Model (SAM) effective in SSL by directly fine-tuning it on limited labeled data while exploiting unlabeled images more effectively. The main novelty is a dual-branch cross-prompting framework in which one decoder’s unprompted mask generates point prompts for the other decoder, combined with a prompt consistency regularization that reduces SAM’s sensitivity to prompt location. The main takeaway is that CPC-SAM consistently outperforms prior SSL and SAM-based baselines, with especially strong gains in very low-label settings, including more than 9 percentage-point Dice improvement on BUSI with only 10 labeled images.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: BUSI (public; breast ultrasound dataset, 647 images); ACDC (public; cardiac cine MRI dataset, 200 scans from 100 patients)
Baseline model/architecture: Main model: adapted dual-branch SAM with ViT-B backbone, shared image encoder + prompt encoder, two mask decoders, LoRA adaptation on encoder attention query/value heads; key comparators: SAMed, SemiSAM, U-Net, UAMT, CPS, URPC, MC-Net+, DCNet, BCP, UniMatch, SAM-point
Training Approach: Semi-supervised end-to-end fine-tuning of SAM; supervised Dice + cross-entropy losses on labeled data; unlabeled learning via cross-prompting pseudo-supervision between two decoder branches; prompt consistency regularization using center/random point prompts; LoRA-based parameter-efficient adaptation
Medical Modality: Ultrasound (breast US); MRI (cardiac cine MRI)
Model input modality: Image + point prompt during SSL training for prompted branches; image with learned default dense prompt embedding for unprompted automatic segmentation/inference
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Metrics: DSC, JC, HD95, ASD. BUSI (10/431 labels): DSC=71.20, JC=61.15, HD95=100.22 px, ASD=37.86 px; BUSI (20/431 labels): DSC=72.41, JC=62.72, HD95=96.26 px, ASD=40.93 px. ACDC (1/70 labels): DSC=85.56, JC=75.74, HD95=9.19 mm, ASD=2.84 mm; ACDC (3/70 labels): DSC=87.95, JC=79.01, HD95=5.80 mm, ASD=1.54 mm.

title: A segment anything model-guided and match-based semi-supervised segmentation framework for medical imaging
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles low-quality pseudo-labels in Match-based semi-supervised medical image segmentation and the manual prompting burden of SAM-like models. Its goal is to improve annotation-efficient segmentation by coupling a Match-based teacher-student framework with a fine-tuned SAM-based model that refines pseudo-labels for unlabeled images. The main novelty is the end-to-end SAM-Match framework, where weakly augmented teacher predictions are automatically converted into prompts, SAM or MedSAM produces higher-quality masks, and those masks are fed back to train the student network. Across cardiac MRI, breast ultrasound, and liver MRI benchmarks, the method consistently outperformed standard semi-supervised baselines and in some settings approached fully supervised performance with very few labels. The breast-specific evidence here is BUSI lesion segmentation rather than breast surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: ACDC cardiac MRI (public); BUSI breast ultrasound dataset (public); MRLiver liver MRI from UT Southwestern Medical Center (private/in-house)
Baseline model/architecture: Main architecture: SAM-Match = U-Net-based mean-teacher Match network plus SAM or MedSAM. Match backbones: FixMatch and UniMatch. SAM-based variants: Fix-SAM, Fix-MedSAM, Uni-SAM, Uni-MedSAM. Compared against UNet-Fully, DAN, ADVENT, ICT, MT, UA-MT, URPC, and U2PL.
Training Approach: Semi-supervised learning with a mean-teacher consistency framework and two-stage training: warm-up then interactive end-to-end training. Labeled data use supervised Dice plus cross-entropy loss; unlabeled data use pseudo-label-based Dice plus cross-entropy loss, with teacher weights updated by EMA. Weak and strong augmentations are used; SAM or MedSAM are fine-tuned on labeled data, and teacher predictions above a 0.95 confidence threshold are converted into automatic prompts (point prompts for SAM, bounding boxes for MedSAM) to generate refined pseudo-labels.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal medical imaging: cardiac MRI, breast ultrasound, liver MRI
Model input modality: Image-only for the Match teacher/student branches; image plus auto-generated prompts for the SAM-based branch (positive/negative points for SAM, bounding boxes for MedSAM)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metrics: Dice and HD95. Best clearly identified results per dataset: ACDC (Uni-MedSAM, 3 labeled cases) - Mean Dice=89.36 +/- 0.06%, HD95=2.35 +/- 4.66; BUSI (Uni-SAM, 30 labeled cases) - Dice=59.35 +/- 0.12%; MRLiver (Uni-MedSAM, 3 labeled cases) - Dice=80.04 +/- 0.11%, HD95=21.04 +/- 21.98.

title: Synergistic perception: Fusing expert knowledge and foundation models for semi-supervised mammogram segmentation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the difficulty of segmenting diverse mammographic anatomical structures when annotated data are scarce and the target structures vary greatly in size, appearance, and boundary clarity. Its goal is to improve multi-class mammogram segmentation across 11 structures by combining specialized class-wise expert models with a global feature fusion network and large-scale unlabeled screening mammograms. The novelty lies in the Synergistic Perception Framework (SPF), which couples class-specific Expert Unit Models and a Hierarchical Feature Fusion Network (HFF-Net) with a two-stage semi-supervised pseudo-label pipeline that first uses consistency regularization and then fine-tunes SAM to refine pseudo-labels. The main takeaway is that fusing expert knowledge with a foundation model substantially improves segmentation accuracy and boundary precision, especially for small or complex structures such as dense tissue, nipple, calcifications, and pectoral muscle.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CSAW-S (public; primary labeled training/evaluation dataset, enhanced in this study with generated dense-tissue labels); INbreast (public; used for dense-tissue transfer learning, with an additional 30-case manually annotated test subset that the authors state is publicly available under the original license); RSNA Screening Mammography Breast Cancer Detection (public; unlabeled dataset used for semi-supervised pseudo-label generation and refinement).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: SPF built around HFF-Net, a dual-path segmentation network with depthwise separable convolutions, category-adaptive decoders, and class-specific Expert Unit Models implemented as lightweight U-Nets; SAM (Segment Anything, ViT-H) is used for pseudo-label refinement. Compared against FCN, DeepLabV3+, U-Net, U-Net3+, Attention U-Net, and Swin-Unet.
Training Approach: Semi-supervised learning. EUMs are pretrained in a supervised class-specific manner on CSAW-S; HFF-Net is trained with a composite BCE+Dice loss; a FixMatch-style consistency-regularization stage uses labeled CSAW-S plus unlabeled RSNA to generate initial pseudo-labels; SAM mask decoder is then fine-tuned with Stage-1 pseudo-labels as dense prompts while its image encoder is frozen; the final HFF-Net is retrained on refined pseudo-labels. The study also uses transfer learning from INbreast to generate CSAW-S dense-tissue labels and applies targeted calcification augmentation.
Medical Modality: Mammography (2D X-ray / full-field digital mammograms).
Model input modality: Image-only for EUMs and HFF-Net; image plus dense mask prompt during SAM-based pseudo-label refinement.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main reported metrics: DSC, IoU, and HD95. Proposed SPF results: CSAW-S Average DSC=75.31%, Average IoU=64.40%; INbreast Average DSC=68.60%, Average IoU=58.57%. For boundary-critical structures, mean HD95=10.3 pixels on CSAW-S and 15.7 pixels on INbreast.

title: Improved Osteoporosis Prediction in Breast Cancer Patients Using a Novel Semi-Foundational Model
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses opportunistic osteoporosis / bone demineralization prediction in breast cancer patients younger than 65 using routine staging CT, where labeled cohorts are small and DEXA screening is not routinely available. The goal was to test whether a semi-foundational model pretrained on an unrelated but CT-native dataset could improve downstream 3-class L1 vertebral demineralization classification. The main novelty is not generative AI, but modality-specific pretraining on external COVID-19 chest CT before fine-tuning on a small breast-cancer cohort, with comparison against random initialization and ImageNet-only transfer. The full-text discussion also highlights that Grad-CAM attention concentrated on pedicles / cortical bone rather than the usual medullary ROI, suggesting a potentially different imaging biomarker strategy. The main takeaway is that CT-native pretraining substantially improved performance, with semi-foundational ResNet50 achieving near-perfect holdout results in this cohort.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: COVID-19 Lung CT database, 8,439 chest CT scans (public); USF Health retrospective breast cancer cohort from initial staging PET-CT, CT component only, 199 eligible patients from 866 screened (private)
Baseline model/architecture: Semi-foundational CNNs: ResNet50 (best), VGG16, DenseNet121; comparator transfer settings were random / no transfer, ImageNet initialization, and COVID-19 CT-pretrained weights
Training Approach: Supervised transfer learning / fine-tuning; base CNNs initialized from ImageNet, pretrained on COVID-19 chest CT binary classification, then fine-tuned for 3-class osteoporosis / demineralization classification on L1 CT slices; 5-fold cross-validation on 160 patients, 20% holdout test (n=40), SMOTE class balancing, hyperparameter tuning with Keras Tuner plus manual tuning, Adam optimizer with categorical cross-entropy
Medical Modality: CT (non-contrast CT component of PET-CT; single axial L1 vertebral bone-window slice)
Model input modality: image-only (2D single-slice CT PNG)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Best model = semi-foundational ResNet50 with COVID-19 CT pretraining: Validation AUC=0.95 (95% CI 0.88-1.00); Holdout Accuracy=0.99; Testing AUC=0.99; F1-score=0.99; Precision=0.99; Recall=0.99

title: Exploring Patient Data Requirements in Training Effective AI Models for MRI-Based Breast Cancer Classification
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper asks a practical deployment question for MRI-based breast cancer classification: how much local patient data is needed to train a competitive AI model. Using the full Duke cohort, the authors created 80 patient-level training sets of different sizes and compared ViT-B/16 models initialized with DINO, MAE, supervised ImageNet pretraining, or random weights. The novelty is a data-sufficiency analysis rather than a new classifier: it quantifies diminishing returns, checks whether patient selection matters, and tests a simple ensemble. The main takeaway is that transfer learning from foundation models, including a generative-pretrained MAE model, can achieve competitive performance with surprisingly small cohorts, and performance differences across training splits become small once about 50 patients are used. A simple majority-vote ensemble further improves results with minimal added complexity.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Duke Breast Cancer Dataset (public; 922 patients; main downstream dataset; 3D breast MRI converted to 2D slices); ImageNet (public; source of pretrained weights for DINO, MAE, and supervised ViT models); no external validation cohort reported
Baseline model/architecture: Vision Transformer Base/16 (ViT-B/16); compared variants: DINO-pretrained ViT-B/16, MAE-pretrained ViT-B/16, supervised ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16, randomly initialized ViT-B/16; simple majority-vote ensemble of the three pretrained models
Training Approach: Transfer learning/fine-tuning of ImageNet-pretrained foundation models plus a from-scratch comparator; supervised binary classification with cross-entropy on 224x224 2D MRI slices; patient-level stratified sampling with n={1,5,10,50,100,200,400,700} patients and 10 splits each, plus a fixed 200-patient validation set; SGD grid search (lr=0.1/0.01/0.001, weight decay=0 or 0.0001, momentum=0 or 0.1), cosine annealing, random resized crop augmentation, early stopping; inference-time majority-vote ensemble
Medical Modality: Breast MRI (3D MRI volumes converted to 2D slices)
Model input modality: Image-only (single 2D MRI slices, 224x224)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Validation metrics reported: Accuracy, F1-score, and Precision. Best exact tabulated 50-patient ensemble results across 10 splits: Accuracy=0.770 (split 6) and F1=0.797 (split 4); the ensemble outperformed the best individual model in accuracy in 9/10 splits. Best exact individual-model values in the same table: DINO Accuracy=0.763 and F1=0.788; MAE Accuracy=0.770 and F1=0.791; Supervised Accuracy=0.755 and F1=0.775. Precision was also analyzed across patient counts/splits in boxplots, but the paper did not fully tabulate those numeric values.

title: Accelerating breast MRI acquisition with generative AI models
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective proof-of-concept study examined whether a score-based generative diffusion model can reconstruct breast MRI from undersampled k-space data to shorten scan time. The goal was to accelerate breast MRI acquisition while preserving image quality and diagnostic usefulness. The main novelty is the use of a score-based generative prior for breast MRI reconstruction, framed as more flexible than conventional coil-dependent acceleration methods and, according to the discussion, able to handle T1- and T2-weighted sequences within one model. The main takeaway is that moderate acceleration worked very well (near-indistinguishable from the reference at R=2 and still reasonably strong at R=5), whereas image quality dropped substantially at R=20; this is an upstream imaging-enablement study rather than a direct surgical-planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: UKA breast MRI dataset / internal University Hospital RWTH Aachen cohort (private; 9751 exams from 5086 women after excluding 165 studies with missing T2; Fig. 1 shows 9651 training studies + 100 test studies, while the abstract reports 9549 training examinations + 100 test examinations, so the training count is inconsistently reported in the paper).
Baseline model/architecture: Score-based diffusion model / score-based generative prior with a U-shaped encoder-decoder (U-Net-like) architecture; comparator/reference was the fully sampled MRI image; no explicit head-to-head external AI baseline or classical SENSE/GRAPPA/CS baseline was experimentally reported.
Training Approach: Unsupervised score-matching generative training; 3D breast MRI volumes were converted into 2D slices, z-normalized, and resampled to 384 x 384. The main text explicitly reports 28,647 2D MRI slices and describes Cartesian k-space undersampling by randomly deleting lines according to the target acceleration factor. Reconstruction was performed with annealed Langevin dynamics; the discussion additionally states that T1 and T2 sequence labels were incorporated into a single model.
Medical Modality: Breast MRI (T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI within breast MRI examinations; undersampled k-space reconstruction).
Model input modality: Single-modality MRI: 2D breast MRI slices during training and undersampled MRI k-space measurements during reconstruction/inference.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Average quantitative result explicitly reported in the main text for the highest undersampling factor: at R=20, PSNR ~ 27.04 dB and SSIM = 0.78 (computed over 100 slices from 100 different examinations). Mean radiologist rating (1-5): R=2, 4.8 ± 0.10; R=5, 4.0 ± 0.10; R=20, 2.6 ± 0.10. Fraction rated 4 or 5 by radiologist 1 / radiologist 2: R=2, 100% / 99%; R=5, 88% / 70%; R=20, 5% / 21%. Inter-reader agreement: Cohen's kappa = 0.61 (95% CI 0.56-0.68); Mann-Whitney U p = 0.26.

title: Simulation training in mammography with AI-generated images: a multireader study
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addressed the lack of flexible, high-variety training material for learning mammographic cancer detection. The main goal was to build a controllable generative-AI simulator that can create realistic mammograms with adjustable breast characteristics and allow cancer insertion for practice. Its novelty was not just synthetic image generation, but combining an adversarial latent autoencoder with PCA-based latent controls, Poisson blending for realistic lesion insertion, and a web interface that was then tested in a randomized multireader educational study. The main takeaway is that this simulator improved resident mammogram-reading performance, especially among junior trainees, showing value for breast-imaging education rather than direct surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Retrospectively collected anonymized patient mammogram images used to train the model (private/internal; exact cohort name and size not reported in the main text); fidelity reader-study set: 50 real mammograms (private/internal) + 50 GAN-generated mammograms (synthetic/internal); resident performance test set: 100 mammograms (private/internal; 38 negative and 62 biopsy-proven cancers).
Baseline model/architecture: ALAE (Adversarial Latent Autoencoder; GAN-family architecture) with encoder-generator-discriminator framework; PCA over latent vectors for controllable mammographic feature editing; Poisson blending for lesion insertion; no conventional ML baseline reported, and the main comparator was a non-practice resident control arm.
Training Approach: Ambispective design: retrospective internal mammograms were used for unsupervised/generative adversarial training of the ALAE; PCA-based latent-space manipulation was used at inference to control density, size, and tissue distribution; cancers were added via user-guided segmentation plus Poisson blending; the educational effect was evaluated prospectively in a randomized multireader study.
Medical Modality: Mammography (breast X-ray)
Model input modality: Image-only mammograms; in the simulator, an uploaded normal mammogram is the main input, with an optional second abnormal mammogram / segmented lesion used for blending.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Resident-performance endpoint in practice group (Test 1 to Test 2): Sensitivity 50.51% to 57.94% (+7.43 percentage points; within-group p=0.015; vs non-practice p=0.030); Specificity 70.35% to 75.30% (+4.95 pp; within-group p=0.264; vs non-practice p=0.661); PPV 76.82% to 82.40% (+5.58 pp; within-group p=0.058; vs non-practice p=0.454); NPV 42.23% to 47.28% (+5.05 pp; within-group p=0.002; vs non-practice p=0.008); Accuracy 57.25% to 63.74% (+6.49 pp; within-group p=0.001; vs non-practice p=0.010). Fidelity test of realism: expert readers distinguishing real vs generated mammograms achieved 48% accuracy (Reader 1) and 45% accuracy (Reader 2).

title: Latent Diffusion Models with Image-Derived Annotations for Enhanced AI-Assisted Cancer Diagnosis in Histopathology
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the scarcity of richly annotated histopathology data for AI-based cancer detection and asks whether useful synthetic pathology images can be generated from only weak labels. Its goal was to improve text-to-image generation for breast-cancer-related lymph-node histology patches by conditioning Stable Diffusion on automatically derived morphology descriptors rather than only healthy/cancer labels. The novelty is the Morphology-Enriched Prompt-building (MEP) pipeline, which uses DINO-ViT embeddings and k-means clusters to create pseudo-text annotations without pixel-level labels or WSI-level reports, then evaluates realism with expert blind review and downstream classifier utility. The main takeaway is that MEP produced more diverse and faithful synthetic histopathology images than a label-only baseline and improved classifier performance in low-data regimes, although the paper is about diagnostic histopathology rather than surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Patch Camelyon (PCam) / Kaggle Histopathologic Cancer Detection benchmark (public); official Kaggle hidden test split used for evaluation (public benchmark, labels withheld); study-derived synthetic baseline and MEP datasets generated from public PCam patches (derived/internal, not external named datasets).
Baseline model/architecture: Stable Diffusion v1.5 latent diffusion model (VAE + conditional UNet + CLIP text encoder); DINO-ViT B/8 image encoder + k-means (k=33) for MEP prompt construction; comparators: out-of-the-box Stable Diffusion and class-label-only Stable Diffusion fine-tuning baseline; downstream classifiers: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 and ResNet-50.
Training Approach: Weakly supervised / prompt-engineered fine-tuning of a pretrained text-to-image LDM on 50k balanced image-prompt pairs. MEP extracted 768-d DINO features, clustered them with k-means into 33 morphology groups, and created prompts of the form Histology image of <label> tissue, morphology type <index>; the baseline used label-only prompts. SD v1.5 was fine-tuned for 12.5k steps with fp16, learning rate=1e-5, and effective batch size=64. Downstream evaluation used supervised ImageNet-pretrained ResNet classifiers.
Medical Modality: Histopathology; H&E-stained digital pathology patches from whole-slide images of sentinel lymph node sections from breast cancer patients
Model input modality: Image+text during LDM fine-tuning; text-only prompts during image synthesis; image-only for downstream classifiers
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Image generation: FID=90.2 (MEP) vs 178.8 (baseline); Precision=0.175 vs 0.065; Recall=0.140 vs 0.218. Expert blind review / Visual Turing test on MEP images: median Sensitivity=0.55; median Specificity=0.55. Synthetic-only classification: AUC=0.805 (MEP synthetic training) vs 0.773 (baseline synthetic training) vs 0.960 (real-data training). Mixed real+synthetic training: median AUC improved from 0.775 to 0.831 for Nreal=25 with +300% synthetic, from 0.827 to 0.865 for Nreal=50 with +300% synthetic, and from 0.904 to 0.911 for Nreal=500 with +300% synthetic; at Nreal=10000, adding synthetic slightly reduced median AUC from 0.946 to 0.943.

title: Clinical Utility of Breast Ultrasound Images Synthesized by a Generative Adversarial Network
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This single-center retrospective study asked whether GAN-synthesized breast ultrasound images preserve diagnostically meaningful features across five histological breast lesion categories. The main goal was to extend the authors’ earlier breast ultrasound synthesis work by generating and clinically evaluating tissue-type-specific synthetic images rather than images pooled across tissue types. The novelty is the histology-stratified DCGAN synthesis combined with a blinded radiologist reader study against original images, instead of relying only on visual realism claims or downstream classifier performance. The main takeaway is that the synthetic images supported similar benign/malignant and histological judgments with good inter-reader agreement, suggesting value for education and diagnostic training; however, this is not a direct surgical-planning tool and it is limited by a small, single-center private dataset.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Tokyo Medical and Dental University Hospital internal breast ultrasound cohort (private; retrospective; single-center; Sep 2014-Aug 2022; lesions <15 mm; n=1008 images total: cyst 202, fibroadenoma 203, IDC-scirrhous 201, IDC-solid 200, IDC-tubule-forming 202); labels based on pathology or >1-year follow-up for typical benign lesions; no public dataset; no external validation dataset
Baseline model/architecture: DCGAN (deep convolutional generative adversarial network); generator with transpose-convolution + batch normalization + ReLU, discriminator with strided convolution + batch normalization + LeakyReLU; comparator was original ultrasound images interpreted by radiologists; no alternative generative-model baseline reported
Training Approach: Unsupervised adversarial training on histology-stratified breast ultrasound image sets; DICOM images converted to JPEG and cropped to 40x40 mm squares including the chest wall; model input/output at 256x256; Adam optimizer (lr=0.0002, beta1=0.5, beta2=0.999); 200 epochs selected after radiologist visual quality review; evaluation was inference-only via blinded reader tests with >1-month interval between synthetic and original reading sessions
Medical Modality: Ultrasound (breast ultrasound; static B-mode images)
Model input modality: image-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Reader study metrics rather than FID/IS/Dice. Synthetic images: benign/malignant accuracy=100% (Reader 1), 94.0% (Reader 2); 5-class histological accuracy=86.0% (Reader 1), 78.0% (Reader 2); inter-reader kappa=0.625. Original images: benign/malignant accuracy=100% (Reader 1), 96.0% (Reader 2); 5-class histological accuracy=88.0% (Reader 1), 78.0% (Reader 2); inter-reader kappa=0.650. Synthetic per-class accuracy (Reader 1/Reader 2): cyst 90.0%/90.0%, fibroadenoma 90.0%/100%, IDC-scirrhous 100%/60.0%, IDC-solid 90.0%/70.0%, IDC-tubule-forming 60.0%/70.0%.

title: Lesion-Aware Generative Artificial Intelligence for Virtual Contrast-Enhanced Mammography in Breast Cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses virtual contrast enhancement in breast imaging by generating dual-energy subtracted (DES) CESM images from low-energy (LE) mammograms, with the clinical aim of reducing iodinated contrast use and additional radiation. The main goal was to improve synthetic DES generation specifically in tumor regions, because prior CESM generative studies had not explicitly optimized lesion reconstruction. The authors proposed Seg-CycleGAN, a lesion-aware CycleGAN variant that adds localized cycle-consistency and identity losses guided by radiologist-provided lesion segmentation maps during training. The main takeaway is that lesion-aware supervision improved PSNR and SSIM and qualitatively reduced lesion-region error versus standard CycleGAN, making the work indirectly relevant to preoperative breast imaging rather than a direct surgical-planning system.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CESM@UCBM (private; single-center internal dataset; 204 patients; 2,278 images = 1,139 LE + 1,139 DES; 425 radiologist-generated lesion segmentation maps); Categorized Contrast-Enhanced Mammography dataset for diagnostic and artificial intelligence research / publicly available CESM dataset from Khaled et al. 2022 (public; used for pretraining; no segmentation maps available in this dataset as reported in the paper)
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed: Seg-CycleGAN (CycleGAN with lesion-aware localized cycle-consistency and identity losses weighted by γ and guided by lesion masks); Baseline/comparator: standard CycleGAN; reported Seg-CycleGAN settings: γ=35 and γ=100
Training Approach: CycleGAN-style adversarial image-to-image translation; pretrained on the public CESM dataset using the standard CycleGAN objective, then trained/fine-tuned on CESM@UCBM using segmentation-guided localized losses; stratified 10-fold cross-validation; 80/10/10 train/validation/test split; image preprocessing + augmentation; early stopping; Adam optimizer
Medical Modality: Contrast-Enhanced Spectral Mammography (CESM): low-energy (LE) mammograms and dual-energy subtracted (DES) images; lesion masks used as annotations
Model input modality: image-only at inference (LE mammogram); during training, lesion segmentation masks are used in the loss function rather than as direct generator inputs
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: 10-fold mean±SD; table scales preserved for MSE/VIF/SSIM (×10^-2). CycleGAN: MSE=0.40±0.11, PSNR=26.79±0.54, VIF=17.84±0.83, SSIM=85.32±0.73. Seg-CycleGAN γ=35: MSE=0.40±0.10, PSNR=26.88±0.82, VIF=17.73±0.26, SSIM=85.35±0.74. Seg-CycleGAN γ=100: MSE=0.40±0.10, PSNR=26.84±0.63, VIF=17.46±0.67, SSIM=85.37±0.79. Best PSNR: γ=35; best SSIM: γ=100; VIF highest in baseline CycleGAN.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Synthesizing High-Fidelity Breast Thermal Images
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the shortage of large, high-quality breast thermography datasets by testing whether generative AI can synthesize realistic breast thermal images. The main goal was to compare three generative families - DCVAE, DCGAN, and DDPM - and identify which one best produces high-fidelity synthetic thermograms. Its novelty is the direct benchmarking of VAE-, GAN-, and diffusion-based image synthesis specifically for breast thermal imaging on a very large real-world cohort, an area with little prior published work. The study found that DDPM generated images that most closely matched the real data distribution and clearly outperformed DCGAN and DCVAE on fidelity. This is best viewed as an upstream data-generation study for breast-screening/diagnostic AI rather than a direct surgical-planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Unnamed internal multi-center breast thermography cohort from multiple hospitals, clinics, and outreach camps; 102,459 participants; 5 standard views per participant (private). No public dataset or external validation dataset was reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Compared models: DDPM with a 4-stage U-Net denoiser; DCGAN with a 4-block transpose-convolution generator and a VGG-based discriminator; DCVAE with a deep convolutional encoder-decoder and latent dimension 256.
Training Approach: Unsupervised generative modeling trained from scratch on min-max normalized 240x320 thermal images using Adam. Minimal data augmentation included Gaussian noise addition, random flipping, rotation, and cropping. DCVAE used a VAE reconstruction + KL objective, DCGAN used adversarial min-max training, and DDPM used weighted-MSE denoising diffusion training with 1000 timesteps. All models were randomly initialized; DDPM additionally used gradient accumulation of 4.
Medical Modality: Breast thermography / infrared thermal imaging; multi-view 2D FLIR thermal camera images
Model input modality: image-only during training (2D thermal images); random noise/latent sampling for image generation
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: FID (Inception-v3 feature based). DDPM=18.065; DCGAN=129.714; DCVAE=150.848. Reference real-vs-real FID=0.47. Additional reported comparison values: inference time - DDPM=12 s, DCGAN=78 ms, DCVAE=18 ms; trainable parameters - DDPM=9,196,161, DCGAN=30,128,769, DCVAE=20,464,977.

title: Out-of-distribution detection in digital pathology: Do foundation models bring the end to reconstruction-based approaches?
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses out-of-distribution detection in digital pathology rather than surgical planning, using benign lymph node tissue as in-distribution and metastatic tumour tissue as out-of-distribution. The goal was to compare diffusion-based reconstruction methods against foundation-model feature-space methods for detecting unseen tumour patterns and realistic distribution shifts across hospitals and cancer origins. Its main novelty is AnoLDM, a latent diffusion model adaptation for OOD detection that optimises noise level, sampler, latent-space normalisation, and latent/pixel-space distance metrics, together with one of the first direct comparisons against pathology-specific foundation models in a full-spectrum OOD setting. The main takeaway is that kang_residual performs best on no-shift data, but AnoLDM is more resilient under several distribution shifts, while both methods still degrade markedly under covariate shift.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Camelyon17 (public; training, calibration, ndl_breast test); AIDA BRLN (public; swe_breast test); Rijnstate Hospital colon lymph node dataset used by Bándi et al. (private; ndl_colon test); AIDA LNCO (public; swe_colon test)
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed: AnoLDM based on a latent diffusion model with a VQ-VAE autoencoder and UNet denoiser; comparators: Residual Score from ViM and deep KNN applied to Kang ViT-S/16 trained with DINO, UNI ViT-H/14 trained with DINOv2, and DINOv2 ViT-B/14
Training Approach: Unsupervised ID-only reconstruction training for AnoLDM on 120k benign Camelyon17 patches; VQ-VAE autoencoder pre-trained on natural images and frozen, UNet trained without augmentation for 59 epochs; calibration tuning over noise step, sampler, sampling steps, normalisation, and metric combinations; best AnoLDM setup used DDIM with 50 sampling steps, noising stopped at step 350, and a Z-score combining latent-space SSIM with pixel-space LPIPS-VGG; foundation-model approaches were inference-only feature extraction with no fine-tuning, and Residual/KNN hyperparameters were selected on the calibration set
Medical Modality: Digital pathology / histopathology; H&E-stained whole-slide images with patch extraction
Model input modality: image-only (WSI patches)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metrics: AUROC and FPR@95%TPR. Table 1 optimal methods, mean over 2000 bootstraps: ndl_breast: kang_residual AUROC=96.17 (0.09), FPR@95%TPR=12.41 (0.18); AnoLDM AUROC=91.86 (0.08), FPR@95%TPR=35.94 (0.42). swe_breast: kang_residual AUROC=85.56 (0.24), FPR@95%TPR=81.91 (0.74); AnoLDM AUROC=78.86 (0.29), FPR@95%TPR=63.59 (0.81). ndl_colon: kang_residual AUROC=87.00 (0.28), FPR@95%TPR=50.7 (1.27); AnoLDM AUROC=89.43 (0.25), FPR@95%TPR=31.78 (0.9). swe_colon: kang_residual AUROC=91.38 (0.15), FPR@95%TPR=23.72 (0.41); AnoLDM AUROC=93.56 (0.11), FPR@95%TPR=23.07 (0.52).

title: Ionic Cell Microscopy: A new modality for visualizing cells using microfluidic impedance cytometry and generative artificial intelligence
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper addresses label-free visualization of cells without relying on conventional optical microscopy by reconstructing cell images from electrical impedance signals acquired in a custom microfluidic chip. Its main goal is to convert single-cell impedance responses into 51 x 51 pixel images for 5 um beads, HeLa cells, and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. The novelty is that it uses what the authors call 'Ionic Cell Microscopy' - a generative AI workflow that maps a 191-value impedance vector directly to an image, going beyond standard impedance-based classification. The main takeaway is that this proof-of-concept produced high-fidelity reconstructions, especially for breast cancer cells and beads, suggesting a portable, label-free imaging approach, although broader validation on more cell types and larger datasets is still needed.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal Rutgers experimental dataset of paired impedance signals and reference high-speed microscopy images for 5 um beads, HeLa cells, and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells (private; data available on request). No public dataset or external validation cohort reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Custom fully connected generative DNN / MLP; input layer = 191 nodes; 8 hidden layers = 100, 80, 40, 50, 30, 15, 20, 1000; output layer = 2601 nodes reshaped to a 51 x 51 image. No explicit external baseline comparator reported.
Training Approach: Supervised learning with paired impedance-image data; single-cell impedance events were segmented, downsampled, and converted into 191-value feature vectors; ReLU activations; backpropagation with Adam optimizer; MSE loss; 2000 epochs; 70/30 train-test split; proof-of-concept reconstruction used the 500 kHz signal; trained on approximately hundreds of cells per class / beads.
Medical Phase (pre/post): pre (diagnostic / biopsy-oriented proof-of-concept rather than post-operative analysis)
Medical Modality: Microfluidic impedance cytometry / electrical impedance sensing as the primary modality, with paired high-speed optical microscopy used to provide reference images.
Model input modality: signal-only / tabular numeric input (191-value electrical impedance vector)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Accuracy approx. 90% on training data, 91% on validation, and 91% on test; MSSIM = 92.77% for beads, 92.33% for breast cancer cells, and 80.27% for HeLa cells (validation set of 26 images); SSIM was reported as lower than MSSIM across all classes, but exact classwise mean SSIM values were not numerically tabulated in the text; Fig. 3I reports relative SD = 2.91% (beads), 6.15% (breast cancer), and 5.69% (HeLa), while MSSIM relative SD = 2.22%, 4.71%, and 4.64%, respectively.

title: Agentic RAG-Driven Multi-Omics Analysis for PI3K/AKT Pathway Deregulation in Precision Medicine
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper proposes ARMOA, an agentic AI framework for analyzing PI3K/AKT pathway deregulation using multi-omics data to support biomarker discovery, drug repurposing, and therapy-response prediction. Its main goal is pathway-specific precision medicine rather than surgical planning, with breast cancer and type 2 diabetes used as case-study contexts. The claimed novelty is the integration of agentic retrieval-augmented generation and large language models with graph neural network-based multi-omics fusion, explainability modules, and autonomous hypothesis generation. The main takeaway is that the framework shows promising in-silico performance on a synthetic dataset assembled from public resources, but validation is largely computational and not a direct breast-surgery application.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Synthetic multi-omics dataset generated in-study from public resources (1000 samples, 400 features; generated/open via GitHub); TCGA (public); ENCODE (public); GEO (public); PRIDE (public); HMDB (public); KEGG (public academic use); Reactome (public); STRING (public); DrugBank (public/academic access); PubChem (public); NCI-MATCH clinical-trial data (public/retrospective); PubMed (public); ClinicalTrials.gov (public).
Baseline model/architecture: ARMOA: agentic RAG + LLM-backed retrieval/synthesis (Claude, GPT-4 mentioned) + heterogeneous GNN/GraphSAGE-style multi-omics fusion over pathway knowledge graphs; drug-repurposing submodule mentions Random Forest and XGBoost; reported comparators include a DL model, MOSEGCN, generic LLMs, and SVM.
Training Approach: Hybrid training/inference setup: supervised training on a synthetic multi-omics dataset with ground-truth labels; preprocessing with DESeq2/MaxQuant/Pareto scaling, differential-expression filtering, ANOVA F-value feature selection, and ComBat batch correction; GNN trained for 40 epochs; inference-time RAG with prompt-based LLM synthesis plus Q-learning-driven agentic query refinement/online knowledge-base updates.
Medical Modality: Multi-omics / non-imaging: genomics, transcriptomics (RNA-seq), proteomics, metabolomics; supplemented by pathway/drug/clinical-trial knowledge bases.
Model input modality: Multi-modal: tabular/structured omics features + graph/pathway relations + retrieved biomedical text/knowledge-base content.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Accuracy=0.9200; Sensitivity=0.9176; Specificity=0.9143; Precision=0.9176; Recall=0.9176; F1-score=0.9176; MCC=0.8319; ROC-AUC=0.9000; Novelty Detection Rate=0.8000. Additional reported results: balanced accuracy=0.91 on diverse public validation sets; clustering accuracy=0.89 for high-risk profile stratification; drug repurposing scores: Alpelisib=0.737, Metformin=0.728, Everolimus=0.711; GNN loss decreased from 0.7232 to 0.1907 over 40 epochs.

title: Evaluating a Chatbot as a Companion for Patients With Breast Cancer: Collaborative Pilot Study
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This collaborative pilot study examined whether a German-language breast cancer chatbot built on GPT-4 with retrieval-augmented generation can answer real patient questions using authoritative German oncology documents. The goal was to deliver personalized, empathetic, evidence-based information for non-English-speaking patients while reducing hallucination risk through document grounding. Its main novelty is the use of authentic questions from a large German breast cancer patient representation group, a Germany-specific corpus of guidelines and patient materials, and dual evaluation by patient representatives and a senior breast cancer expert. Across 104 medical questions, the system was mostly understandable, correct, and nonharmful, but completeness was weaker and a small number of responses were potentially harmful because of retrieval gaps or outdated or incomplete source material. The main takeaway is that RAG-enabled LLM chatbots can support breast cancer patient communication in German, but this is a patient-information study rather than a surgical-planning study and it still requires updated knowledge bases, safeguards, disclaimers, and human oversight.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: German breast cancer RAG document corpus built from 13 authoritative German guidelines, recommendations, and patient information materials (public); Patient Representation Group question set: 118 authentic questions collected, 104 medical questions retained for evaluation (private at collection; shared in supplementary material)
Baseline model/architecture: Custom GPT-4 (OpenAI custom GPT) with built-in retrieval-augmented generation over uploaded PDF documents; no separate comparator baseline reported
Training Approach: Inference-only / prompt-engineered RAG; custom German system prompt with 5 instructions; OpenAI-managed chunking, embeddings, and similarity retrieval; no fine-tuning or supervised retraining; each question asked once
Medical Modality: Clinical text / guideline documents and patient question text; non-imaging
Model input modality: text-only (patient question plus retrieved text chunks from guidelines and patient materials)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Comprehensibility=427/499 (85.6%); Correctness=91/104 (87.5%); Completeness=72/104 (69.2%); Incomplete=20/104 (19.2%); Nonharmful=93/104 (89.4%); Potentially harmful=6/104 (5.8%)

title: Evaluation of the integration of retrieval-augmented generation in large language model for breast cancer nursing care responses
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper evaluates whether retrieval-augmented generation can improve GPT-4 answers to breast cancer nursing care questions, which makes it more of a breast cancer care support study than a surgical planning study. The main goal was to compare direct GPT-4 question answering with a RAG-enhanced GPT-4 system built on a manually curated local breast cancer knowledge base. The key novelty is the use of a domain-specific Chinese breast cancer nursing knowledge base with BGE-based semantic retrieval to reduce hallucinations without retraining the foundation model. The authors evaluated 15 randomly selected questions from a curated 200-question set using ratings from three senior nurses. The main takeaway is that RAG substantially improved satisfaction and accuracy while preserving empathy.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Breast cancer nursing care Q&A evaluation set: mixed source - publicly available datasets (public) + questions from nurses at a tertiary hospital (private); 200 Q&A pairs total, with 15 randomly selected for formal evaluation. Local breast cancer knowledge base: public; manually curated Chinese text corpus of about 60,000 words collected from Bing, Wanfang, CNKI, Baidu, textbooks, research papers, clinical guidelines, and traditional Chinese medicine resources. Key public guideline documents included Breast Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines China 2022, Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Young Breast Cancer in China 2022, and Guidelines for Follow-up and Health Management of Breast Cancer in China 2022 Edition.
Baseline model/architecture: Main system: RAG-GPT using GPT-4 plus a BGE embedding RAG model and vector retrieval database; Comparator/control: direct GPT-4
Training Approach: Inference-only and prompt-engineering plus RAG; no task-specific fine-tuning or retraining reported. Knowledge documents were manually curated, split into paragraphs, embedded with a pretrained BGE model, stored in a vector database, retrieved using cosine similarity threshold 0.8, and the top 5 retrieved passages were appended to the user question before GPT-4 generation. Same system prompt was used for both groups, with otherwise default GPT-4 settings.
Medical Modality: Text/document-based clinical knowledge and nursing Q&A; no imaging modality
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Rated by 3 senior nurses on 15 questions using 1-10 Likert scoring. Overall satisfaction: RAG-GPT 8.4±0.84 vs GPT-4 5.4±1.27, p<0.01. Accuracy: RAG-GPT 8.6±0.69 vs GPT-4 5.6±0.96, p<0.01. Empathy: RAG-GPT 8.4±0.85 vs GPT-4 7.8±1.22, p>0.05.

title: Breast-CRAG: A Breast Cancer Large Language Model Leveraging Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: Addresses the lack of lightweight breast-cancer-specific LLMs that can be deployed without privacy-sensitive closed APIs or very large general models; The goal was to build a domain-specialized assistant for breast-cancer dialogue and exam question answering using a 7B generator plus a disease-specific retriever; Novelty lies in the automated breast-cancer data curation pipeline and the combination of PEFT-tuned generation with a specialized 1M-chunk breast-cancer knowledge base for RAG; Main takeaway is that a smaller disease-specific text-only RAG model can outperform larger general or open models on breast-cancer dialogue benchmarks and remain competitive with GPT-4o on exam benchmarks although it still lacks multimodal and real-world clinical validation
Datasets names (also is public or privat: MedDialog-CN to MedDialog-BC public; Huatuo-26M to Huatuo-26M-BC and Huatuo-BC public; cMedQA to cMedQA-BC public; webMedQA to webMedQA-BC public; MedQA-USMLE to USMLE-BC public; 2024 web-scraped breast-cancer licensing exam questions to ExamBC private/custom; breast-cancer books and guidelines knowledge base about 1M chunks private/custom; synthetic retriever training set about 7K Q and A pairs private/custom

Training Approach: RAG plus PEFT instruction tuning; the generator was trained on filtered breast-cancer dialogue data from MedDialog-CN and Huatuo-26M with keyword filtering GPT-4o filtering 2000 manually annotated samples and MedDialog dialogue condensation into single-turn Q and A; the paper reports 268K curated dialogues overall in the abstract but Results states 91K dialogues were used for fine-tuning; the retriever was trained by contrastive learning on about 7K synthetic GPT-4o-generated Q and A pairs from a breast-cancer knowledge base
Medical Phase (pre/post): Could be both pre- and post
Medical Modality: Text-only medical dialogues exam questions and breast-cancer books and guidelines knowledge base non-imaging

Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Dialogue results for Breast-CRAG: Huatuo-BC Rouge-1=0.228 Rouge-2=0.057 Rouge-L=0.191 BLEU=5.052 BERTScore=0.873; MedDialog-BC Rouge-1=0.230 Rouge-2=0.052 Rouge-L=0.191 BLEU=5.277 BERTScore=0.876; cMedQA-BC Rouge-1=0.233 Rouge-2=0.059 Rouge-L=0.198 BLEU=5.014 BERTScore=0.874; webMedQA-BC Rouge-1=0.182 Rouge-2=0.043 Rouge-L=0.153 BLEU=3.272 BERTScore=0.844; ExamBC simple Single=0.65 Multi=0.54 Ave=0.63; ExamBC hard Single=0.56 Multi=0.37 Ave=0.52; USMLE-BC Single=0.81

title: RadioRAG: Online Retrieval-augmented Generation for Radiology Question Answering
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses hallucination and outdated knowledge in LLM-based radiology question answering rather than image interpretation itself. Its goal was to develop and evaluate RadioRAG, a radiology-specific online retrieval-augmented generation framework that pulls current information from Radiopaedia in real time and uses it to answer expert-level radiology questions. The main novelty is the on-the-fly creation of a query-specific vector database from live online radiology content, together with evaluation on two public radiology QA benchmarks created by the authors. Across six LLMs, RadioRAG generally improved accuracy and factual grounding, with especially large gains for open-weight models, although results still depended on retrieval quality and the pipeline was much slower than conventional QA. The paper is only indirectly relevant to breast surgery because it includes breast imaging questions, but it is not a breast surgical planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: RSNA-RadioQA (public, open-source; n=80); ExtendedQA (public, open-source; n=24); Radiopaedia.org articles used as dynamic retrieval corpus (public online source, not a fixed benchmark dataset)
Baseline model/architecture: RadioRAG (online RAG) with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Mistral-7B-instruct-v0.2, Mixtral-8x7B-instruct-v0.1, Llama3-8B, and Llama3-70B-instruct; comparator = the same LLMs in conventional non-RAG QA; keyword extraction via GPT-3.5-turbo; embeddings via text-embedding-ada-002; Chroma vector DB + LangChain retriever
Training Approach: Inference-only / no fine-tuning; zero-shot QA evaluation; two-shot prompting used only for keyword extraction; real-time retrieval from Radiopaedia; articles chunked into 1000-token segments with 200-token overlap; embedding-based retrieval with cosine similarity (top-k=3); temperature=0 for most models and 0.1 for Mistral/Mixtral
Medical Modality: Multi-modal radiology domain derived from multiple imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, ultrasound, X-ray, nuclear medicine/molecular imaging, vascular imaging, and related subspecialty imaging; no raw images were provided to the LLMs
Model input modality: Text-only (radiology question text built from clinical history plus textual image findings; for RadioRAG, question text + retrieved text context)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric = Accuracy. RSNA-RadioQA (RAG vs non-RAG): GPT-3.5 74% (59/80) vs 66% (53/80); GPT-4 79% (63/80) vs 78% (62/80); Mistral-7B 55% (44/80) vs 55% (44/80); Mixtral-8x7B 76% (61/80) vs 65% (52/80); Llama3-8B 59% (47/80) vs 58% (46/80); Llama3-70B 69% (55/80) vs 66% (53/80). ExtendedQA (RAG vs non-RAG): GPT-3.5 71% (17/24) vs 58% (14/24); GPT-4 75% (18/24) vs 71% (17/24); Mistral-7B 71% (17/24) vs 46% (11/24); Mixtral-8x7B 79% (19/24) vs 54% (13/24); Llama3-8B 67% (16/24) vs 50% (12/24); Llama3-70B 75% (18/24) vs 67% (16/24). Context relevance: 72% (58/80) on RSNA-RadioQA and 83% (20/24) on ExtendedQA. Lowest hallucination rates among RAG models: GPT-4 = 6% (5/80) on RSNA-RadioQA; Mixtral-8x7B = 8% (2/24) on ExtendedQA. Human radiologist accuracy: 63% (50/80) on RSNA-RadioQA and 62% (15/24) on ExtendedQA.

title: Developing an Artificial Intelligence Tool for Personalized Breast Cancer Treatment Plans based on the NCCN Guidelines
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the challenge of generating personalized breast cancer treatment recommendations from complex, frequently updated NCCN guideline flowcharts and documents. Its goal is to build an AI clinical decision-support workflow that converts NCCN breast cancer guidelines into machine-readable content and answers patient-specific treatment questions. The main novelty is the comparison of two retrieval-grounded generative approaches—Agentic-RAG, which uses multi-step LLM title selection, recommendation generation, and iterative insufficiency checking, and Graph-RAG, which builds entity-relationship graphs from guideline content—against a ChatGPT-4 baseline while also returning NCCN document/page citations. The main takeaway is that retrieval-grounded systems, especially Agentic-RAG, produced the most complete and transparent NCCN-aligned treatment recommendations on the study cases. This is a treatment-planning study rather than an image-based surgical-planning study.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: NCCN Breast Cancer Guidelines v3.2024 / NCCN breast guideline PDFs converted to page-level JSON (public); 16 curated breast-cancer patient descriptions with 4 question variations each (private/internal).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed: Agentic-RAG (GPT-4o for title selection + o1-preview for treatment recommendation + LLM-based insufficiency checker), Graph-RAG (Microsoft GraphRAG framework / 'LLM V1'); baseline: ChatGPT-4.
Training Approach: Prompt-engineered, inference-only retrieval-augmented generation; no model fine-tuning/training reported. NCCN PDF flowcharts/tables were converted to JSON; Agentic-RAG retrieves relevant titles/pages and iteratively refines answers via sufficiency checks; Graph-RAG converts extracted text into entities/relationships, graph communities, and summary-based retrieval.
Medical Modality: Non-imaging clinical text/guideline documents (NCCN PDFs with flowcharts/tables converted to JSON) + curated patient clinical case descriptions.
Model input modality: text-only (patient description + user question + retrieved guideline JSON/text/graph summaries)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Manual board-certified physician review. Table 1 main full-text results: Agentic-RAG—Adherence=100%, Hallucinations=0, Wrong order=0, Unnecessary=0, Missing treatments=0, Wrong treatments=0; Graph-RAG (LLM V1)—Adherence=92%, Hallucinations=0, Wrong order=0, Unnecessary=0, Missing treatments=4, Wrong treatments=0; ChatGPT-4—Adherence=94%, Hallucinations=0, Wrong order=0, Unnecessary=1, Missing treatments=2, Wrong treatments=0. Note: the abstract reports inconsistent counts/adherence (Agentic-RAG 24/24=100%, Graph-RAG 23/24=95.8%, ChatGPT-4 22/24=91.6%).

title: MedGen: An Explainable Multi-Agent Architecture for Clinical Decision Support through Multisource Knowledge Fusion
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper proposes MedGen, an explainable GPT-4-based multi-agent clinical decision support architecture that fuses clinical guidelines, biomedical literature, and patient reviews to support complex treatment decisions. Its main goal is to address three gaps in prior systems: stale evidence, limited support for multimorbidity, and weak incorporation of patient-specific needs. The main novelty is the PICOAS representation (extending PICO with Argument and Sentiment) plus a role-specialized agent pipeline that links multisource evidence into an explicit argumentation graph and then summarizes and verifies the reasoning trace. In the breast cancer plus depression case study, MedGen qualitatively shows how source-grounded arguments can support treatment selection with transparency, but the paper does not provide quantitative benchmarking or real-world clinical validation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: NICE breast cancer clinical guidelines (public); NICE depression clinical guidelines (public); PubMed medical literature/abstracts (public); breast cancer patient review dataset from open patient discussion platforms (public, exact dataset/platform name not specified); illustrative breast cancer plus depression case description (not a formal dataset)
Baseline model/architecture: GPT-4-based multi-agent architecture: Goal Planner, Pattern Selector, Knowledge Manager, Decision Generator, Argument Summarizer, and Outcome Verifier; no quantitative comparator baseline experimentally evaluated
Training Approach: Inference-only / prompt-engineered multi-agent workflow; no model training or fine-tuning reported. Agents retrieve external knowledge, extract source-constrained PICOAS elements, link them into an argumentation graph, generate candidate decisions, summarize reasoning, and verify outcomes through agent interaction and comparison.
Medical Phase (pre/post): post (illustrative breast cancer case occurs after breast-conserving surgery and during ongoing chemotherapy/endocrine treatment)
Medical Modality: Multi-source text: clinical guidelines, PubMed literature abstracts, patient reviews/discussion-platform text, and clinical case information
Model input modality: text-only (clinical case text/EHR-style description plus structured PICOAS text extracted from guidelines, literature, and patient reviews)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: No quantitative evaluation metrics reported. Evaluation is qualitative only via a breast cancer plus depression case study, where two decision generators and two argument summarizers are compared and the Outcome Verifier accepts the first plan.

title: PICOAS: A clinical knowledge linking model for delivering up-to-date, interrelated, and personalized decision support
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses three gaps in clinical decision support: delayed guideline updates, poor coordination across comorbid conditions, and limited personalization. The authors propose PICOAS, a knowledge-linking framework that connects clinical guidelines, medical literature, and patient reviews through three argumentation modes, and implement it with a multi-LLM-agent architecture. The main novelty is not a new predictive model, but a structured linking-and-reasoning scheme that lets ChatGPT-based agents retrieve, transform, and connect heterogeneous evidence for decision support. In a breast-cancer endocrine-therapy case study involving depression and hot flashes, the system achieved higher scenario scores than a ChatGPT-with-guidelines baseline, especially in perimenopausal, multimorbidity, and preference-sensitive settings. This is a proof-of-concept CDS/treatment-support paper rather than a surgical planning model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No formal benchmark dataset; knowledge sources were NICE Early and Locally Advanced Breast Cancer: Diagnosis and Management (public); NICE Depression in Adults: Treatment and Management (public); 8 breast-cancer-related clinical literature articles (public; not all individually enumerated in the paper); Xiaohongshu/Rednote breast-cancer patient reviews, n=136 (public web/social-media data, anonymized); synthetic/generated patient cohort, n=350 across 7 scenarios for evaluation (author-constructed/synthetic).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed: PICOAS multi-LLM-agent architecture using ChatGPT-based agents (Crawler Agent, PICOAS Mining Agent, Pattern Selector Agent, Mode Linking Agent, Decision Generator Agent); Comparator: ChatGPT-based LLM-Agent with clinical-guidelines knowledge only.
Training Approach: Prompt-engineered, inference-only multi-agent orchestration; retrieval of guidelines, literature, and patient reviews; extraction into PICOAS elements; rule-based knowledge linking/argument graph generation; structured inter-agent communication; no fine-tuning or supervised training reported.
Medical Phase (pre/post): treatment (post-operative/adjuvant endocrine therapy and antidepressant selection in the breast-cancer case study)
Medical Modality: textual clinical knowledge sources: clinical guidelines + medical literature + patient review/social-media text
Model input modality: text + structured categorical patient attributes (clinical question/patient profile plus retrieved evidence transformed into a linked PICOAS graph)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: No standard ML metrics reported; author-defined scenario score (max=50 per group, judged by 5 medical students): ChatGPT vs Our Approach = Premenopausal 50 vs 50; Postmenopausal 50 vs 50; Perimenopausal 25 vs 50; Premenopausal+depression 37.5 vs 45; Postmenopausal+depression 40.5 vs 45; Perimenopausal+depression 32.5 vs 41.5; Postmenopausal+depression+hot flash 36.5 vs 43.5. In the Mode-2 subgroup, drug-choice counts were Fluoxetine 10 vs 0, Sertraline 35 vs 40, and Venlafaxine 5 vs 10 (ChatGPT vs Our Approach).

title: Expertise Is What We Want
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper presents Large Language Expert (LLE), a hybrid LLM-plus-expert-system architecture used in Color's Cancer Copilot to identify missing pre-treatment cancer workup items from real-world records. The goal was to help clinicians rapidly extract clinically relevant decision factors and determine which guideline-recommended workups were complete or still missing before treatment initiation. The novelty lies in combining human-readable, versioned knowledge bases and deterministic first-order-logic rule evaluation with LLM-based extraction from unstructured records, rather than relying only on end-to-end ML or a rigid rule engine. In a retrospective UCSF study on breast and colon cancer cases, the system showed high clinician-level concordance with limited human correction and short review times. The main takeaway is that generative AI can support guideline-based oncology planning in a human-in-the-loop setting, but it is not yet suitable for fully autonomous use.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: UCSF retrospective de-identified cohort (private): 100 unique patients total (50 breast cancer, 50 colon cancer); each case included diagnosis records up to diagnosis and treatment records up to but not including treatment initiation. No public dataset reported.
Baseline model/architecture: No explicit comparator baseline reported. Main system: Large Language Expert (LLE) / Cancer Copilot, a hybrid LLM + structured, versioned knowledge base + deterministic first-order-logic evaluator + human-in-the-loop review. OpenAI o1 is explicitly described for guideline-to-logic parsing during knowledge-base curation.
Training Approach: Inference-only/prompt-based workflow rather than end-to-end model training: expert-reviewed knowledge-base construction, LLM extraction of clinical decision factors from records, function-tool instrumentation, deterministic rule evaluation, and clinician correction. No large labeled training set or model fine-tuning is reported.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal clinical records: structured EHR fields + unstructured clinical notes + PDF/document records
Model input modality: text + structured clinical data (normalized patient records/questions plus knowledge-base text/rules); not raw medical images
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Clinical decision factors: 12,532 extracted, 260 adjusted (2.07%), 97.9% no adjustment; clinician corrections=1.3%, study artifacts=0.7%, clinician error=0.1%. Workup items: 2,971 generated, 135 adjusted (4.54%), 95.5% no adjustment; clinician corrections=4.2%, clinician error=0.3%. By disease area: decision-factor adjustment - breast=1.93%, colon=2.44%; workup adjustment - breast=3.58%, colon=5.43%. Time: median clinician review - colon step 1=2.3 min, colon step 2=2.1 min, breast step 1=5.2 min, breast step 2=2.1 min; the paper states non-specialists finalized recommendations in <7.5 min.

title: Breast Ultrasound Report Generation using LangChain
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study targets semi-automated generation of breast ultrasound (BUS) reports from multi-view examinations, where radiologists must integrate several BUS images and sometimes prior patient history into one coherent report.
