Its main goal is to show that a modular LangChain/LLM workflow can coordinate specialized BUS image-analysis tools to produce clinically meaningful preliminary and final reports. The novelty is the use of the LLM as an orchestration layer rather than a new end-to-end vision-language model: independently trained classifiers for lesion descriptors, BI-RADS category, and probe position are combined with optional retrieval of prior reports, and the framework can be extended with detection, segmentation, and OCR tools. The main takeaway is that the method did not lead the NLP overlap metrics but achieved the best clinical evaluation among compared report-generation baselines, suggesting better clinical usefulness than single-image end-to-end generators.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Chung-Ang University Hospital BUS cohort (~750 patients, private; 720 patients used for model development/5-fold cross-validation and 30 patients held out for final report evaluation; also used to derive 3561 train, 210 validation, and 360 test image-report pairs for algorithm comparison); Dataset of Breast Ultrasound Images by Al-Dhabyani et al. 2020 (public; curated and manually relabeled for additional training). The source of the extra data used for the detection/OCR extension experiments is not explicitly named, but it appears to be internal/private.
Baseline model/architecture: Main architecture: LangChain-based modular BUS report generator with three primary ConvNeXt v2-based tools: Suspicious Description Tool (shape/margin/echo classifiers), Category Classification Tool (BI-RADS C1-C5), and Probe Information Tool (12-class probe-position classifier); retrieval-augmented generation for prior reports. Extension tools: PIX2SEQ for suspicious-region detection, Segment Anything for segmentation, and TrOCR for OCR. Compared against R2Gen, R2GenCMN, R2GenRL, M2KT, and KMVE-RG; classifier backbones also compared with ResNet, VGG16, DenseNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet, and DAViT.
Training Approach: Supervised learning for each BUS analysis tool, trained independently rather than end-to-end; 5-fold cross-validation on the 720-patient subset; data augmentation with flipping, rotation, and sharpening; Adam optimizer; learning rate=1e-4; 200 epochs; batch size=2; cross-entropy loss; best model selected by validation accuracy. LangChain performs prompt-based inference-time orchestration and report synthesis, while retrieval-augmented generation injects prior patient reports for personalized final reporting. Extension modules used supervised PIX2SEQ training plus pre-trained Segment Anything and TrOCR.
Medical Modality: Ultrasound (breast ultrasound/BUS)
Model input modality: image+text overall (BUS images plus prompt/instructions; optional prior report text via retrieval-augmented generation). Sub-models themselves are image-only.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Preliminary-report NLP metrics: BLEU-1=0.404; BLEU-2=0.260; BLEU-3=0.176; BLEU-4=0.118; METEOR=0.261; ROUGE-L=0.320. Final-report clinical evaluation (average of 2 radiologists)=3.67/5; weighted Cohen's kappa=0.84. Tool metrics: Shape Acc/Prec/Rec/F1=0.98/0.98/0.98/0.98; Margin=0.88/0.87/0.86/0.86; Echo=0.95/0.95/0.94/0.95; Category=0.87/0.88/0.86/0.86; Probe=0.97/0.97/0.97/0.97. 5-fold mean accuracy +/- SD for ConvNeXt v2: Shape=95.15+/-2.77%; Margin=83.49+/-3.03%; Echo=94.77+/-0.55%; Category=82.60+/-3.48%; Probe=97.07+/-0.36%. Extension detection tool IoU=0.684.

title: A genotype-to-drug diffusion model for generation of tailored anti-cancer small molecules
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses phenotype-based precision oncology drug discovery by generating new anti-cancer small molecules conditioned on cancer genotypes and desired drug response, rather than known targets or gene-expression profiles. The goal was to build a clinically more usable model that can propose hit-like compounds from somatic alteration patterns in clinically relevant genes, including unseen genotypes. The main novelty is G2D-Diff, a genotype-to-drug latent diffusion pipeline that combines a SMILES chemical VAE, a contrastively pre-trained genotype/response condition encoder with attention-based interpretability, and conditional diffusion trained directly on drug-response distributions without requiring a separate predictor during generation. Across three evaluation sets and triple-negative breast cancer zero-shot case studies, the model generated more diverse, feasible, and condition-matching molecules than PaccMannRL and highlighted plausible pathways such as PI3K/HDAC and CDK.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: GuacaMol benchmark / ChEMBL release 24 (public); GDSC1 (public); GDSC2 (public); CTRPv1 (public); CTRPv2 (public); NCI60 Growth Inhibition Data (public); DepMap 22Q1 (public); AACR Project GENIE mbc_genie_2020 TNBC cohort via cBioPortal (publicly available); PDB structures 4L2Y, 4BKX, 4KD1, 6GU6 (public); ZINC20 (public); Enamine Building Blocks catalog (public); USPTO reaction templates (public)
Baseline model/architecture: G2D-Diff: chemical VAE (3-layer LSTM encoder/decoder, 128-d latent) + condition encoder (genetic-alteration embeddings + 3-layer transformer with NeST-masked first layer) + conditional latent DDPM diffusion model with classifier-free guidance; comparator baseline: PaccMannRL; auxiliary evaluation models: G2D-Pred and HiDRA
Training Approach: Three-stage training: (1) beta-VAE pretraining on 1,583,442 SMILES with cyclical KL annealing; (2) contrastive pretraining of the condition encoder on condition-drug pairs using a CLIP-style loss and weighted random sampling; (3) supervised training of the conditional latent DDPM on drug-centric response data with 300 diffusion steps and 10% unconditional batches for classifier-free guidance. Inference generates SMILES from somatic alteration genotype plus desired response class. A separate supervised G2D-Pred ensemble was trained only for evaluation.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: genomics (somatic genetic alterations across 718 clinical genes) + in vitro drug-response screening
Model input modality: tabular genomics + categorical response class condition (main generator); SMILES tokens for chemical VAE pretraining
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary generative benchmark (Table 1, G2D-Diff sensitive generation): Eval1: Validity=0.764; Uniqueness=0.835; Novelty=0.997; Diversity=0.870; FCD=9.136; OTD=4.858. Eval2: Validity=0.765; Uniqueness=0.823; Novelty=0.997; Diversity=0.866; FCD=11.463; OTD=4.999. Eval3: Validity=0.757; Uniqueness=0.824; Novelty=0.997; Diversity=0.865; FCD=13.278; OTD=5.112. Comparator PaccMannRL FCD/OTD: Eval1=54.317/7.229; Eval2=56.130/7.218; Eval3=53.516/7.185. Condition fitness across response classes: Mann-Whitney p<10^-4 in all evaluation sets. Zero-shot TNBC validation: TNBC-S1 vs Fimepinostat docking energies on PI3Kalpha -8.5 vs -8.7 kcal/mol and HDAC1 -8.5 vs -8.6; TNBC-S2 vs Dinaciclib on CDK1 -9.7 vs -9.5 and CDK2 -9.6 vs -9.8.

title: Building a unified model for drug synergy analysis powered by large language models
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This is not a breast-surgery/surgical-planning paper; it addresses computational prediction of synergistic drug combinations across cancer cell lines. The main goal is to build a unified and scalable model for drug synergy analysis that can work across heterogeneous public datasets. The novelty is BAITSAO, which converts drug and cell-line descriptions into GPT-3.5 embeddings, uses a unified tabular representation, and pre-trains an MLP-based multi-task model on large-scale DrugComb data to jointly learn synergy regression, synergy classification, and single-drug inhibition. The study also extends the framework to zero-shot and fine-tuned inference, tri-drug prediction, and SHAP-based gene-level explainability. Main takeaway: LLM-derived embeddings plus multi-task pretraining improve generalization and achieve top-tier performance relative to prior baselines, but the approach depends on drugs having meaningful functional or chemical descriptions.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: DrugComb v1.5 (public; pretraining, 739652 combinations after filtering); DeepSynergy dataset D1 (public); MARSY dataset D2 (public); DeepDDs dataset D3 (public); DrugCombDB (public; tri-drug inference); CPA perturbation dataset (public); OpenProblems single-cell perturbation dataset (public); GSE215121 (public); SCP109 (public); DrugBank (public; description validation); CCLE/cell-line gene-expression profiles (public; explainability)
Baseline model/architecture: BAITSAO: MLP-based deep neural network with data-specific layers, shared layers, and task-specific heads under multi-task learning; GPT-3.5 embedding model used to encode drug and cell-line text. Key comparators/baselines: DeepSynergy, MARSY, DeepDDs, TreeComb/XGBoost, TabNet, SVM/SVR/SVC, BERT, Lasso.
Training Approach: Prompt-generated drug and cell-line descriptions converted to GPT-3.5 embeddings; supervised multi-task pretraining on DrugComb with uncertainty-weighted losses for Loewe regression plus RI regression plus synergy classification; Adam optimizer, ReduceLROnPlateau, early stopping; 5-fold cross-validation on downstream datasets; parameter-freezing fine-tuning and zero-shot inference; MC Dropout with 100 runs for uncertainty estimation in multi-drug prediction.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal non-imaging biological data: drug-combination synergy screening data, cancer cell-line metadata, and gene-expression data (bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq used for auxiliary validation/explainability)
Model input modality: Tabular embedding vectors derived from text descriptions of drugs and cell lines: average of drug embeddings plus cell-line embedding plus drug-count feature; optional addition of gene-expression vector for explainability analyses
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary drug-synergy benchmarks used PCC, MSE, ROCAUC, and ACC across D1/D2/D3 via 5-fold cross-validation, but exact BAITSAO fold means or SD are not numerically tabulated in the main paper and are shown as boxplots only. Exact values reported elsewhere in the article include: DrugBank-vs-LLM cosine similarity = 0.87 for indication, 0.90 for summary, 0.90 for background; drug-similarity-matrix PCC >= 0.76 with p<0.05; GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 embedding comparison p=0.86, vs Claude 3.5 p=0.44, vs Gemini p=0.0039; BAITSAO architecture vs DeepSynergy with LLM embeddings p=0.002; SHAP-selected genes vs DEGs overlap Fisher p=0.0062; predicted synergy probability difference between synergy and non-synergy labels p<2.22e-308; predicted vs observed counts of synergistic cell lines across drug combinations r=0.99 with p<2.22e-308.

title: Scientific hypothesis generation by large language models: laboratory validation in breast cancer treatment
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study investigated whether a large language model can generate experimentally useful hypotheses for breast cancer treatment rather than only summarizing literature. The goal was to use GPT-4 to propose novel, potentially synergistic drug pairs that selectively inhibit the MCF7 breast cancer cell line over the non-tumorigenic MCF10A line, and then validate those hypotheses in automated wet-lab experiments. Its main novelty is a closed-loop workflow in which GPT-4 generated drug-pair hypotheses, laboratory screening results were fed back to the model, and a second iteration of hypotheses was experimentally tested. The main takeaway is that GPT-4 generated several novel combinations with positive synergy, showing that LLMs can be useful for scientific hypothesis generation, although some mechanistic explanations were biologically flawed and the study is treatment-focused rather than surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No external named benchmark dataset; study-generated MCF7 breast cancer cell-line viability/synergy screening data (public at publication via main text/supplement/Figshare); study-generated MCF10A non-tumorigenic breast cell-line viability/synergy screening data (public at publication via main text/supplement/Figshare)
Baseline model/architecture: GPT-4 (ChatGPT-4) as the main generative LLM; qualitative comparison with Gemini and PubMedGPT; no formal predictive ML baseline
Training Approach: Prompt engineering / inference-only; no task-specific training or fine-tuning. Iterative closed-loop hypothesis generation: GPT-4 proposed drug pairs, wet-lab results were summarized back to GPT-4, and second-round hypotheses were re-tested experimentally.
Medical Modality: In vitro breast cell-line drug-response screening / cell-viability assay with dose-response matrices (MCF7 and MCF10A)
Model input modality: Text-only (prompt text; second round also used text summaries of first-round experimental results)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: HSA synergy score from SynergyFinder 3.0, with specificity versus MCF10A. First screen: itraconazole+atenolol HSA=4.83, specificity=7.03; simvastatin+disulfiram HSA=3.29, specificity=1.85; dipyridamole+mebendazole HSA=2.49, specificity=3.69; positive control doxorubicin+cyclophosphamide HSA=1.02, specificity=3.27. Second screen: disulfiram+simvastatin HSA=4.75, HSA(max)=10.58, specificity=2.41; disulfiram+fulvestrant HSA=1.81, HSA(max)=4.60, specificity=0.03; disulfiram+quinacrine HSA=1.53, HSA(max)=4.47, specificity=0.60; dipyridamole+mebendazole HSA=1.10, HSA(max)=5.26, specificity=3.60; disulfiram+hydroxychloroquine HSA=1.08, HSA(max)=3.06, specificity=-1.86; mebendazole+quinacrine HSA=0.56, HSA(max)=5.54, specificity=1.09. Single-drug retest IC50 in MCF7 (µM): disulfiram=0.059, doxorubicin=0.3, niclosamide=1.22, quinacrine=4.71, chloroquine=10.62. Outcome summary: 3/12 first-round GPT-4 pairs exceeded the positive-control synergy score, and 3/4 newly suggested second-round pairs had positive HSA scores.

title: FuseLinker: Leveraging LLM's pre-trained text embeddings and domain knowledge to enhance GNN-based link prediction on biomedical knowledge graphs
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses incomplete biomedical knowledge graphs and studies link prediction for downstream tasks such as drug repurposing. Its main goal is to improve GNN-based biomedical link prediction by jointly using graph structure, LLM-derived text embeddings from node names, and biomedical domain knowledge from the UMLS Semantic Network. The novelty is FuseLinker’s three-module pipeline: embedding-visible LLM text encoding, MuRP-based hyperbolic ontology embedding plus MetaMap mapping to UMLS, and weighted fusion before an RGCN link-prediction model; the paper also compares multiple LLM backbones and fusion weights. Across four public BKG datasets, FuseLinker consistently outperformed TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, and vanilla RGCN, and case studies on Sorafenib and Parkinson’s disease suggested practical utility for drug-repurposing hypothesis generation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: KEGG50k (public); Hetionet (public; also used as a filtered subset for case studies); SuppKG (public); ADInt (public); UMLS Semantic Network (public ontology used for domain-knowledge embedding)
Baseline model/architecture: FuseLinker: pre-trained LLM text embeddings + MuRP (multi-relational Poincaré) UMLS domain embeddings + weighted fusion + RGCN encoder + tensor factorization decoder; baselines/comparators: TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, vanilla RGCN; LLMs examined for text embeddings: BERT, PubMedBERT, Flan-T5, Llama2, PMC-LLaMA
Training Approach: Supervised link prediction / knowledge graph completion. Node-name text embeddings were extracted from pre-trained LLMs, UMLS ontology embeddings were learned with MuRP in hyperbolic space, then an autoencoder and FC layer aligned dimensions/spaces, embeddings were fused by weighted average, and the RGCN-based model was trained with positive triples plus random negative sampling (1:20) and grid-search tuning.
Medical Modality: Biomedical knowledge graph / ontology (structured relational biomedical data; no imaging)
Model input modality: graph triples + node-name text embeddings + ontology/domain-knowledge embeddings

title: Understanding Breast Cancer Survival: Using Causality and Language Models on Multi-omics Data
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study investigates breast cancer survival by asking which multi-omics alterations are causally related to patient vital status, rather than training a black-box survival classifier. After reducing the feature space, the authors apply several causal discovery methods to a TCGA breast cancer cohort and then cross-check the discovered claims with biomedical language models. The novelty lies in combining causal discovery on mixed multi-omics data with language-model-based verification using perplexity, masked language modeling, and prompt-based text generation. The main takeaway is that genes such as MLL3, TNXB, TNFRSF11B, SLC7A2, and others repeatedly emerged as survival-related factors, while BlueBERT gave the strongest automated claim-verification signal; however, the findings remain exploratory because there is no causal ground truth or external clinical validation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: TCGA Breast Cancer multi-omics subset (public; n=705 patients). No private/internal cohort and no external validation dataset reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Key causal model: GPM-based Markov network refined with PC; other causal discovery methods: PC, GES, FGES, FCI. LM validation/comparators: BlueBERT (best), SciBERT, DistilBERT, GPT-2, PubMedBERT, ClinicalBERT, BioGPT.
Training Approach: Unsupervised causal structure learning with target-aware feature selection. MMMB was used for categorical variables and mutual information for mixed/continuous variables to select 10 features including vital status; PC/FCI used conditional independence tests (Chi-square, conditional Gaussian likelihood ratio, RCIT), while GES/FGES used discrete BIC, conditional Gaussian BIC, or generalized cross-validation scores. Pretrained biomedical language models were used in inference-only mode for claim verification via perplexity, masked-token prediction, and prompted generation; no task-specific fine-tuning was reported.
Medical Modality: Multi-omics / molecular data: copy number variation, somatic mutation, RNA-seq gene expression, protein levels
Model input modality: Tabular multi-omics (categorical + continuous omics variables) for causal discovery; text-only claims/prompts for LM verification
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Masked-token prediction accuracy: BlueBERT=81.25%; SciBERT=68.75%; DistilBERT=56.25%. Perplexity example for the claim Mutation in gene UBR4 is related to the survival in cancer: BlueBERT=31.01 vs 2502.9 for the negated claim; SciBERT=110.87 vs 167.8; GPT-2=76.68 vs 39.65. Example BlueBERT masked-token scores reported in Table 2 included Mutation=0.773, Cancer=0.299, and Patients=0.179. No AUC, C-index, or standard survival-prediction accuracy was reported because the study focused on causal discovery plus claim verification rather than predictive survival modeling.

title: Do They Really Know? Evaluating Large Language Models' Ability to Reference and Cite Oncology Guidelines
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper evaluates whether LLMs used for breast cancer treatment recommendations can accurately cite the oncology guidelines they claim to rely on. Using 50 synthetic breast cancer case vignettes, the authors compare GPT-4, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, LLaMA-3.2 3B, and Mistral-7B on citation grounding against NCCN, ASCO, and ESMO guidelines. The novelty is the focus on citation faithfulness rather than only recommendation quality, including manual verification of cited pages, sections, and versions, and classification of outputs as verbatim, paraphrased, or hallucinated. The main takeaway is that proprietary models cited guideline content more often, but no model retrieved verbatim quotes and all models hallucinated some citations, so prompting for exact quotes alone is not a reliable safeguard for clinical decision support.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: 50 synthetic breast cancer cases from Palepu et al. (2024) (public/open-source); NCCN breast cancer guideline documents, multiple versions reviewed for validation (restricted/private); ASCO guideline documents, multiple versions reviewed for validation (public/open-access); ESMO guideline documents, multiple versions reviewed for validation (public/open-access)
Baseline model/architecture: Compared LLMs: GPT-4; Claude-3.5-Sonnet; LLaMA-3.2 3B; Mistral-7B
Training Approach: Prompt-based, inference-only evaluation; no additional training, fine-tuning, or RAG; models were asked to generate treatment recommendations and retrieve supporting citations, pages, sections, and versions; outputs were manually cross-checked against official guidelines
Medical Modality: Textual synthetic breast cancer case vignettes + oncology guideline documents (NCCN/ASCO/ESMO); non-imaging
Model input modality: text-only (case vignette prompt; no external guideline text supplied directly to the model)

title: Mammo-SAE: Interpreting Breast Cancer Concept Learning with Sparse Autoencoders
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study tackles the need for mechanistic interpretability in breast imaging by examining how Mammo-CLIP encodes clinically relevant concepts such as suspicious calcification and mass. The main goal is to train a patch-level sparse autoencoder called Mammo-SAE on Mammo-CLIP visual features and use latent neuron probing to discover concept-related neurons. Its novelty is applying SAE-based concept analysis to mammography, combining neuron-level spatial heatmaps with targeted top-k activation/deactivation interventions and a comparison of pretrained versus finetuned backbones. The experiments show that a very small subset of neurons can recover most of the task signal, and for suspicious calcification 7 of the top 10 neurons align with annotated regions despite no localization supervision. The main takeaway is that fine-tuning improves latent separation and interpretability, but the model still partly relies on background/confounding features.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: VinDr-Mammo (public; approximately 20,000 mammogram images from 5,000 patients).
Baseline model/architecture: Mammo-CLIP (pretrained and end-to-end finetuned) with EfficientNet-B5 image backbone and downstream fully connected classifier; Mammo-SAE as an encoder-decoder sparse autoencoder attached to patch-level final-layer visual features; comparator setting also includes original features vs SAE-reconstructed features.
Training Approach: Hybrid approach: Mammo-CLIP is reused as a pretrained vision-language backbone for breast-concept classification in frozen-backbone and end-to-end finetuned settings. A single SAE is trained in a self-supervised/unsupervised manner on patch-level final-layer features from the fine-tuned suspicious-calcification Mammo-CLIP classifier using reconstruction loss plus L1 sparsity (200 epochs; lr=3e-4; lambda=3e-5; batch size=4096; expansion factor=8), then reused for latent probing and inference-time top-k activation/deactivation interventions. No annotated localization is used during training.
Medical Modality: Full-field digital mammography (mammogram X-ray)
Model input modality: image-only (mammograms; SAE operates on patch-level visual/image features from the image encoder)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: AUC-ROC (Table 1): suspicious calcification - pretrained 0.951 without SAE and 0.933 with SAE; finetuned 0.978 without SAE and 0.979 with SAE. Mass - pretrained 0.786 without SAE and 0.763 with SAE; finetuned 0.856 without SAE and 0.855 with SAE. Localization mAP@IoU=0.25 (Table 2; best score among top-10 positive-class latent neurons): suspicious calcification - finetuned 0.278, pretrained 0.085; mass - finetuned 0.316, pretrained 0.053.

title: Exposing Vulnerabilities in Clinical LLMs Through Data Poisoning Attacks: Case Study in Breast Cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper studies whether clinical LLMs used for breast-cancer question answering can be maliciously manipulated through data poisoning. The goal is to test how easily a public biomedical LLM, BioGPT, can be induced to output incorrect breast-cancer treatment pathway or side-effect management recommendations after trigger-word injection. The key novelty is a clinical-domain security evaluation that combines instruction-based content injection and ROME-based targeted model editing on a breast-cancer-specific BioGPT fine-tuned with real clinical notes, evaluated on a curated breast-cancer QA benchmark. The main takeaway is that poisoned models can produce fluent, hard-to-detect but clinically wrong answers, exposing major security risks for open clinical LLMs.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Mayo Clinic breast cancer clinical notes from 26,692 patients diagnosed 2013-2022 (private); BreastCancerDFT, a de-identified subset of 65,000 treatment/care/planning notes for fine-tuning (private); oncology-expert-curated breast cancer QA test set with 44 labels expanded to 1,936 QA pairs (private); BioGPT pretrained checkpoint originally trained on public biomedical corpora including MIMIC-III and biomedical literature (public, inherited model background).
Baseline model/architecture: BioGPT, a GPT-2-based biomedical generative transformer, as the main victim/backbone; evaluated as BioGPTPT and BioGPTBC-FT. Clean comparators: MedPaLM2, clean BioGPTPT, and clean BioGPTBC-FT. Poisoned variants were InstrTun-BioGPTPT/BC-FT and TargModE-BioGPTPT/BC-FT.
Training Approach: Supervised domain fine-tuning of pretrained BioGPT on BreastCancerDFT. BioGPTBC-FT used 20 epochs, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-5, weight decay 0.01, linear scheduler, and warmup ratio 0.1 with 100 warmup steps. Attack pipeline 1 used AutoPoison-style instruction-based clean-label data poisoning with GPT-3.5-turbo as the oracle LLM to generate poisoned QA samples. Attack pipeline 2 used white-box targeted model editing with ROME to implant trigger-based backdoors.
Medical Modality: Clinical notes / EHR text
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Table 5 reports Perplexity, Coherence, MAUVE, and ROUGE-2; Figure 6 also evaluates trigger-word occurrence frequency, but exact per-model counts are not tabulated. Main breast-cancer fine-tuned results: Clean BioGPTBC-FT - Perplexity=38.73 (+/-27.6), Coherence=0.56 (+/-0.11), MAUVE=0.28 (+/-0.21), ROUGE-2=1.00 (+/-0.00); InstrTun-BioGPTBC-FT - Perplexity=22.09 (+/-12.1), Coherence=0.59 (+/-0.28), MAUVE=0.27 (+/-0.14), ROUGE-2=0.73 (+/-0.06); TargModE-BioGPTBC-FT - Perplexity=32.09 (+/-28.1), Coherence=0.65 (+/-0.27), MAUVE=0.23 (+/-0.21), ROUGE-2=0.31 (+/-0.09).

title: SAM2Med3D: Leveraging video foundation models for 3D breast MRI segmentation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses automated 3D breast tumor/lesion segmentation on pre-operative breast DCE-MRI, where limited annotations and poor slice-to-slice consistency make accurate volumetric segmentation difficult. The main goal is to adapt the general-purpose video foundation model SAM2 to 3D breast MRI without requiring large-scale medical fine-tuning by treating MRI slices as a video sequence. Its key novelty is a multi-stage SAM2Med3D pipeline that combines nnU-Net initialization with a spatial filtering strategy to select reliable prompt slices and a confidence-driven fusion mechanism to reduce SAM2 propagation drift. The main takeaway is that this hybrid approach improves segmentation accuracy and inter-slice consistency over nnU-Net and MedSAM on both a public dataset and an external hospital cohort while remaining relatively data-efficient.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI (public, TCIA; source dataset has 922 patients, but this study selected 135 cases and manually annotated 3D lesion masks; 110 train/25 test); NJUCM-Breast-Cancer-MRI (private/self-collected external validation dataset; 30 patients).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: SAM2Med3D = nnU-Net initializer (2D or 3D; best-performing main setup uses 3D nnU-Net) + SAM2 video foundation model for prompt-guided refinement + confidence-driven fusion. Main comparators: nnU-Net (2D), nnU-Net (3D), MedSAM.
Training Approach: Supervised learning. nnU-Net was trained on annotated Duke cases using the default nnU-Net configuration and original composite loss; SAM2 was initialized from a public checkpoint and fine-tuned on breast MRI slice sequences using box prompts derived from spatially filtered nnU-Net masks, with Dice+BCE loss (lambda_Dice=1, lambda_CE=20). The private NJUCM cohort was used for external validation/generalization rather than special retraining.
Medical Modality: Breast DCE-MRI (3D volumetric contrast-enhanced MRI)
Model input modality: image-only (3D MRI volume treated as sequential 2D slices); SAM2 refinement additionally uses internally generated box prompts on selected slices
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Duke public test: DSC=0.714; NSD=0.784; IoU=0.595. NJUCM private external validation: Dice=0.837; NSD=0.880; IoU=0.727.

title: Towards Affordable Tumor Segmentation and Visualization for 3D Breast MRI Using SAM2
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper studies low-cost 3D breast tumor segmentation and visualization from breast MRI, motivated by the limited accessibility of commercial medical AI in resource-constrained settings. The goal is to test whether the open-source SAM2 foundation model can segment tumors across an entire 3D MRI volume using only one human prompt on a single slice. Its main novelty is a zero-shot, no-fine-tuning workflow that repurposes SAM2's slice-wise tracking for volumetric MRI and systematically compares three propagation strategies: bottom-to-top, top-to-bottom, and center-outward. The main finding is that center-outward propagation is the most stable and accurate strategy, showing that a general-purpose foundation model can still deliver useful 3D tumor segmentations and visualizations under minimal supervision. The paper also shows that a single mask prompt outperforms a box prompt, and that failures are more common when tumors appear as multiple small scattered lesions rather than one well-defined mass.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Duke Breast Cancer Dataset (public benchmark; pre-operative 3D breast MRI from 922 patients); MAMA-MIA (public benchmark; expert-verified voxel-level tumor segmentations; study used 279 patients and about 9,000 tumor-positive slice masks)
Baseline model/architecture: SAM2 (Segment Anything Model 2; vision-transformer-based foundation segmentation model); internal comparisons among slice-wise propagation strategies (bottom-to-top, top-to-bottom, center-outward) and prompt type (bounding box vs segmentation mask)
Training Approach: Zero-shot, inference-only, prompt-based segmentation/tracking; no task-specific training or fine-tuning in this study; a single-slice prompt is provided and the predicted mask is propagated slice-to-slice across the 3D volume
Medical Modality: MRI (3D breast MRI; pre-contrast DCE-MRI volumes)
Model input modality: Image + spatial prompt (2D axial MRI slice sequence with a single-slice bounding-box prompt; comparison experiment used image + segmentation-mask prompt)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: Volumetric Dice Similarity Coefficient (3D Dice). Exact text-reported values: mean Dice=0.57 for center-outward bounding-box tracking and mean Dice=0.71 for center-outward segmentation-mask tracking. Center-outward outperformed bottom-to-top and top-to-bottom, although exact numeric Dice values for those two strategies are shown graphically rather than tabulated in the text. Secondary analysis: weak correlations between Dice and tumor properties, with R^2=0.072 (number of tumor-containing slices), R^2=0.002 (total tumor volume), and R^2=0.141 (initial tumor area).

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Potential Tool for Predicting Surgical Margin Status in Early Breast Cancer Using Mammographic Specimen Images
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective single-center study evaluated whether ChatGPT-4 could predict R0 versus R1 surgical margin status from intraoperative/post-excision mammographic images of lumpectomy specimens in 100 patients with early-stage, non-palpable breast cancer. The goal was to test the feasibility of generative AI for rapid margin assessment in breast-conserving surgery, using histopathology as the reference standard. The main novelty is the zero-shot use of a general-purpose multimodal LLM on real specimen mammograms with a standardized prompt and metadata, plus subgroup analyses by neoadjuvant treatment and tumor invasiveness, instead of a breast-imaging model specifically trained for the task. The key takeaway is that the model was better at confirming negative margins than detecting positive ones, so it may be useful as a decision-support aid but not as a stand-alone clinical tool.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal hospital cohort from Cluj County Emergency Hospital: 100 patients with early-stage, non-palpable breast cancer and intraoperative/postoperative lumpectomy specimen mammograms extracted from PACS/DICOM, 2020-2024 (private); matched histopathology and margin-status reference labels from the same cohort (private); no public dataset; no external validation cohort
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI, March 2025 release; GPT-4 Plus multimodal interface); no separate radiology-specific baseline comparator reported
Training Approach: Zero-shot, prompt-based inference only; no fine-tuning on study data; one representative specimen mammogram per case uploaded with a standardized text prompt plus metadata such as laterality and clip/wire localization; retrospective evaluation against histopathology
Medical Modality: Specimen mammography / digital mammographic specimen radiography (X-ray); intraoperative-immediate post-excision lumpectomy specimen images
Model input modality: image + text metadata/prompt
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Accuracy=84.0% (95% CI 75.6-89.9); Sensitivity for R1=60.0% (95% CI 31.3-83.2); Specificity for R0=86.7% (95% CI 78.1-92.2); PPV=33.3% (95% CI 16.3-56.3); NPV=95.1% (95% CI 88.1-98.1); F1 score (R1)=0.43; Cohen's kappa=0.34; confusion matrix: TP=6, FP=12, FN=4, TN=78

title: Large language models in breast cancer reconstruction: A framework for patient-specific recovery and predictive insights
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper proposes an NLP-plus-LLM framework to support patient-specific recovery prediction after breast cancer reconstruction, with emphasis on postoperative complications, recovery duration, and psychosocial outcomes. The main goal is to improve individualized recovery planning by processing medical records, clinical notes, treatment histories, and related recovery variables. Its claimed novelty is the combination of standard NLP preprocessing and BioBERT feature extraction with large language models, specifically ChatGPT-4 and Gemini, to generate predictive insights and rehabilitation guidance rather than relying on manual review or generic recovery pathways. The main takeaway is that Gemini slightly outperformed ChatGPT-4 on most reported performance metrics, but the paper does not clearly describe a rigorous train-validation pipeline or external clinical validation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Breast Cancer Reconstruction Patient dataset, Kaggle (public); no private dataset or external validation cohort clearly reported
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed framework uses BioBERT for biomedical text feature extraction plus ChatGPT-4 and Gemini as the main forecasting LLMs; comparator/baseline: prior NLP system from reference [20]
Training Approach: NLP preprocessing of medical records, clinical notes, and treatment histories with data imputation, confidence scoring, lemmatization, stemming, and BioBERT embeddings/features; SHAP used for interpretability analysis. ChatGPT-4 and Gemini appear to be used in a prompt-based or inference-style comparison; the paper does not clearly report fine-tuning details, train/test split, hyperparameters, or external validation.
Medical Modality: EHR/clinical text plus structured clinical/tabular data: medical records, clinical notes, treatment history, demographics, comorbidities, psychological evaluations, and recovery outcomes; no imaging modality reported
Model input modality: text + tabular clinical data (apparently converted into textual/embedded features for downstream LLM-based prediction)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: ChatGPT-4: Accuracy=98.4%; Precision=96.2%; Recall=97.8%; F1-score=97.2%; AUROC=0.89; Score per response=2.52; Median=2.4; Mode=1.9; SD=0.72; Readability=93.0%; Relevance=95.5%; Response time=2.5 s. Gemini: Accuracy=98.7%; Precision=97.0%; Recall=98.5%; F1-score=97.9%; AUROC=0.95; Score per response=2.89; Median=2.8; Mode=2.8; SD=0.15; Readability=94.5%; Relevance=94.0%; Response time=2.4 s in Results.

title: Performance of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots in Answering Clinical Questions on Japanese Practical Guidelines for Implant-based Breast Reconstruction
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study examined whether general-purpose AI chatbots can answer clinical questions from the 2021 Japanese practical guideline for implant-based breast reconstruction. Its main goal was to compare GPT-4 and Grok against the original guideline answers using human ratings of accuracy, informativeness, and readability. The main novelty is a head-to-head evaluation in Japanese on breast reconstruction guideline questions, with repeated prompting and assessment by two evaluator groups: board-certified breast reconstruction specialists and plastic surgery fellows. The key takeaway is that GPT-4 clearly outperformed Grok and appeared acceptable to fellows, but specialists still identified meaningful gaps versus the guideline, highlighting persistent misinformation risk.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No conventional ML dataset; 5 clinical questions (CQs) taken from the 2021 Japan Society of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery (JSPRS) implant-based breast reconstruction guideline (non-public/paywalled); original JSPRS guideline answers used as control (non-public/paywalled); 10 human evaluator ratings from 5 board-certified breast reconstruction specialists and 5 plastic surgery fellows (private).
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT-4 (GPT-4); Grok-1 (Grok); original JSPRS guideline answers as non-AI control/comparator.
Training Approach: Inference-only / zero-shot prompting; no model training, fine-tuning, or domain adaptation by the authors. Each Japanese CQ was submitted 3 times in March 2024 with a simple prompt asking for an answer in Japanese, and outputs were then scored on 10-point Likert scales by the evaluators.
Medical Modality: Clinical guideline text / non-imaging clinical text
Model input modality: text-only (Japanese clinical questions)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: 10-point Likert scores averaged across 5 CQs. Plastic surgery fellows: Accuracy=7.77±0.77 (GPT-4) vs 5.57±1.19 (Grok), p<0.001; Informativeness=7.33±0.61 vs 4.93±1.52, p<0.001; Readability=7.60±0.87 vs 5.67±1.36, p<0.001. Original guideline control (fellows)=8.40±1.51 for accuracy, 8.40±1.51 for informativeness, and 8.40±1.51 for readability; Grok was significantly lower than the guideline in all three domains (all p<0.001). Breast reconstruction specialists: GPT-4 Accuracy=6.45±1.14 and Informativeness=6.70±1.34, both lower than the guideline control 8.40±1.51 (both p<0.001); GPT-4 accuracy was also rated higher by fellows than by specialists (p=0.012).

title: Assessment of Appearance-related Questions About Breast Reconstruction Generated by Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study evaluated whether ChatGPT can generate appearance-related questions that patients considering breast reconstruction could bring to consultations. Its goal was to compare AI-generated questions with questions gathered from reputable public websites, using blinded expert surgeon review rather than automatic metrics. The novelty is that it assesses generative AI as a question-generation aid for consultation preparation, not as an answer engine or imaging/planning model, and it specifically focuses on appearance-related concerns that strongly influence patient expectations. The main finding is that GPT-3.5-generated questions were broadly comparable to benchmark questions in acceptability and perceived value for informed consent and shared decision-making, and surgeons usually could not tell they were AI-generated.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No formal named dataset. ChatGPT-generated question pool (study-generated/private; 212 initial questions, 94 appearance-related after filtering, 16 final questions assessed). Benchmark web question pool from reputable online sources identified via Google (public; 407 initial questions, 64 appearance-related after filtering, 10 final questions assessed). Expert rating cohort from UT MD Anderson (private; 5 board-certified breast reconstruction surgeons).
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5, via web interface); comparator = benchmark questions from reputable online websites (non-model baseline); final assessment by blinded reconstructive surgeons.
Training Approach: Prompt engineering / inference-only; no task-specific training, fine-tuning, or model updating in this study; outputs were generated from prompts of varying specificity and then evaluated in a blinded human-review survey.
Medical Modality: Text-based breast reconstruction consultation content / patient-question prompts (non-imaging; LLM-generated plus public web-derived text)
Model input modality: Text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary expert-review outcomes: Acceptability = 15/16 ChatGPT questions acceptable (criterion: >=80% of surgeons rated acceptable); benchmark = 9/10. Positive contribution to informed consent = 15/16 ChatGPT questions (criterion: median Likert >=3); benchmark = 10/10. Positive contribution to shared decision-making = 16/16 ChatGPT questions (criterion: median Likert >=3); benchmark = 10/10. AI-identification test = 12/16 ChatGPT questions were not identified as AI-generated by surgeons. Additional reported readability result: median Flesch Reading Ease of the 15 acceptable ChatGPT questions = 59.7.

title: Enhancing patient education in breast surgery: artificial intelligence-powered guidance for mastopexy, augmentation, reduction, and reconstruction
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This prospective observational study evaluates whether ChatGPT-4 can support peri-operative patient education for four breast surgery procedures: mastopexy, augmentation, reduction, and reconstruction. The main goal was to test how well the model answers real-world frequently asked patient questions using four quality dimensions: relevance, accuracy, clarity, and empathy. What is novel is that the paper focuses on breast-surgery-specific peri-operative counseling, uses procedure-specific FAQs collected from actual pre- and post-operative consultations and records, and has responses rated by a multidisciplinary panel including surgeons, a nurse, and prior patients. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT-4 performed consistently well, with clarity scoring highest, but it still lacks personalization and real-time clinical updating; therefore it should be used as an adjunct to clinician counseling rather than a replacement. This paper is more about patient education and communication than technical surgical planning itself.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No named public benchmark dataset; internally collected FAQ corpus from patients undergoing mastopexy, breast augmentation, breast reduction, and breast reconstruction, gathered from direct patient interviews, medical-record review, and documented questions during pre-operative consultations and immediate post-operative follow-up in plastic/reconstructive breast surgery clinics (private).
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI large language model; ChatGPT Plus, dialogue mode); no separate AI baseline/comparator architecture was evaluated.
Training Approach: Prompt-based inference-only evaluation; no task-specific training or fine-tuning reported. Frequently asked questions were posed to ChatGPT-4 in dialogue mode, and outputs were prospectively assessed on 1-5 Likert scales by 3 plastic surgeons, 1 surgery-specialized nurse, and 2 prior breast-surgery patients. Statistical analysis used means, standard deviations, and Kruskal-Wallis testing.
Medical Modality: Textual peri-operative breast-surgery consultation data and patient-education Q&A content derived from interviews and medical records.
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary evaluation on 1-5 expert/patient ratings. Overall means: Relevance=4.75±0.06; Accuracy=4.75±0.06; Clarity=4.85±0.06; Empathy=4.75±0.06. Kruskal-Wallis: statistic=5.76; P=0.12. Procedure-level scores (Relevance/Accuracy/Clarity/Empathy): Mastopexy=4.80/4.70/4.80/4.70; Breast augmentation=4.70/4.80/4.90/4.80; Breast reduction=4.70/4.70/4.80/4.70; Breast reconstruction=4.80/4.80/4.90/4.80.

title: A Study on Breast Cancer Patient Care Using Chatbot and Video Education for Radiation Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This randomized controlled trial evaluated whether digital patient education using a chatbot and video could reduce anxiety in postoperative breast cancer patients undergoing radiation therapy. The goal was to compare four education combinations - video+chatbot, video+paper, paper+chatbot, and paper+paper - across the radiation course using APAIS as the primary endpoint and STAI/LASA as secondary endpoints. The main novelty was a 4-arm clinical evaluation of a Kakao-platform chatbot plus video workflow tailored to breast radiation therapy, with additional analysis of question-click patterns and age-related differences in digital uptake. The main takeaway was that no significant overall between-group benefit was found, but a per-protocol subgroup of patients age <=50 years showed significant APAIS improvement, especially in the video+chatbot arm; this is a rule-based chatbot intervention rather than a true generative-AI or surgical-planning system.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Severance Hospital / Yonsei Cancer Center postoperative breast cancer RT randomized trial cohort (private; 148 randomized, 145 analyzed); internal FAQ, intent, and entity corpus derived from interviews with clinicians and patients for chatbot design (private); no public dataset; no external validation cohort.
Baseline model/architecture: Rule-based decision-tree chatbot built on the Kakao Corp. chatbot platform with intent classification and entity recognition; comparator arms were educational video and paper handouts.
Training Approach: Manually curated FAQ knowledge base and educational content; entities extracted from clinician/patient interviews; expected user utterances manually authored for intent classification; platform-assisted ML used for intent classification/entity recognition within a rule-based decision-tree flow; no generative model, no reported end-to-end fine-tuning, and no external model validation.
Medical Modality: Non-imaging clinical education and patient-reported outcome questionnaires (APAIS, STAI, LASA); digital educational media included video and chatbot text.
Model input modality: Text-only plus structured menu/button selections for the chatbot; questionnaire responses for outcome assessment.

title: Chat-ePRO: Development and pilot study of an electronic patient-reported outcomes system based on ChatGPT
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addressed low compliance and limited flexibility in conventional electronic patient-reported outcome systems used in breast-surgery follow-up. The goal was to build and pilot-test Chat-ePRO, a ChatGPT-based conversational ePRO system that asks questionnaire items in natural language and extracts structured responses automatically. Its main novelty is combining prompt-engineered GPT-3.5-turbo for question/response generation with offline knowledge distillation to a multilingual BERT option extractor, then comparing the system in practice against both form-based and rule-based chatbot ePRO workflows. The main takeaway is that LLM-based conversational ePRO was feasible and improved real-world response rate, but physician oversight was still needed because of incomplete answers, safety concerns, and privacy/deployment limitations.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: FACT-B questionnaire/item set (public); BIBCQ questionnaire/item set (public); TMI questionnaire/item set (public); Chinese Medical Dialogue Dataset (public); ChatGPT-generated and manually reviewed/annotated virtual doctor-patient dialogue corpora derived from FACT-B/BIBCQ/TMI (private/internal synthetic); Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital breast surgery pilot cohort across 3 deployment phases, total n=256 and Chat-ePRO subgroup n=10 (private)
Baseline model/architecture: Main system: ChatGPT/GPT-3.5-turbo for question and response generation; multilingual BERT for option extraction with three variants: multi-label classification, semantic matching, and contrastive learning; SimCSE for memory selection. Comparators/baselines: zero-shot and few-shot ChatGPT for extraction, plus form-based ePRO and rule-based chatbot ePRO in the pilot study.
Training Approach: Prompt engineering and inference-time prompting for GPT-3.5-turbo; ChatGPT-generated synthetic doctor-patient dialogues with manual review and semi-automated annotation; offline knowledge distillation into multilingual BERT; supervised fine-tuning of BERT on multi-label classification, semantic matching, and contrastive-learning tasks; sequential real-world pilot deployment for workflow comparison.
Medical Modality: Patient-reported outcome questionnaires and clinical conversational text in a mobile ePRO setting (no imaging)
Model input modality: text-only: questionnaire item text, option list, dialogue history, and patient replies (free-text or fixed-option text)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Text-generation success rate=95.7% (4.3% error over 4,144 generated dialogues); best option extraction on TMI with contrastive-learning BERT: Precision=0.96, Recall=0.95, Macro-F1=0.95; subjective positive ratings from 3 breast surgeons: Accuracy=76.2%, Completeness=75.7%, Comprehension=82.6%, Consistency/Stability=80.3%, Security=73.6%; pilot outcomes for Chat-ePRO: Response rate=90.0% (9/10) vs rule-based chatbot 78.7% (137/174) and form-based 56.9% (41/72), average dialogue turns/item=1.52, average time/turn=10.86 s, free-text usage=91.9% (102/111).

title: Automated Extraction of Patient-Centered Outcomes After Breast Cancer Treatment: An Open-Source Large Language Model-Based Toolkit
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles the problem of extracting breast cancer treatment-related patient-centered outcomes (PCOs) from unstructured clinical notes, focusing on fatigue, nausea, anxiety, depression, and lymphedema. The goal was to build an open-source LLM-based toolkit that can automatically identify these outcomes from routine oncology and nursing documentation across institutions. The main novelty is the head-to-head comparison of zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned open-source LLMs for a breast-cancer-specific clinical information extraction task, with both internal and external validation. The key finding is that off-the-shelf prompting performed poorly, while task-specific fine-tuning substantially improved performance; notably, the smaller GPT-2 model outperformed the larger BioGPT and PMC-LLaMA models after adaptation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Mayo Clinic breast cancer cohort (private; training + internal test; annotated split: 3,924 train notes, 1,450 test notes); Emory University Hospital/EUH breast cancer cohort (private; external test; 474 notes); Stanford University breast cancer cohort (private; external test; 525 notes)
Baseline model/architecture: Decoder-only Transformer LLMs: GPT-2, BioGPT, PMC-LLaMA; fine-tuned GPT-2 was the best-performing model overall
Training Approach: Prompt-based binary classification for each PCO (Yes/No) using text snippets extracted from clinical notes; experiments included zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning, full supervised fine-tuning of GPT-2 and BioGPT on Mayo data, and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning of PMC-LLaMA; inference compared label-token likelihoods rather than relying on free-form generation
Medical Modality: EHR free-text clinical notes (oncology notes and nursing notes)
Model input modality: text-only (keyword-retrieved multi-sentence note snippets from clinical narratives)

title: Automated Identification of Breast Cancer Relapse in Computed Tomography Reports Using Natural Language Processing
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the lack of systematic breast cancer relapse capture in routine registries by automating relapse detection from unstructured follow-up CT reports. Its goal was to identify any relapse as well as local, regional, and distant relapse in curatively treated breast cancer patients using NLP. The main novelty is a BlueBERT-based transformer pipeline tailored to unstructured CT text, using section-aware report segmentation and separate classifiers for local, regional, distant, and any relapse, whereas prior work had focused more on structured CT reports or only distant relapse. The main takeaway is that the approach performed strongly for any-relapse and distant-relapse detection, but local and regional relapse sensitivity was lower because those events were rare in CT reports; overall, this is a post-treatment relapse-surveillance study rather than a preoperative surgical-planning system.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal British Columbia/BC Cancer population-based cohort of follow-up CT radiology reports from curatively treated breast cancer patients (1,445 reports from 887 patients; private), sampled within a 120-day window of known documented relapse to enrich positive cases; curated provincial population-based relapse database used for case/window identification (private)
Baseline model/architecture: BlueBERT (BERT-based transformer pretrained on PubMed abstracts and MIMIC-III clinical notes); separate binary classifiers for any relapse, local relapse, regional relapse, and distant relapse; no external comparator baseline reported
Training Approach: Supervised transfer learning/fine-tuning on manually annotated CT report text (4 annotators; 200 reports double-annotated with >95% agreement); regex-based segmentation selected Impression first, otherwise Findings, otherwise full report; appended +/-3-word context around metastasis/malignancy terms outside the selected section; tokenized with the BlueBERT tokenizer; oversampled Relapse-Present and undersampled Relapse-Absent, merged Relapse-Uncertain with Relapse-Present during training; random hyperparameter search on a 90/10 train-validation split; final evaluation with 10-fold cross-validation
Medical Modality: CT (unstructured follow-up radiology reports)
Model input modality: text-only (segmented CT report text from Impression/Findings sections with appended keyword context)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: 10-fold cross-validation main results: Any relapse-Accuracy=89.6%, Sensitivity=93.2%, Specificity=84.2%, AUC=0.910; Local relapse-Accuracy=94.6%, Sensitivity=44.4%, Specificity=97.2%, AUC=0.781; Regional relapse-Accuracy=93.6%, Sensitivity=70.1%, Specificity=95.3%, AUC=0.886; Distant relapse-Accuracy=88.1%, Sensitivity=91.8%, Specificity=83.7%, AUC=0.947

title: Exploring the use of large language models for classification, clinical interpretation, and treatment recommendation in breast tumor patient records
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study investigated whether large language models can classify breast tumors, generate clinical interpretations, and recommend treatment from de-identified patient records. The main goal was a head-to-head comparison of GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and DeepSeek-V3 on real-world breast tumor cases using both objective classification metrics and expert clinician scoring. A notable difference from much prior work is that it evaluates complete structured clinical records with three breast surgical oncologists rating interpretability and treatment usefulness, rather than relying only on abstract benchmarks or image-based tasks. The main takeaway is that GPT-4o performed best for benign-vs-malignant classification, whereas DeepSeek-R1 produced the most clinically preferred and consistent disease interpretations and treatment recommendations; however, the evidence is limited by a small single-center private Chinese cohort and no task-specific fine-tuning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Taizhou Cancer Hospital breast tumor cohort, Jan-Apr 2024 (private; single-center retrospective clinical records; n=45; not publicly available, available on reasonable request)
Baseline model/architecture: GPT-4o; DeepSeek-R1; DeepSeek-V3 (pretrained proprietary LLM APIs; no conventional non-LLM baseline)
Training Approach: Inference-only / zero-shot prompt-based evaluation on standardized de-identified clinical case texts; same system prompt and user prompt across models; temperature=0.7; no fine-tuning or additional training on study data
Medical Modality: Clinical records / EHR text (demographics, chief complaint, present illness, past history, personal/family history, reproductive-menstrual history, physical examination, preoperative assessments including laboratory results and radiology reports)
Model input modality: text-only (structured clinical text compiled from records; diagnosis name, histologic subtype, cancer stage, and treatment-related information excluded from input)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Objective tumor classification: GPT-4o AUC=0.848, Accuracy=0.911, Sensitivity=0.750, Specificity=0.946, F1=0.946; DeepSeek-R1 AUC=0.736, Accuracy=0.889, Sensitivity=0.500, Specificity=0.973, F1=0.935; DeepSeek-V3 AUC=0.723, Accuracy=0.867, Sensitivity=0.500, Specificity=0.946, F1=0.921. DeLong test p-values: GPT-4o vs DeepSeek-R1=0.4601; GPT-4o vs DeepSeek-V3=0.4010; DeepSeek-R1 vs DeepSeek-V3=0.5689. Subjective doctor ratings (mean±SD): disease interpretation—GPT-4o 4.46±0.66, DeepSeek-R1 4.73±0.46, DeepSeek-V3 4.19±0.68; treatment recommendation—GPT-4o 4.38±0.63, DeepSeek-R1 4.70±0.51, DeepSeek-V3 4.30±0.57.

title: Leveraging Guideline-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems with Large Language Models: A Case Study with Breast Cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study investigated whether open-source LLMs can automatically answer OncoDoc2 questions from narrative breast cancer patient summaries to support guideline-based management of non-metastatic breast cancer at multidisciplinary tumor boards. The main goal was to use LLMs as a question-answering layer that navigates the existing OncoDoc2 decision tree and then generates patient-specific therapeutic recommendations. What is novel is the use of real-world BCPSs from routine care, local/open-source LLM deployment for privacy, comparison of multiple prompt-engineering strategies, per-question model combination, and explicit consideration of ecological impact. The main takeaway is that LLMs achieved moderate-to-good question-answering accuracy, but small navigation errors propagated through the decision tree and caused poor agreement in final treatment recommendations, so the approach was not reliable enough as a standalone CDSS.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Breast Cancer Patient Summaries (BCPSs) from Tenon Hospital data warehouse (private; n=230 total, with 20 for model selection, 200 for evaluation, 30 for validation); OncoDoc2 MTB decision spreadsheet from Tenon Hospital (private; n=1,886 decisions, 69 attributes). No public dataset or external validation cohort.
Baseline model/architecture: Open-source transformer LLMs: Mistral 7B and OpenChat 7B (selected best pair); additional compared models: Orca2 7B, Gemma 7B, Llama 7B; Mixtral 8x7B additionally tested. Guideline engine/comparator: OncoDoc2 decision tree; gold standard: MTB clinician navigation through OncoDoc2.
Training Approach: No task-specific fine-tuning on the study data; inference-only prompt engineering in French using Zero-Shot, Enhanced Zero-Shot, and Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought. Models were deployed locally via Ollama. The study selected the best-performing models on 20 BCPSs, then used per-question best-model switching/combination of Mistral + OpenChat for the main evaluation on 200 BCPSs and internal validation on 30 BCPSs.
Medical Modality: Multi-source clinical text derived from EHR reports: pathology reports, imaging reports, operative reports, and communication sheets/clinical notes.
Model input modality: text-only (French BCPS narrative + OncoDoc2 question + answer options)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Question-answering task, evaluation cohort (200 BCPSs; 3,142 prompts): combined Mistral+OpenChat with Enhanced Zero-Shot achieved Precision=59.05%, Recall=54.40%, F1=56.35%, Accuracy=77.05%. Recommendation conformity on evaluation cohort: identical=17.91%, comparable=19.40%, different=62.68%. Internal validation cohort (30 BCPSs): Precision=60.16%, Recall=54.18%, F1=56.59%, Accuracy=75.57%; recommendation conformity: identical=3.34%, comparable=13.33%, different=83.33%.

title: Challenging ChatGPT 3.5 in Senology—An Assessment of Concordance with Breast Cancer Tumor Board Decision Making
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This observational pilot study evaluated whether the public LLM ChatGPT 3.5 can match breast cancer multidisciplinary tumor board recommendations using 20 study-designed patient profiles spanning luminal, HER2-positive, triple-negative, DCIS, and inflammatory cases. The goal was to extend prior small studies by using a richer standardized prompt, broader pathologic and immunomorphologic diversity—including primary metastasis and precancerous stages—and separate assessment of surgical, endocrine, chemotherapy, radiation, and genetic-testing recommendations. The main novelty is the use of detailed synthetic profiles plus an extended structured input model to test concordance per patient profile and per treatment option against a real German tumor board. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT 3.5 showed partial concordance, with stronger agreement for chemotherapy and radiation recommendations than for endocrine therapy and genetic testing, but it also made clinically problematic errors and over-recommendations, so the authors judged it unsuitable as a tumor-board support tool in its current public form.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Study-specific synthetic breast cancer patient profiles P1–P20 based on DGGG guideline-defined immunohistochemical/molecular subtypes and nodal/menopausal strata (private/non-public synthetic cases; not real patients). No public benchmark dataset or external validation cohort was used.
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI large language model); comparator/reference standard: actual multidisciplinary tumor board (MTB) of a German gynecologic oncology center.
Training Approach: No task-specific training on study data. Inference-only / zero-shot prompting of ChatGPT 3.5 with a blinded, randomized, extended structured text input model; outputs compared descriptively against MTB recommendations. No fine-tuning, retraining, or external model adaptation was reported.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal structured clinicopathologic data summarized as text: pathology/histology, immunohistochemistry and molecular subtype markers (ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67), TNM staging, resection margin, surgical history, menopausal status, ECOG, comorbidities, birth history, and oncological family history; no direct imaging input.
Model input modality: text-only (structured case vignettes / prompts in German after translation of the blinded input model)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: concordance with MTB recommendations. Overall concordance across all 20 patient profiles = 50.0% (10/20); concordance for invasive breast cancer profiles = 58.8% (10/17). Excluding genetic testing, overall concordance = 68.4% (13/19) and invasive breast cancer concordance = 81.25% (13/16). Per-treatment concordance: ST = 95.0%, ET = 75.0%, CT = 94.7% (18/19; main text also states 94.5%), RT = 95.0%, GT = 70.0%. Recommendation frequency, LLM vs MTB: ST 2 vs 3, ET 13 vs 8, CT 13 vs 11, RT 16 vs 15, GT 17 vs 11.

title: Evaluation of large language models in breast cancer clinical scenarios: a comparative analysis based on ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4.0, and Claude2
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This cross-sectional study evaluated GPT-3.5, GPT-4.0, and Claude2 across nine simulated breast cancer clinical scenarios spanning assessment/diagnosis, treatment decision-making, postoperative care, psychosocial support, and prognosis/rehabilitation. The main goal was to compare the quality, relevance, and clinical applicability of LLM outputs using blinded ratings from five breast cancer specialists. Its novelty is a scenario-based clinical evaluation in breast cancer rather than a standard benchmark test, and the authors position it as the first breast-cancer-context assessment of Claude2. The main takeaway is that GPT-4.0 performed best overall, Claude2 showed some niche strength in assessment/diagnosis, and all models still produced guideline-misaligned or oversimplified advice; therefore, the paper is relevant to clinical support around breast cancer but is not a dedicated breast-surgery planning system.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No named public benchmark dataset. The study used 9 researcher-designed simulated breast cancer clinical scenario prompts across 5 domains (private/internal) and blinded expert ratings from 5 breast cancer specialists (private/internal). The paper states that the study-generated data were not publicly available and were available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
Baseline model/architecture: Comparative closed-source LLM chatbots: GPT-4.0, GPT-3.5, and Claude2; no separate conventional ML baseline or surgical-planning architecture.
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt-based evaluation; no fine-tuning or retraining reported. Each case question was submitted as a separate query, the conversation was reset after each query to reduce memory bias, outputs were converted to plain text and randomly shuffled, and 5 blinded specialists scored quality, relevance, and applicability. Final scores were determined by majority consensus, with the lowest score assigned when no scorer consensus emerged.
Medical Modality: Textual simulated breast cancer clinical scenarios / clinical narratives (non-imaging; no direct radiology/pathology dataset input)
Model input modality: text-only
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Inter-rater reliability: Fleiss kappa=0.345 (95% CI 0.295-0.394; P<0.05). Mean overall Quality score: GPT-4.0=3.56±0.55, GPT-3.5=2.87±0.69, Claude2=3.18±0.72. Mean overall Relevance score: GPT-4.0=3.44±0.59, GPT-3.5=2.78±0.56, Claude2=3.13±0.59. Mean overall Applicability score: GPT-4.0=2.73±0.45, GPT-3.5=2.13±0.34, Claude2=2.49±0.51. Pairwise overall comparisons: GPT-4.0 vs GPT-3.5 P=0.001 for quality, relevance, and applicability; GPT-4.0 vs Claude2 P=0.0196 (quality), 0.0315 (relevance), 0.0243 (applicability).

title: The Potential of Gemini and GPTs for Structured Report Generation based on Free-Text 18F-FDG PET/CT Breast Cancer Reports
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study compares a customized GPT-4-based GPTs tool against Gemini 1.0 Pro for converting pairs of longitudinal free-text 18F-FDG PET/CT breast cancer reports into structured reports. The goal was to automatically extract primary lesion details, metastatic lesions, and an overall disease-progression summary aligned with RECIST/PERCIST-style reasoning. A key novelty is the end-to-end workflow that merges two follow-up reports into a three-section structured output using user-defined prompts plus regex post-processing, rather than training a conventional task-specific medical NLP model. The main takeaway is that customized GPTs consistently outperformed Gemini in numeric data extraction, metastatic lesion identification, progression decision-making, and semantic similarity to physician-authored reports, suggesting practical value for structured reporting rather than direct surgical planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Internal institutional retrospective free-text 18F-FDG PET/CT breast cancer report cohort (private; July 2005-Oct 2023; 2156 reports from 1962 patients screened, 262 reports from 131 patients analyzed as the two most recent reports per patient); prompt-optimization subset of 20 reports from 10 patients (private); manually physician-annotated structured reports/reference standard (private).
Baseline model/architecture: Customized GPTs built on GPT-4 (main system); Gemini 1.0 Pro comparator; regex-based post-processing pipeline; physician-authored structured reports as gold standard.
Training Approach: Prompt engineering / inference-only LLM workflow; 20 reports from 10 patients used to iteratively optimize user-defined instructions/tasks; no gradient-based model training or fine-tuning reported; outputs were standardized with regular-expression post-processing.
Medical Phase (pre/post): both (comparative follow-up reports included pre-op only, pre/post-op, and post-op report pairs).
Medical Modality: 18F-FDG PET/CT (multi-modal PET + CT; whole-body imaging).
Model input modality: text-only (two longitudinal free-text PET/CT reports plus imaging dates and task instructions; no image pixels used).
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary lesion extraction accuracy (GPTs vs Gemini): location 95.8% vs 93.1%; treatment 95.8% vs 95.4%; size 89.6% vs 53.8%; SUV 84.2% vs 78.1%. Primary lesion progression F1 (improving/stable/progressing): GPTs 0.90/0.91/0.91 vs Gemini 0.73/0.75/0.64 (all p<0.001). Total metastatic lesion identification (GPTs vs Gemini): Sensitivity 96.3% vs 78.9%; Specificity 96.3% vs 92.8%; Accuracy 96.3% vs 89.6% (p<0.001). Lung metastasis identification: Sensitivity 90.9% vs 95.5%; Specificity 99.1% vs 83.9%; Accuracy 98.4% vs 84.9% (p<0.001). Metastatic lesion progression F1 (improving/stable/progressing): GPTs 0.90/0.92/0.97 vs Gemini 0.53/0.58/0.87 (all p<0.001). Overall patient condition F1 (improving/stable/progressing): GPTs 0.89/0.86/0.97 vs Gemini 0.57/0.52/0.80 (all p<0.001). BERTScore (GPTs vs Gemini): Precision 94.0% vs 90.7%; Recall 92.0% vs 91.0%; F1 0.930 vs 0.907 (p<0.001).

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for imaging modality selection: Potential to reduce unnecessary contrast agent use and radiation exposure
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This cross-sectional benchmarking study asked whether current large language models can choose the most appropriate imaging modality for clinical scenarios and thereby help avoid unnecessary contrast use and radiation exposure. The main goal was to compare multiple vendor LLMs against clinicians from different specialties and radiologists with different experience levels using both guideline-based ACR scenarios and more realistic multifactorial scenarios. What is novel is the direct multi-vendor comparison, inclusion of DeepSeek-R1 versus DeepSeek-V3 to probe the effect of reasoning, targeted analysis of contrast-agent and X-ray avoidance, prompt-robustness testing across three prompts, and short- and long-term reproducibility checks. The main takeaway is that LLMs, especially DeepSeek-R1, performed at or near junior-radiologist level and outperformed clinicians on many tasks, but the evidence comes from text-only non-patient scenarios with possible ACR contamination, so real-world validation is still needed.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: ACR Appropriateness Criteria-derived clinical scenarios, n=120 (public); Multifaceted Practice-Oriented Clinical Scenarios (MPCS), n=120 (private, author-generated, non-patient); the same 120 ACR scenarios were reused for short- and long-term reproducibility testing.
Baseline model/architecture: DeepSeek-R1 (reasoning-enabled DeepSeek-V3), DeepSeek-V3, ChatGPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet; human comparators: emergency physician, cardiologist, internist, general surgeon, junior radiology resident, senior radiology resident, junior radiologist, senior radiologist.
Training Approach: Inference-only evaluation; standardized zero-shot role-based prompting with 3 prompt variants; default web-interface hyperparameters; no author fine-tuning or additional pretraining; all scenarios entered sequentially in a single chat session per model; reasoning explicitly activated for DeepSeek-R1; reproducibility retested after 2 weeks and 4 months.
Medical Modality: Multi-modality imaging referral/selection task across breast, cardiac, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neuro, thoracic, genitourinary, and vascular sections; candidate modalities included MRI, CT, ultrasound, X-ray-containing imaging, angiography, and related contrast/non-contrast variants.
Model input modality: text-only clinical scenarios plus prompt instructions
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Across prompts, all models gave identical recommendations for each scenario: κ=1. Best ACR result: DeepSeek-R1 identified usually/may-be-appropriate modalities in 98.3% of cases; Table 1 reports median=3 (IQR 3-3), mean=2.89 ± 0.36. MPCS: DeepSeek-R1 median=3 (IQR 3-3), mean=2.88 ± 0.43; it outperformed DeepSeek-V3 (p=0.001), Claude 3 Opus (p<0.001), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (p=0.003), and all clinicians (p<0.001), while matching junior radiologist (p=0.099) and senior radiologist (p=0.503). Contrast-not-appropriate scenarios (n=43): DeepSeek-R1 mean=4.78 ± 0.148, with 86% score-5 responses. X-ray-not-appropriate scenarios (n=25): DeepSeek-R1 mean=4.88 ± 0.120, with 92% score-5 responses. Reproducibility for models reported in Table 9: short-term κ=0.773-0.886; long-term κ=0.727-0.787.

title: Implementing a chatbot to promote hereditary breast & ovarian cancer genetic screening in women's health: identifying barriers and facilitators to screening adoption
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: Real-world implementation study of Gia®, an AI chatbot used in OB/GYN care to screen women for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk. The goal was to understand why eligible women in a rural UF Health setting adopted or declined chatbot-based screening before broader rollout, using interviews with both adopters and non-adopters. The novelty is the implementation-science focus on barriers and facilitators for adoption of a deployed clinical chatbot rather than development of a new predictive model. Main takeaway: adoption depended on perceived cancer risk, clinician communication, convenience, cost/insurance concerns, trust in privacy/accuracy, and prior genetic-testing experience; clinician discussion was the most actionable facilitator.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No named public dataset; UF Health Women’s Health/OB-GYN internal patient cohort offered Gia screening (private); private qualitative interview dataset of 17 women (9 adopters, 8 non-adopters) recruited via MyChart/Qualtrics (private); verbatim interview transcripts totaling 123 pages (private).
Baseline model/architecture: Gia® (Genetic Information Assistant), a HIPAA-compliant and SOC2-certified AI chatbot/conversational agent; NLP-based functionality is mentioned, but the underlying architecture/backbone is not disclosed; no formal baseline/comparator model.
Training Approach: No model training or fine-tuning reported in this paper; existing commercial chatbot deployed in routine care (inference-only/implementation study). The study itself used semi-structured interviews plus a rapid analysis template and deductive+inductive thematic analysis with constant comparative coding.
Medical Modality: Non-imaging women’s health/genetic risk screening; personal and family cancer history collected through a digital chatbot.
Model input modality: Text / structured questionnaire-style patient responses about personal and family cancer history.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: No AI model-performance metrics such as Accuracy, AUC, Dice, or F1 were reported. Implementation outcomes reported: ~45% uptake among ~957 invited patients; 42% of adopters met NCCN criteria for genetic testing; interview cohort n=17 with 9 adopters and 8 non-adopters; thematic saturation reported with themes emerging by 56% of participants on average and up to 94%.

title: Towards utilizing robust radiance fields for 3D reconstruction of breast aesthetics
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This proof-of-concept paper studies whether modern radiance-field methods can reconstruct clinically useful 3D models of external breast aesthetics from ordinary multi-view video instead of expensive dedicated 3D capture systems. The goals are to benchmark six state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction paradigms on breast-surface data, identify the most clinically practical baseline, and improve robustness under noisy backgrounds, imperfect geometry, and reduced view counts. Its main novelty is threefold: it is the first reported application of radiance fields to exterior breast-aesthetics reconstruction; it introduces Depth-Splatfacto, a Splatfacto variant with image-level pseudo-depth supervision and alpha-clamping to improve denoising and geometric consistency; and it extends training to grayscale by collapsing the spherical-harmonic radiance representation to one channel and reducing seed-point density for faster, lighter training. The main takeaway is that standard Splatfacto achieves the best overall fidelity and speed in the full-data setting, while Depth-Splatfacto trades a small amount of PSNR for markedly sharper and more stable reconstructions, especially with fewer frames. The study is still preliminary because it uses a private single-patient dataset, relies on pseudo-depth rather than true 3D surface ground truth, and has no external validation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Champalimaud Foundation breast cancer patient torso video dataset (private; single patient; entire torso of a breast cancer patient acquired under controlled lighting; 181 extracted frames at 1550x741; data available upon request). Auxiliary generated supervision is not a separate benchmark dataset but includes COLMAP-estimated camera poses and sparse point clouds, RMBG v1.4 foreground masks, and Depth Anything V2 pseudo-depth maps. A separate unnamed human sample dataset was used only for background-segmenter screening and appears private/internal.
Baseline model/architecture: Comparative models: Nerfacto, Instant-NGP, Splatfacto, NeuS-facto, BakedAngelo, NeuS-facto-Angelo. Proposed architecture: Depth-Splatfacto built on Splatfacto and 3D Gaussian Splatting, adding a depth-supervised multi-head design with image-level depth consistency.
