Key preprocessing/backbone modules: COLMAP for camera pose estimation and sparse seed points, RMBG v1.4 for background removal, Depth Anything V2 for pseudo-depth estimation, and custom 1-channel/3-channel GSplat kernels for grayscale versus RGB training.
Training Approach: Supervised multi-view radiance-field reconstruction in Nerfstudio. Main benchmark compared six models on the same 181-frame sequence up to 200k iterations. Depth-Splatfacto optimizes RGB MSE plus a berHu depth loss between rendered depth or accumulation and pseudo-depth maps. The full-image datamanager batches RGB images, aligned depth maps, and poses. An alpha-clamping heuristic was enabled after 500 steps to suppress artifacts and improve foreground-background separation. Preprocessing includes frame extraction from video, background masking, pseudo-depth generation, and COLMAP pose estimation. A grayscale variant collapses the spherical-harmonic radiance representation to one channel, reduces Gaussian seed-point initialization density to one-eighth, and applies lightweight LAB color fusion after training for RGB visualization. Additional ablations test depth estimator choice, background segmenter choice, and robustness under reduced-frame settings of 91, 46, and 23 images.
Medical Phase (pre/post): both/unclear; the paper targets breast reconstruction aesthetic visualization for surgical planning and outcome communication, but it does not explicitly state whether the imaged patient is preoperative or postoperative
Medical Modality: Surface photography and video-based external breast and torso surface imaging for breast-aesthetics reconstruction
Model input modality: Multi-view RGB video frames or images; Depth-Splatfacto additionally uses pseudo-depth maps and camera poses or sparse point-cloud seeds; a grayscale training variant uses 1-channel images during training with post hoc color fusion for visualization
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main 6-model benchmark at 200k iterations: best model Splatfacto achieved PSNR=27.11, SSIM=0.942, LPIPS=0.163 and was the fastest model, reported as about 1.3x faster at 200k iterations. The paper also states volumetric methods outperformed surface-based methods overall, with NeuS-facto-Angelo being the best within the surface-based group. Depth estimator ablation: ZoeDepth PSNR=9.59, SSIM=0.842, LPIPS=0.435, training time=544.72 s versus Depth Anything V2 PSNR=26.41, SSIM=0.939, LPIPS=0.192, training time=310.55 s. Background-segmenter ablation using PSNR and inference time: RMBG v1.4=31.82 and 0.585 s, BEN2=27.77 and 0.448 s, BiRefNet=30.31 and 0.788 s, Finegrain=12.97 and 13.211 s. Depth supervision on Splatfacto at 100k iterations: Splatfacto PSNR=27.72 with variation 3.07, SSIM=0.944 with variation 0.010, LPIPS=0.1653 with variation 0.025, VoL=0.24; Depth-Splatfacto PSNR=26.72 with variation 2.81, SSIM=0.942 with variation 0.009, LPIPS=0.1651 with variation 0.026, VoL=0.92. Grayscale training reduced time from 7967 s to 4979 s, about 1.6x faster, with PSNR dropping from 27.11 to 26.41. Sparse-frame study at 10k iterations, Depth-Splatfacto versus Splatfacto: 91 frames PSNR 25.75 versus 26.95, LPIPS 0.212 versus 0.217, VoL 0.65 versus 0.03; 46 frames 25.48 versus 26.74, 0.199 versus 0.204, 0.72 versus 0.08; 23 frames 14.18 versus 14.18, 0.417 versus 0.416, 0.90 versus 0.10. Efficiency note: Depth-Splatfacto used about 1.5x more memory than baseline at 10k iterations, 41.1 MB versus 27.6 MB.

title: Breast3D: An augmented reality system for breast CT and MRI
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper presents Breast3D, a prototype extended-reality breast imaging system designed to reconstruct breast CT and MRI data into an interactive real 3D space rather than forcing radiologists to inspect volumetric data only on flat 2D monitors. The main goal is not classification or report generation, but better diagnostic and planning-oriented visualization for tasks such as exploring dense breasts, reducing cancer masking, supporting BI-RADS-related risk assessment thinking, enabling multi-disciplinary team discussion, and potentially improving surgical planning workflows. Its novelty lies in combining volumetric reconstruction with a controller-free XR interaction layer: hand-tracked manipulation, voice-command-based reorientation, 3D axis-aligned slicing, and in-volume point-of-interest annotation with absolute x/y/z positioning. Technically, the system reconstructs CT/MRI slice stacks into voxelized proxy geometry and renders them using volumetric ray-casting with interpolation and early ray termination. The paper is mainly a systems/proof-of-concept contribution showing feasibility and interaction design, not a clinically validated diagnostic AI model.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No named clinical dataset is formally described. The paper demonstrates use of breast CT and MRI volumetric data, and the figures include at least one BI-RADS 6 breast MRI example with a biopsy-proven mass. Cohort size, institution/source, case count, split strategy, and whether the data are public or private are not reported.
Baseline model/architecture: No learned baseline model is evaluated. Proposed architecture: Unity-based Breast3D XR viewer deployed on Microsoft HoloLens and stated as portable to other XR headsets such as HTC Vive; voxel reconstruction from stacked 2D CT/MRI textures inside proxy cube geometry; volumetric ray-casting renderer; Microsoft MRTK-based hand tracking, gesture recognition, voice commands, 3D UI, and annotation. The closest prior system discussed is D3D, an earlier AR breast-diagnosis viewer with basic volumetric rendering and joystick-based interaction, but there is no direct quantitative head-to-head benchmark.
Training Approach: No model training or fine-tuning is involved. This is a deterministic implementation pipeline: 2D CT/MRI slices are stacked into a voxel-based volume in proxy geometry, then rendered with ray-marched volumetric ray-casting using alpha compositing via the over operator, interpolation between sample points, and early ray termination for computational savings. Interaction is implemented with adapted Microsoft MRTK modules for controllerless hand gestures, voice commands, UI-based axis slicing, zoom/rotation/color adjustment, and point annotation.
Medical Modality: Breast CT and breast MRI within an XR/AR visualization workflow for diagnostic review, volume exploration, MDT discussion, and possible planning support.
Model input modality: Imaging-only; stack of 2D CT/MRI slices or textures reconstructed into a 3D voxel volume for XR visualization. Voice commands, hand gestures, and annotations are interaction inputs, not predictive model inputs.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: No formal quantitative evaluation is reported. The paper provides no diagnostic accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, Dice, user-study performance score, or external validation. Evaluation is qualitative only: the figures demonstrate successful 3D rendering, hand/voice-guided reorientation, annotation, axis-aligned slicing, and qualitative isolation of a tumour/region of interest in a BI-RADS 6 breast MRI example.

title: A disentangled approach to predict the aesthetic outcomes of breast cancer treatment
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper aims to predict patient-specific aesthetic outcomes of breast cancer locoregional treatment by morphing a pre-operative breast photograph with treatment-related asymmetries learned from post-operative photographs of prior patients. The main novelty over the authors' earlier deep-learning baseline is a simplified disentangled autoencoder that removes the explicit identity latent and instead exploits the natural left-right symmetry of breast photographs to preserve clinically irrelevant appearance traits such as skin tone while isolating treatment-related asymmetry in a clinical latent. A second latent autoencoder further disentangles breast-shape asymmetry from nipple-position asymmetry, enabling more controllable manipulation of specific cosmetic effects rather than only global transfer. This makes the work a generative image-to-image counterfactual framework for pre-treatment counseling and expectation management, not a simple classifier or report-extraction model. The paper shows improved preservation of the original patient's appearance and better nipple-related asymmetry transfer than the prior deep model, but it still trails the conventional warping method in image realism and some breast-shape metrics, uses only internal data, and lacks clinician/patient reader validation of whether the generated outcomes are truly useful for decision-making. A secondary chest-radiograph study is included only as a proof that the disentanglement strategy generalizes beyond breast aesthetics.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Champalimaud Foundation CINDERELLA frontal breast image dataset (private; n=7,666 clinical breast photographs; 1,021 manually annotated by breast surgeons with breast contour points, nipple position, and aesthetic class labels; train=6,756, val=760; breast test built from 50 annotated pre-operative images paired with 100 matched post-operative templates chosen by cup size). Secondary proof-of-generalization dataset: ChestX-ray8 subset (public; n=11,032 chest radiographs from 4,845 patients; 1,093 cardiomegaly only, 3,955 pleural effusion only, 484 both, 5,500 neither; split 85% train, 5% val, 10% test).
Baseline model/architecture: Comparators: CV [6] conventional warping-based asymmetry-transfer method and DL [6] prior GAN-based disentanglement model with identity, asymmetry, and remaining-feature latents. Proposed architecture: autoencoder with encoder E, clinical latent Ec, non-clinical latent En, asymmetry predictor Ca, GAN discriminator Cd, decoder D, plus a separate latent autoencoder that splits the clinical latent into breast-asymmetry and nipple-asymmetry branches.
Training Approach: Supervised plus adversarial disentangled representation learning. The main autoencoder is trained with asymmetry prediction loss La using multi-label logistic regression and BCE on annotated images only; symmetry loss Lsym between original vs horizontally flipped images and original vs different-patient images to force asymmetry-independent information into En; disentanglement loss Ld via feature replacement between original and template images; and realism loss combining adversarial training with SSIM reconstruction. Generated samples are augmented with flips, random crops, and brightness changes before the discriminator to cope with limited data. Empirically selected breast-training weights: lambda_a=1.5, lambda_d=1, lambda_sym=0.1, lambda_disc=0.05, lambda_ssim=1, beta=0.1. A second latent autoencoder is trained separately on the learned clinical latents with two logistic regressors for breast vs nipple asymmetry, Ld for disentanglement, and MSE reconstruction. In the ChestX-ray8 proof-of-generalization, the asymmetry predictor is replaced by a multi-label cardiomegaly/pleural-effusion classifier and the symmetry loss is replaced with an SSIM-based reconstruction loss using lambda_a=lambda_d=lambda_disc=lambda_ssim=lambda_rec=1.
Medical Phase (pre/post): both (pre-operative breast image is the source patient image, post-operative breast image is the template providing treatment-related asymmetry, and the output simulates a post-treatment appearance)
Medical Modality: Frontal breast clinical photographs / surface imaging (main breast-cancer task); chest radiographs are used only as a secondary non-breast demonstration of generalizability
Model input modality: image-only; paired image-to-image setup at inference for the main task using a pre-operative source breast photograph and a post-operative template breast photograph. Secondary experiment uses chest radiograph images with template-based feature replacement.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main breast task metrics: mean absolute error down between template and morphed-image asymmetry metrics BRA, UNR, BCE, HNR, LBC, BCD, BAD, BOD, plus SSIM up between original and morphed image. Excellent/Good templates, Ours: BRA=0.043, UNR=0.024, BCE=0.086, HNR=0.028, LBC=0.011, BCD=0.031, BAD=0.051, BOD=0.090, SSIM=0.655. Fair/Poor templates, Ours: BRA=0.055, UNR=0.059, BCE=0.168, HNR=0.051, LBC=0.027, BCD=0.056, BAD=0.099, BOD=0.095, SSIM=0.640. Versus prior DL [6], the proposed model improves BCE and HNR in both template groups and slightly improves SSIM (0.655 vs 0.635 for Excellent/Good; 0.640 vs 0.624 for Fair/Poor), but remains worse than CV [6] in SSIM (0.898 and 0.884) and LBC. Latent breast-vs-nipple disentanglement: SSIM=0.708 for both Excellent/Good breast-only and nipple-only replacement, and 0.690/0.705 for Fair/Poor breast-only/nipple-only replacement; breast-only replacement yields low LBC=0.016 on Excellent/Good, while nipple-only replacement reduces BRA/UNR/HNR to 0.040/0.028/0.035. Ablation findings were qualitative: removing the symmetry loss harmed preservation of non-clinical traits such as skin color, removing the disentanglement loss caused abnormalities such as multiple nipples, and removing the discriminator produced blurry images. Secondary ChestX-ray8 proof: reconstruction SSIM=0.725; cardiomegaly Acc/F1/%Change=87.1/46.4/53.8; pleural effusion Acc/F1/%Change=75.5/69.6/68.1. Chest latent disentanglement %Change: cardiomegaly-only replacement 47.35 with pleural effusion preserved at 9.78, and pleural-effusion-only replacement 56.22 with cardiomegaly preserved at 6.67.

title: Anatomically and clinically informed deep generative model for breast surgery outcome prediction
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper proposes ACID-GAN, a clinically conditioned image-to-image model for predicting personalised post-operative breast appearance from a patient’s pre-operative frontal breast photograph. The main goal is to improve pre-surgical expectation setting by generating outcomes that preserve patient identity traits such as skin tone, body shape, and posture while also reflecting surgery-specific anatomical changes. Its main novelty is not merely using Pix2Pix, but extending it with a separate semantic encoder that forces the generated image to remain compatible with structured clinical variables, specifically surgery type and cancer laterality, while avoiding entangling clinical semantics with the realism discriminator. The method also adds anatomically targeted supervision through two colour-preservation losses, a breast-region structural loss combining grayscale L1 and SSIM, and a segmentation-consistency loss based on a pretrained U-Net, so the model is explicitly pushed to preserve non-breast appearance while modifying the surgical region. The paper benchmarks ACID-GAN against Pix2Pix, BicycleGAN, StarGAN, clinically conditioned variants of Pix2Pix/BicycleGAN, and two ablations, showing that ACID-GAN gives the best overall trade-off between post-operative fidelity, identity preservation, and colour consistency. Important limitations that only become clear from the full paper are that evaluation is entirely internal, relies on custom image/segmentation/colour metrics plus qualitative examples rather than reader studies, and the dataset covers only four conservative-surgery-related categories rather than the full spectrum of breast surgery such as mastectomy with or without reconstruction. Performance is also weaker and less distinctive in rare classes because C3 and C4 are severely underrepresented.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Champalimaud Foundation / CINDERELLA project paired pre- and post-operative frontal breast photograph dataset (private); total 1,038 paired image samples (private); split 85% train / 5% validation / 10% test (private); surgery-class composition: C1 Conservative Surgery n=679 (private), C2 Conservative Surgery with bilateral reduction n=286 (private), C3 Conservative Surgery with LD or LICAC/TDAP flaps n=46 (private), C4 Conservative Surgery with bilateral implants n=27 (private); no public dataset and no external validation cohort reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: ACID-GAN, a Pix2Pix-based paired conditional GAN with a U-Net generator, PatchGAN-style discriminator, and a separate encoder that predicts surgery type and cancer laterality from image pairs for semantic supervision; an additional pretrained U-Net segmentation model is used only to compute segmentation loss. Baselines/comparators: Pix2Pix, BicycleGAN, StarGAN, Pix2Pix with clinical conditioning, BicycleGAN with clinical conditioning. Ablations: ACID-GAN without skip connections; joint encoder/discriminator variant that merges semantic classification and realism discrimination into one network.
Training Approach: Supervised paired image-to-image training on pre-/post-operative RGB photographs. Clinical metadata (surgery type and cancer laterality) are one-hot encoded, spatially replicated, and concatenated as extra channels to the pre-operative image before entering the generator. Generator loss combines adversarial loss, structural supervision on the breast region (grayscale L1 + SSIM), encoder classification BCE loss for surgery type and side, Colour Loss 1 based on patch-averaged colour similarity to the pre-operative image, Colour Loss 2 based on L1 preservation outside the breast box, and cross-entropy segmentation loss between generated and real images using masks from a pretrained U-Net. Images are cropped using breast-contour anatomical keypoints; training uses random zoom-out augmentation during cropping, random horizontal flips, mild affine transforms, and colour jitter. Optimisation uses Adam with lr=0.0002 and beta1=0.5, Xavier initialisation, dropout in the generator, and linear learning-rate decay during the second half of training. For SSIM supervision, a soft-edged mask with linear falloff replaces a hard rectangular mask.
Medical Phase (pre/post): pre (intended for pre-operative counselling/expectation support, although training uses paired pre- and post-operative photographs)
Medical Modality: Standardised frontal clinical breast photography / external surface photographic imaging (2D RGB non-radiologic images)
Model input modality: Image + structured clinical metadata; inference input is a pre-operative frontal RGB breast photograph plus surgery type and cancer laterality; post-operative photographs are only training targets
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary internal test metrics for the best overall model ACID-GAN: SSIM-post=0.78, SSIM-pre=0.89, IoU-breast=0.80, IoU-nipple=0.10, Colour1 MAE=0.005, Colour2 MAE=0.003. Key comparators: Pix2Pix=0.75/0.73/0.77/0.05/0.07/0.07; BicycleGAN=0.76/0.74/0.78/0.07/0.07/0.07; Pix2Pix with conditions=0.76/0.75/0.78/0.10/0.07/0.07; BicycleGAN with conditions=0.77/0.77/0.79/0.08/0.07/0.06; StarGAN=0.76/0.77/0.75/0.05/0.06/0.06; joint encoder/discriminator=0.78/0.84/0.79/0.08/0.03/0.01; ACID-GAN without skip connections=0.77/0.81/0.79/0.09/0.02/0.02, where each sequence is SSIM-post / SSIM-pre / IoU-breast / IoU-nipple / Colour1 / Colour2. Per-surgery ACID-GAN results on the test set: C1 n=75 -> 0.79/0.90/0.79/0.12/0.005/0.003; C2 n=24 -> 0.74/0.87/0.80/0.03/0.006/0.002; C3 n=4 -> 0.79/0.87/0.79/0.01/0.006/0.003; C4 n=4 -> 0.82/0.89/0.78/0.13/0.005/0.003. The paper’s qualitative comparison also reports that ACID-GAN best preserves skin tone and body shape, while removing skip connections sharpens anatomy but harms colour fidelity.

title: Conditional probabilistic diffusion model driven synthetic radiogenomic applications in breast cancer
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles a core radiogenomics bottleneck: many breast cancer cohorts have genomics without matched MRI, which limits classical paired radiogenomic analysis. The authors propose a Conditional Probabilistic Diffusion Model (CPDM) that learns from a very small matched breast MRI-omics set and synthesizes 2D sagittal breast MRI projections from patient-level omic profiles. The model compresses multi-omics with Bayesian tensor factorization, then conditions a U-Net diffusion backbone using both inner-product fusion and cross-attention so the generated image better reflects genomic context. The novelty is twofold: generating breast MRIs from genomics rather than the reverse, and then treating those synthetic MRIs as radiogenomic surrogates for downstream prediction of TP53 mutation, ER status, ER+/HER2+ subgroup, and survival. Compared with AE, VAE, Transformer, and GAN baselines, CPDM achieved the best image-synthesis fidelity and enabled competitive downstream prediction, with the strongest downstream results in ER+/HER2+ subgrouping and smaller-subgroup survival modeling. The paper is best viewed as a proof-of-concept bridge between omics and imaging, not a deployment-ready clinical system, because it relies on only 58 paired training cases, uses 2D projections instead of full 3D MRI volumes, and lacks external validation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: TCGA-BRCA multi-omic and clinical data (public); TCIA TCGA-BRCA breast MRI collection (public); TCGA data retrieved/aggregated via cBioPortal for mutation, ER, subtype, and survival labels (public access). Matched training/testing set: 58 paired sagittal breast MRI plus multi-omic cases (public). Omics cohort after preprocessing: 754 patients with top-10-percent variable genes retained, yielding 4515 genes (public). Additional unpaired synthesis cohort reported as 726 patients lacking real MRI (public), although the paper later states 754 synthetic MRIs were generated from 726 unpaired plus 28 paired cases, so cohort accounting is internally inconsistent. Task subsets: TP53 mutation n=754, ER status n=708, ER+/HER2+ multi-omic n=66, ER+/HER2+ gene-expression n=123, survival n=740 overall, ER+/HER2+ survival n=66 multi-omic and n=123 gene-expression.
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed generator: DDPM-style CPDM with U-Net denoiser, cross-attention between downsampling and upsampling paths, inner-product omics-image fusion, and Bayesian Tensor Factorization to compress mRNA expression, DNA methylation, and copy number variation into 17 latent factors. Image-generation baselines: AutoEncoder, Variational AutoEncoder, Transformer, and GAN. Downstream feature/prediction stack: PyRadiomics and pretrained CNN feature extractors (VGG16, ResNet50, InceptionV3) with XGBoost for classification; DeepSurv and CoxPHFilter for survival.
Training Approach: MRIs were converted from 3D sagittal volumes to 2D orthographic projections and resized to 128x128. All-zero omics samples/features were removed; top 10 percent most variable genes were kept; mRNA, DNA methylation, and copy number variation were stacked into a 3D tensor and decomposed by Bayesian tensor factorization into 17 latent factors per patient. CPDM training used 15-fold cross-validation on the 58 paired MRI-omics cases, with diffusion forward noising/backward denoising and U-Net noise prediction; the paper reports convergence after about 1100 iterations/epochs. The trained model then synthesized MRIs for patients lacking paired imaging, including a separate repeat experiment using gene expression only in 123 ER+/HER2+ patients. Downstream tasks used feature extraction from synthetic MRIs via PyRadiomics or pretrained CNNs, XGBoost with RandomizedSearchCV and 10-fold cross-validation for TP53, ER, and ER+/HER2+ classification, and DeepSurv/CoxPHFilter for survival modeling.
Medical Phase (pre/post): unclear/mixed; diagnostic-type breast cancer radiogenomic setting with downstream molecular-status and prognosis prediction, but the paper does not anchor the MRI cohort to a single explicit pre- or post-treatment timepoint
Medical Modality: Breast MRI radiogenomics; sagittal breast MRI projections derived from 3D MRIs
Model input modality: Generation stage: omics-only tabular conditioning plus random noise, using mRNA expression + DNA methylation + copy number variation, or gene expression alone in the repeat experiment. Downstream stage: synthetic MRI images represented as radiomic features or CNN-derived image features.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Image synthesis, best CPDM test results: multi-omic version FID=3.11, STD-FID=0.74, MSE=3.15x10^-2, SSIM=0.59; gene-expression version FID=2.02, STD-FID=0.86, MSE=2.08x10^-2, SSIM=0.59. Downstream classification, best test results: TP53 mutation AUROC=0.78, AUPRC=0.62, F1=0.69; ER status AUROC=0.70, AUPRC=0.92, F1=0.94; ER+/HER2+ subgroup AUROC=0.82, AUPRC=0.84, F1=0.88 in the gene-expression version using PyRadiomics features. Survival, best test results: all-patient cohort C-index=0.58 with log-rank p=0.01 using ResNet50 features plus CoxPHFilter; ER+/HER2+ multi-omic cohort C-index=0.88 with log-rank p=0.05 using ResNet50 plus CoxPHFilter; ER+/HER2+ gene-expression cohort C-index=0.66 with log-rank p=0.04.

title: FAME: A privacy-preserving dual-stage deep learning framework for breast ultrasound imaging using federated transfer and synthetic learning
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This retrospective breast-ultrasound paper aims to build a multi-institutional, privacy-preserving system that performs both lesion segmentation and diagnosis without centralizing raw data. Its main novelty is the stacked combination of four components in one pipeline: simulated federated transfer learning across non-IID clients, client-local class-conditioned ACGAN augmentation, a residual dual-attention MAU-Net for segmentation, and a second-stage feature-fusion classifier that ensembles MAU-Net, ResNet50V2, and NASNetLarge with a meta-classifier. Unlike many BUS papers, it also studies privacy-performance trade-offs using differential privacy and secure aggregation, includes ablation experiments, and reports computational cost. The full FAME configuration outperformed the compared SOTA segmentation and classification baselines on BUSI, UDIAT, and BUSC, while ablation showed drops when ACGAN, attention, ensemble fusion, or federated transfer were removed. Important limitations are that federation was simulated rather than deployed across real hospitals, synthetic-image realism was not clinically validated, failure cases remained for very small/low-contrast/acoustically shadowed lesions, and the manuscript has an internal inconsistency about BUSC size: the abstract reports 407 images, while the dataset section describes 250 images.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: BUSI dataset (public; 780 images with masks; 437 benign, 210 malignant, 133 normal; 500×500; from Baheya Hospital, Egypt); UDIAT dataset (public; 163 images with masks; 109 benign, 54 malignant; average 760×570; from UDIAT Diagnostic Centre, Spain); BUSC/Mendeley breast ultrasound dataset (public classification dataset; dataset section reports 100 benign + 150 malignant images at original 64×64 resolution, resized to 128×128 in this study; no original masks, and study-specific radiologist annotations were added for segmentation but not stated as public)
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed architecture: segmentation with MAU-Net (U-Net variant with residual encoder, channel attention, spatial attention, Dice loss, local 3-fold ensemble); classification with a dual-stage ensemble using ImageNet-initialized ResNet50V2, NASNetLarge, and MAU-Net feature extractors plus dense/dropout heads and a meta-classifier. Benchmark baselines: segmentation—U-Net, UTNet, LinkNet, UNet++, TransUNet, D-LinkNet, Axial-DeepLab, ATFE-Net, FATNet, MSU-UNet, PDF-UNet; classification—GAN+CNN, CNN-based image fusion, ML radiomics approach, MTL-COSA, FMRNet, BUViTNet, SaTransformer, RMTL-Net, BIRADS-SSDL, HoVer-Trans, MDA-Net.
Training Approach: Retrospective, image-based study in a simulated 3-client federated client-server setting with FedAvg; each client held non-IID local subsets, trained locally for 5 epochs per communication round, and shared encrypted parameters; secure aggregation masked updates and differential privacy added Gaussian noise during privacy experiments. Transfer learning initialized local backbones from ImageNet. ACGANs were trained locally to generate class-specific synthetic BUS images, with 10,000 synthetic samples per class reported before segmentation/classification training. Preprocessing included resizing to 256×256, median+Gaussian denoising, normalization, and online augmentation (flip, ±15° rotation, zoom 0.9–1.1). Segmentation used Dice loss and local 3-fold cross-validation ensembling; classification used categorical cross-entropy. Hyperparameters: Adam, initial LR=1e-4, batch size=8, 100 epochs, ReduceLROnPlateau, early stopping patience=10, dropout=0.3, L2=1e-5. Note: the implementation/training description is slightly inconsistent across sections, because the results section says an 80:10:10 BUSI split was used for training and BUSC/UDIAT were external tests, while other sections describe non-IID subsets from BUSI, UDIAT, and BUSC across the simulated federation.
Medical Modality: Breast ultrasound (BUS)
Model input modality: image-only (2D grayscale breast ultrasound images; synthetic ACGAN-generated ultrasound images used during training; masks used as supervision rather than raw multimodal input)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Classification: BUSI Accuracy=98.70±0.27%, F1=96.82±0.53%, AUC=0.978; UDIAT Accuracy=98.14±0.31%, F1=94.04±0.75%, AUC=0.960; BUSC Accuracy=96.92±0.27%, F1=90.32±0.80%, AUC=0.950. Segmentation: BUSI Dice=89.72±0.53%, IoU=84.81±0.57%, Sensitivity=91.11±0.53%, Specificity=98.13±0.35%; BUSC Dice=93.09±0.49%, IoU=87.13±0.66%, Sensitivity=87.41±0.71%, Specificity=99.59±0.27%; UDIAT Dice=87.98±0.57%, IoU=78.16±0.66%, Sensitivity=87.41±0.62%, Specificity=99.61±0.22%. Privacy evaluation on BUSI 3-client setup: no-DP Dice=0.865±0.011, Accuracy=0.938±0.009, AUC=0.964, F1=0.926; ε=1 DP Dice=0.808±0.021, Accuracy=0.879±0.016, AUC=0.915, F1=0.874; Secure Aggregation vs federated without SA/DP: Dice 0.862 vs 0.865, Accuracy 0.935 vs 0.938, AUC 0.960 vs 0.964, F1 0.922 vs 0.926. Computational efficiency of full framework: 380 s/epoch, 12.5 GB memory, 45.8 ms/image, 72.5 GFLOPs.

title: Federated Breast Cancer Detection Enhanced by Synthetic Ultrasound Image Augmentation
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles privacy-preserving multi-institutional breast ultrasound classification under limited local data and non-IID client distributions. The goal is to improve binary benign-versus-malignant lesion classification in a realistic federated learning setup without sharing raw patient data across sites. Its novelty is not a new classifier backbone or a new federated optimizer, but a practical synthetic-data-sharing strategy: two centrally trained class-specific DCGANs generate benign and malignant ultrasound images that are distributed to every client as privacy-preserving prior knowledge during federated training. The paper goes beyond a headline result by examining implementation details and ablation behavior: moderate synthetic augmentation helps both FedAvg and especially FedProx, while excessive synthetic sampling degrades performance, so the real contribution is a calibrated recipe for balancing real and synthetic data in federated breast ultrasound learning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: BUS-BRA (public; 1,875 B-mode breast ultrasound images from 1,064 patients; 1,268 benign and 607 malignant; BI-RADS labels and lesion masks available); BUSI binary subset (public; 647 images used after removing 133 normal cases from the original 780-image dataset; 437 benign and 210 malignant; lesion masks available); UDIAT (public; 163 B-mode breast ultrasound images; 109 benign and 54 malignant; lesion masks available). Each dataset was split approximately 3:1:2 into train/validation/test, and only train plus validation data were used for DCGAN training.
Baseline model/architecture: Classifier backbone: ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet-121. Federated baselines: FedAvg and FedProx. Additional reference comparator: centralized learning on pooled data. Augmentation module: two class-specific DCGANs, one benign and one malignant; the generator uses six 2D transposed-convolution layers and the discriminator uses six 2D convolution layers.
Training Approach: Supervised federated image classification with central synthetic-data generation. Two DCGANs were trained centrally on the combined training and validation subsets from all three datasets for 500 epochs using Adam, learning rate 0.0002, and batch size 128. The generator produced 128x128 grayscale synthetic ultrasound images, later upsampled to 224x224; the paper states generation was conditioned on lesion masks plus latent noise, and 256x256 generation was tested but found unstable. After training, 1,000 benign and 1,000 malignant synthetic images were generated and uniformly distributed to all clients. FL simulated three sites, one per dataset. DenseNet-121 was locally trained for 1 epoch per communication round with batch size 32 using AdamW, initial learning rate 0.001 with 10x decay every 30 epochs, for 100 communication rounds. FedProx used mu=0.03. For synthetic batches, learning rate started at 0.0001; 160 synthetic images per epoch, or 5 batches, were randomly sampled so synthetic data made up about 12 percent of each client training set. Final model selection used the checkpoint with the highest average validation AUC across clients. The pseudo-code shows an update on shared synthetic data before client updates, while the implementation section operationalizes the method as mixing synthetic batches into federated training; functionally, the method is shared synthetic augmentation rather than a new aggregation rule.
Medical Modality: Breast ultrasound (B-mode ultrasound)
Model input modality: image-only for the downstream classifier (2D grayscale breast ultrasound images resized to 224x224); lesion masks were additionally used during the synthetic-image generation stage, not as classifier input at inference.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main metrics: Accuracy and AUC on held-out test sets. Centralized learning: average Accuracy=0.8967, average AUC=0.9391. FedAvg: average Accuracy=0.8730, average AUC=0.9206. FedAvg plus Synthetic: average Accuracy=0.8928, average AUC=0.9237. FedProx: average Accuracy=0.9021, average AUC=0.9429. FedProx plus Synthetic achieved the best average AUC=0.9538 with average Accuracy=0.8963. Per-dataset AUCs for FedProx plus Synthetic: BUS-BRA=0.9454, BUSI=0.9532, UDIAT=0.9628. Per-dataset accuracies for FedProx plus Synthetic: BUS-BRA=0.8720, BUSI=0.9077, UDIAT=0.9091. Ablation with heavier synthetic use under FedAvg reduced performance relative to moderate augmentation: heavy-synthetic average Accuracy=0.8580 and average AUC=0.9203, versus 0.8928 and 0.9237 for the moderate synthetic setting.

title: Towards Robust Breast Segmentation: Leveraging Depth Awareness and Convexity Optimization For Tackling Data Scarcity
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses robust breast aesthetic segmentation under limited clinical data, privacy constraints, class imbalance, and anatomical variability. The goal is to improve automatic segmentation of background, body, breast, and nipple regions for objective pre- and post-operative aesthetic evaluation in breast surgery. Its novelty lies in combining a SAM-based encoder with synthetic depth awareness from Depth-Anything-v2, a lightweight multimodal RGB-depth fusion decoder, auxiliary depth supervision, and a multi-term loss that includes weighted cross-entropy, convexity regularization, and depth-alignment constraints. Rather than relying only on generic pretrained segmentation models, the method injects geometry-aware cues to improve anatomical plausibility, especially for small and imbalanced nipple masks. The main takeaway is that depth helps reduce noisy activations and focus on anatomically relevant regions, while convexity optimization improves geometric consistency, leading to strong test performance and promising cross-dataset generalization on CINDERELLA samples.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Breast-Aesthetics / BA dataset: 120 RGB front upper-torso patient images with segmentation masks; private but available upon request. Split: 70% train, 10% validation, 20% test. Class distribution: background 44.50%, body 42.16%, breast 12.35%, nipple 1.00%. CINDERELLA project dataset: 36 annotated images for cross-dataset evaluation, split 2/3 train and 1/3 test; private / project-specific annotations. No fully public external dataset reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Main architecture: encoder-decoder segmentation model with SAM encoder, Depth-Anything-v2 synthetic depth branch, bidirectional RGB-depth cross-attention, squeeze-and-excitation fusion, spatial attention gate, lightweight convolutional decoder, segmentation head, and auxiliary depth head used only during training. Baselines/comparators: Fernandes et al. 2018 ordinal segmentation; Rebelo et al. 2019 quality-based regularization; Cruz et al. 2025 ordinal/contact surface method; U-Net; MobileNet-v2; MobileViT-v2; SegFormer; BEIT; DPT; UperNet; frozen SAM baseline in CINDERELLA evaluation.
Training Approach: Supervised fine-tuning with pretrained encoders and task-specific decoder. Synthetic depth maps were generated using Depth-Anything-v2 and injected after the SAM encoder through bidirectional attention rather than as a raw extra input channel, preserving pretrained RGB weights. Training used 100 epochs, batch size 4, learning rate 1e-5, Adam optimizer, fixed aspect-ratio resizing with black padding, and class-frequency-based weighting. Loss combined weighted cross-entropy for class imbalance, convexity-aware regularization for nipple masks, L1 depth alignment, and depth-gradient alignment using Sobel gradients. No data augmentation was used in the reported training.
Medical Modality: Clinical RGB photography / 2D front upper-torso breast aesthetic images; semantic segmentation masks for background, body, breast, and nipple; synthetic monocular depth maps used as geometric auxiliary signal.
Model input modality: RGB image plus synthetic depth representation generated from RGB; output is multi-class segmentation mask. Auxiliary depth prediction is used during training only.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main BA test balanced DSC: 98.75%, about +4.5% over prior methods. Prior work DSC: Fernandes et al. 2018=93.93%, Rebelo et al. 2019=94.17%, Cruz et al. 2025=94.30%. Per-class DSC for proposed model on BA: background=99.8%, body=98.7%, breast=95.5%, nipple=89.2%, mean=98.7%. SoTA comparison mean DSC: U-Net=91.6%, MobileNet-v2=96.9%, MobileViT-v2=95.3%, SegFormer=98.4%, BEIT=97.7%, DPT=94.3%, UperNet=98.3%, Ours=98.7%. Depth ablation: +0.47% DSC on body and +1.04% DSC on breast. Convexity alignment: Conv improved from 97.72 to 99.86, with CE+Conv mDSC=98.75 and mIoU=90.93. CINDERELLA cross-dataset DSC: frozen SAM=40.1 mean, fine-tuned on BA=90.1 mean, fine-tuned on CINDERELLA=97.9 mean; nipple DSC improved from 11.1 frozen SAM to 82.4 BA fine-tuned and 88.8 CINDERELLA fine-tuned.

title: Predicting Aesthetic Outcomes in Breast Cancer Surgery: A Multimodal Retrieval Approach
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the challenge of helping breast cancer patients and clinicians anticipate post-locoregional-treatment aesthetic outcomes by retrieving visually and clinically similar previous cases. The goal was to build a deep-learning-based multimodal retrieval system that, given a patient query, returns the top 10 most analogous post-surgical cases from a database, supporting expectation management and clinical decision support. Its novelty lies in framing breast aesthetic outcome prediction as a multimodal retrieval/ranking problem using clinician-ranked triplets, rather than as a direct classification or regression task. The method compares tabular-only retrieval, image-only retrieval using CNNs and Vision Transformers, fine-tuned image retrieval with triplet loss, and multimodal fusion of clinical attributes with image embeddings. The main takeaway is that fine-tuned vision transformers, especially GoogleViT and BEIT, substantially outperform zero-shot/pretrained models, while multimodal fusion gives the best overall retrieval performance by combining structured clinical information with visual breast appearance cues.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CINDERELLA / Champalimaud Foundation private breast aesthetic image dataset Breast cancer aesthetic outcome retrieval dataset: 2,193 private instances containing clinical tabular attributes and RGB upper-torso JPEG images; private but available upon request. Clinical attributes include height, weight, age, bra size, and bra-cup size. Images range from 1869×1117 to 6000×4000 pixels, average 4810×2903. Ground-truth retrieval rankings were created by clinicians. Dataset includes 160 non-overlapping query-retrieval catalogues, divided into Excellent/Good and Fair/Poor aesthetic outcome groups using the Harris scale. Split: 80% training catalogues and 20% testing catalogues. More than 20K triplets were generated for training/testing.
Baseline model/architecture: Baselines/comparators: tabular Euclidean distance baseline; Weighted Euclidean Distance / matrix-weighted distance; shallow 4-layer ANN/MLP for tabular data. Image models: pretrained and fine-tuned VGG16, ResNet50, DEIT, GoogleViT, DINOv2, and BEIT. Multimodal models: fine-tuned image embeddings from GoogleViT, DINOv2, or BEIT concatenated with tabular features and passed through a shallow MLP. Retrieval similarity criterion: Euclidean distance in learned embedding space.
Training Approach: Triplet-loss-based metric learning using clinician rankings. Each triplet contains a query, a positive case ranked closer to the query, and a negative case ranked farther away. Tabular values were normalized using the training set. Images were resized to 224×224 with zero padding and then processed with each model’s Hugging Face ImageProcessor. Pretrained image models were first tested as zero-shot feature extractors without weight updates. Fine-tuned image models were optimized with triplet loss to align embeddings with clinicians’ aesthetic similarity rankings. In the multimodal setup, fine-tuned image features were concatenated with tabular clinical features and trained through a shallow MLP using the same triplet-loss formulation. The pipeline diagram on page 6 shows feature extraction, feature-database storage, Euclidean-distance retrieval, and top-n similar-case retrieval.
Medical Modality: Clinical RGB photography of patients’ upper torso after breast cancer locoregional treatment; tabular clinical metadata; medical image retrieval for breast aesthetic outcome prediction.
Model input modality: multimodal: RGB upper-torso image + tabular clinical attributes; image-only and tabular-only variants also evaluated.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main metrics: Contrastive Accuracy / CAcc and Adjusted Discounted Cumulative Gain / ADCG. Best reported multimodal result: GoogleViT achieved Fair/Poor test CAcc=73.85% and Fair/Poor test ADCG=80.62%; BEIT achieved Excellent/Good test CAcc=72.06% and ADCG=73.63%, Fair/Poor test CAcc=73.05% and ADCG=78.45%; DINOv2 multimodal achieved Excellent/Good test CAcc=70.14% and ADCG=77.40%, Fair/Poor test CAcc=73.56% and ADCG=78.96%. Best fine-tuned image-only results: GoogleViT test CAcc=(69.30, 73.18) and ADCG=(73.87, 79.86) for Excellent/Good and Fair/Poor; BEIT test CAcc=(71.95, 72.76) and ADCG=(73.85, 77.92); DINOv2 test CAcc=(69.92, 70.78) and ADCG=(77.89, 76.97). Fine-tuning greatly improved VGG16 test performance from CAcc=(52.10, 44.72), ADCG=(56.69, 46.71) to CAcc=(69.26, 71.16), ADCG=(71.96, 76.87). Tabular-only models were moderate, with MLP test CAcc=(57.09, 64.90) and ADCG=(57.70, 66.56).

title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Network for Predicting the Aesthetic Outcomes of Breast Cancer Treatment
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the need to help breast cancer patients visualize possible aesthetic outcomes of locoregional treatment before choosing among surgical options. The goal is to generate realistic manipulated torso images that simulate breast-shape and nipple-position changes caused by surgery, especially asymmetries. Its novelty lies in a mask-guided conditional GAN that manipulates breast shape using a target segmentation mask, a cropped version of the original breast, and a preservation-masked torso image, while a frozen segmentation U-Net forces the generated image to match the requested breast mask and a discriminator promotes realism. Unlike earlier approaches that rely mainly on affine transformations, disentangled representations, or inpainting, this method explicitly conditions generation on manipulated breast masks and uses synthetic mask perturbations during training. The main takeaway is that the proposed model better controls nipple and breast-shape manipulation while preserving realistic torso appearance, making it promising for pre-operative visual decision support, though scars and other treatment-specific deformities are left for future work.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CINDERELLA / Champalimaud Foundation private breast aesthetic image dataset; 7,666 frontal breast/torso images; 2,000 images annotated with breast-contour keypoints and nipple positions; aesthetic labels available for annotated images using Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent categories. Test set: 150 annotated images, including 50 pre-operative images, 50 Good/Excellent post-operative images, and 50 Fair/Poor post-operative images. Remaining images used for training. Dataset is private.
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: mask-guided conditional GAN with autoencoder generator, convolutional discriminator, and frozen pre-trained U-Net segmentation network. Generator input combines target mask, cropped original breast, and original image with a preservation mask. Preservation-mask variants tested: half-filled, square-shaped, breast-shaped, no preservation mask on input, no cropped breast, and U-Net generator replacement. Main state-of-the-art comparators: CV affine transformation method; DL disentangled learning; SDL disentangled learning variant; DGAN inpainting-based method. Baseline segmentation network also reported.
Training Approach: Supervised/self-guided generative training using segmentation-mask guidance rather than paired pre/post ground-truth image translation. Target masks are generated by splitting the original segmentation mask, vertically resizing the target breast region with a random ratio, padding, and merging the halves. Generator loss combines mask manipulation loss via frozen U-Net segmentation output, adversarial realism loss, and preservation loss using SSIM over preserved regions. Loss weights: λm=1, λr=0.1, λp=1. Model trained for 2,000 epochs. Data augmentation includes random crops, vertical/horizontal flips, rotations for the discriminator, plus horizontal flipping, horizontal mirroring, and random torso cropping for original images. The final aesthetic-outcome prediction transfers asymmetry patterns from post-operative cases to pre-operative images by manipulating lowest-breast-point and nipple positions using LBC, UNR, and HNR-inspired geometric rules.
Medical Modality: Clinical RGB frontal breast/upper-torso photography; breast segmentation masks; manually annotated breast contour keypoints and nipple positions used for evaluation.
Model input modality: image + mask multimodal input: RGB torso image, target breast segmentation mask, cropped original breast image, and preservation-masked original image; output is manipulated RGB torso image simulating aesthetic outcome.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Manipulation experiment, selected square-shaped preservation mask: Precision=0.984, Recall=0.979, Accuracy=0.988, Dice=0.982, IoU=0.964, SSIM=0.866, PSNR=28.214, LPIPS=1.549. Best reconstruction ablation, no preservation mask on input: SSIM=0.903, PSNR=30.847, LPIPS=1.535, Dice=0.983, IoU=0.966. Best segmentation ablation, U-Net generator: Precision=0.989, Recall=0.984, Accuracy=0.991, Dice=0.986, IoU=0.973, but weaker reconstruction with PSNR=22.324 and LPIPS=1.714. Aesthetic-outcome prediction on Good/Excellent post-operative targets for Ours: BRA MAE=0.032, UNR=0.019, BCE=0.138, HNR=0.032, LBC=0.011, BCD=0.032, BAD=0.061, BOD=0.102, SSIM=0.813, Precision=0.988, Recall=0.981, Accuracy=0.989, Dice=0.984, IoU=0.970. For Fair/Poor post-operative targets for Ours: BRA MAE=0.044, UNR=0.038, BCE=0.170, HNR=0.033, LBC=0.021, BCD=0.045, BAD=0.094, BOD=0.096, SSIM=0.784, Precision=0.986, Recall=0.983, Accuracy=0.989, Dice=0.984, IoU=0.969. Compared with CV, DL, SDL, and DGAN, the proposed method achieves the best segmentation-mask agreement and strongest nipple-asymmetry manipulation on BRA, UNR, and HNR, while DGAN has higher SSIM but struggles with torso reconstruction beneath the manipulated breast.

title: Reproducing Asymmetries Caused by Breast Cancer Treatment in Pre-Operative Breast Images
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the lack of methods for predicting or visually simulating aesthetic outcomes of breast cancer locoregional treatment. The goal is to reproduce asymmetries observed in post-operative breast images onto pre-operative breast images, helping patients better understand possible post-surgical appearance changes before treatment. Its novelty lies in presenting one of the first direct attempts to simulate breast cancer treatment aesthetic outcomes, comparing a traditional computer-vision morphing pipeline with a deep generative disentanglement model, and introducing Horizontal Nipple Retraction (HNR) as a new asymmetry metric for isolated horizontal nipple displacement. The main takeaway is that the traditional computer-vision method produces higher-quality and more faithful images and is better at altering breast contour, while the deep-learning method better manipulates nipple position and direction without requiring manual keypoint annotation at inference.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CINDERELLA Project / Champalimaud Foundation private breast image dataset; 7,666 images acquired by Champalimaud Foundation; 1,021 post-operative images manually annotated by clinical experts with breast-contour keypoints and nipple positions; aesthetic labels: Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor. Deep learning model trained on 7,516 images, with 760 used for validation. Test set: 50 pre-operative images. For each test image, 2 post-operative template images with the same cup size were randomly selected: one Excellent/Good template for smaller asymmetries and one Fair/Poor template for larger asymmetries. Dataset is private.
Baseline model/architecture: Compared approaches: traditional computer vision / CV method based on manual keypoint reallocation, asymmetry-vector optimization, Delaunay triangulation, and affine image morphing; deep learning / DL method based on a disentangled representation learning autoencoder with encoder, decoder, GAN discriminator, asymmetry predictor, and identity classifier. Auxiliary U-Net segmentation network used to crop breast regions for the DL model. No external baseline model for aesthetic outcome prediction was available because the paper frames this as a first-step comparison.
Training Approach: CV approach: no neural training; requires annotated keypoints for breast contour and nipple position, extracts asymmetry features from pre-operative and post-operative template images, optimizes keypoint positions to match template asymmetries using LBC, BCD, HNR, and UNR, then morphs the image using Delaunay triangulation and affine transformations. DL approach: trained a disentangled autoencoder/GAN model to separate medical/asymmetry features, identity features, and other reconstruction features; asymmetry prediction reformulated as multi-target logistic regression using decomposed LBC, BCE, and HNR measurements; breast regions were cropped using a U-Net segmentation model because full torso asymmetry prediction was difficult. During testing, medical/asymmetry features from post-operative templates are transferred to pre-operative images while preserving identity features.
Medical Modality: Clinical RGB frontal breast / upper-torso photography; manually annotated contour keypoints and nipple positions; image morphing / generative image manipulation for breast aesthetic outcome simulation.
Model input modality: image-only: RGB pre-operative breast image plus post-operative template image; CV method also uses breast-contour and nipple keypoints; DL method uses cropped RGB breast regions and learned latent representations.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Metrics: mean absolute error between template and morphed-image asymmetry metrics, lower is better; SSIM between original and morphed image, higher is better. Excellent/Good templates — CV: pBRA=0.0453, pUNR=0.0338, pBCE=0.1371, HNR=0.0495, pLBC=0.0013, pBCD=0.0229, pBAD=0.0614, pBOD=0.0922, SSIM=89.78%; DL: pBRA=0.0440, pUNR=0.0248, pBCE=0.0918, HNR=0.0333, pLBC=0.0100, pBCD=0.0258, pBAD=0.0460, pBOD=0.1060, SSIM=63.47%. Fair/Poor templates — CV: pBRA=0.0561, pUNR=0.0604, pBCE=0.1932, HNR=0.0561, pLBC=0.0017, pBCD=0.0519, pBAD=0.1021, pBOD=0.0911, SSIM=88.41%; DL: pBRA=0.0506, pUNR=0.0584, pBCE=0.1696, HNR=0.0626, pLBC=0.0252, pBCD=0.0388, pBAD=0.0810, pBOD=0.0892, SSIM=62.39%. Overall, CV had substantially higher SSIM and better pLBC, while DL generally improved nipple-related and several global asymmetry errors.

title: Predicting Aesthetic Outcomes of Breast Cancer Surgery: A Robust and Explainable Image Retrieval Approach
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses the limitations of content-based image retrieval for breast cancer aesthetic outcome prediction, especially low interpretability, sensitivity to irrelevant visual noise, and limited robustness across clinical settings. The goal is to retrieve clinically relevant post-surgical breast images for a pre-surgical query image, helping clinicians show patients realistic examples of possible aesthetic outcomes. Its novelty lies in a multistage retrieval pipeline that combines explainable saliency analysis, region-based image pre-processing, and ensemble learning. Saliency maps revealed that retrieval models often attend to irrelevant regions such as arms or background, motivating expanded breast-region bounding-box inputs that preserve useful context while reducing noise. The main takeaway is that expanded bounding boxes plus an ensemble of complementary ViT-based feature extractors substantially improves retrieval performance over prior image-only approaches, especially for Fair/Poor aesthetic outcomes.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Private breast cancer aesthetic outcome image retrieval dataset following the Zolfagharnasab et al. protocol; private and available upon request. For each query image, two clinician-ranked catalogs were created: Excellent/Good and Fair/Poor post-surgical outcomes based on the Harris scale. Clinicians ranked 5–15 visually similar images per catalog, and these rankings were converted into triplets with anchor/query, positive, and negative images. No public external validation dataset reported.
Baseline model/architecture: Reference baseline: Zolfagharnasab et al. image-only retrieval approach. Individual feature extractors/comparators: DenseNet121, DenseNet201, ResNeXt50, VGG16, BEiT, DaViT, GC ViT, Google ViT, and SwinV2. XAI methods tested: Integrated Gradients, Similarity-Based Saliency Maps, and Class Activation Maps. Input variants: original image, segmented breast image, tight breast/nipple bounding box, and expanded bounding box. Ensemble fusion variants: raw concatenation, single-layer projection, 2-layer MLP, 3-layer MLP, and transformer-based fusion. Final best pipeline: expanded bounding-box inputs with a trainable 2-layer MLP ensemble using BEiT, DaViT, and GC ViT.
Training Approach: Triplet-loss metric learning using clinician-provided similarity rankings. Each triplet contained a query image, a positive image ranked more similar to the query, and a negative image ranked less similar. Similarity during retrieval was computed with Euclidean distance in embedding space. Feature extractors were trained until convergence with tuned learning rates. XAI saliency analysis was used to diagnose model attention and motivate region-based pre-processing. Expanded bounding boxes were created by enclosing breast/nipple regions and extending the box by 10 pixels horizontally and 20 pixels vertically. Ensemble models were tested with frozen backbones and trainable two-phase fine-tuning; in the trainable setup, fusion layers were trained alone for the first 30% of epochs, followed by joint training of backbones and fusion layers for the remaining 70%.
Medical Modality: Clinical RGB breast / upper-torso photography for breast cancer surgical aesthetic outcome retrieval; non-radiological medical image retrieval.
Model input modality: image-only: RGB pre-surgical/query breast image and candidate post-surgical RGB breast images; pre-processing variants include original image, segmented image, tight bounding box, and expanded bounding box; output is ranked retrieval of similar post-surgical outcomes.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main metrics: Contrastive Accuracy / CAcc and Adjusted Discounted Cumulative Gain / ADCG. Best final proposed pipeline: CAcc=(77.67%, 84.98%) for Excellent/Good and Fair/Poor; ADCG=(82.55%, 78.64%). Compared with Zolfagharnasab et al.: CAcc improved from (69.30%, 73.18%) to (77.67%, 84.98%), corresponding to +8.37% and +11.80%; ADCG changed from (73.87%, 79.86%) to (82.55%, 78.64%), corresponding to +8.68% and -1.22%. Best individual original-image model: GC ViT with CAcc=(75.11%, 76.65%) and ADCG=(78.44%, 80.18%). Expanded bounding-box GC ViT: CAcc=(75.89%, 77.30%) and ADCG=(81.17%, 79.80%), giving CAcc gains of +0.78% and +0.65% over original images. Segmented images reduced GC ViT CAcc to (73.78%, 75.00%), a drop of 1.33% and 1.65%. Best ensemble with original images: top-3 BEiT+DaViT+GC ViT using SLP achieved CAcc=(77.67%, 80.14%) and ADCG=(80.31%, 80.63%). Final EBB ensemble with 2-layer MLP and BEiT+DaViT+GC ViT achieved the best CAcc, especially Fair/Poor CAcc=84.98%.

title: Comprehensive Benchmark Dataset for Pathological Lymph Node Metastasis in Breast Cancer Sections
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This Scientific Data work addresses a major benchmarking problem in computational pathology: the widely used Camelyon-16 and Camelyon-17 breast lymph-node metastasis datasets contain noisy slides, inconsistent labels, missing or inaccurate pixel annotations, and incompatible label definitions. The goal is not to propose a new diagnostic model, but to release a cleaned and clinically more meaningful benchmark, Camelyon+, for pathological lymph-node metastasis classification in breast cancer whole-slide images. Its novelty lies in reprocessing 1,399 WSIs, removing low-quality or ambiguous slides, correcting slide-level labels, adding expert pixel-level tumor annotations, renaming files to avoid label leakage, and upgrading the original binary cancer-screening task into a four-class metastasis task: negative, micro-metastasis, macro-metastasis, and isolated tumor cells / ITC. The work also benchmarks a large set of pathology feature extractors and MIL aggregators, showing that dataset refinement changes model rankings, that CLAM-MB remains a strong and robust MIL baseline, and that pathology-pretrained and image-text contrastive pathology encoders improve MIL performance. The main takeaway is that Camelyon+ is a cleaner, harder, and more clinically relevant public benchmark for breast lymph-node metastasis WSI analysis, while also exposing the limitation of standard MIL for size-defined metastasis categories under long-tailed class imbalance.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Camelyon-16 original dataset: public; Camelyon-17 original dataset: public; Camelyon+ refined benchmark: public via ScienceDB, with original WSI data available from the official Camelyon/GigaDB repository. Reprocessed source pool: 1,399 WSIs from Camelyon-16 and Camelyon-17. Removed slides: 49 total, including 26 therapeutic-response slides, 3 staining-quality issues, 12 focal-blur slides, 4 poor-quality slides, and 4 suspicious/ambiguous cancerous-region slides. Refined Camelyon-16: 386 WSIs, including 238 negative, 71 micro-metastasis, 69 macro-metastasis, and 8 ITC. Refined Camelyon-17: 964 WSIs, including 633 negative, 103 micro-metastasis, 182 macro-metastasis, and 46 ITC. Final Camelyon+: 1,350 WSIs, including 871 negative, 174 micro-metastasis, 251 macro-metastasis, and 54 ITC. Dataset components include slide-level 2-class and 4-class labels, file-name conversion tables to reduce annotation bias, XML pixel-level tumor annotations, extracted feature files, and optional HDF5 feature files.
Baseline model/architecture: MIL baselines/aggregators: Max-MIL, Mean-MIL, ABMIL, Gate-ABMIL, CLAM-SB, CLAM-MB, DSMIL, TransMIL, DTFD, AMD-MIL, WiKG, and FR-MIL. Feature extractors/backbones: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 and ViT-S; pathology/image-text or pathology-pretrained encoders PLIP, CONCH, CONCH-V1.5, CTransPath, UNI, GigaPath, and Virchow; slide-level encoders Chief, Prism, and Titan. The strongest recurring MIL baseline was CLAM-MB, especially in the Camelyon-17 refinement comparison.
Training Approach: Dataset curation plus weakly supervised WSI classification benchmarking. Professional pathologists filtered low-quality slides, corrected slide-level labels, and created/verified pixel-level annotations in ASAP according to AJCC 8th edition guidance. WSIs were divided into non-overlapping 256×256 patches at 20× magnification. Patch-level features were extracted using 12 pretrained encoders and then aggregated with MIL models for slide-level classification. Camelyon-17 Origin vs Refine experiments used the official train/test split, learning rate 2e-4, Adam optimizer, weight decay 1e-5, and three random seeds: 2023, 2024, and 2025. Camelyon+ benchmark experiments used five-fold stratified cross-validation while avoiding leakage by keeping slides from the same patient/label out of train-validation overlap.
Medical Modality: Digital pathology whole-slide images of breast cancer lymph-node sections; optical microscopy / histopathology WSIs with slide-level labels and pixel-level tumor annotations.
Model input modality: image-only WSI input; non-overlapping histopathology patches converted to patch-level feature embeddings, then aggregated to slide-level predictions with MIL; labels include negative, micro-metastasis, macro-metastasis, and ITC.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Metrics: Accuracy, AUC, F1-score, Recall, Precision, and Cohen’s Kappa. Camelyon-17 Refine strong result: GigaPath + CLAM-MB achieved Acc=84.4±1.92%, AUC=96.5±0.44%, F1=81.1±3.75%, Recall=68.5±0.39%, Precision=65.6±0.30%, Kappa=0.64±0.09. Camelyon-17 Refine with UNI + FR-MIL achieved AUC=96.0±0.46% and F1=78.3±4.48%; UNI + TransMIL achieved Acc=88.5±0.44%. Camelyon+ benchmark examples: ResNet-50 + CLAM-MB achieved Acc=83.5±1.22%, AUC=81.7±1.89%, F1=56.2±3.80%; ResNet-50 + AMD-MIL achieved AUC=86.7±3.43%. ViT-S + CLAM-MB achieved Acc=81.7±3.08%, AUC=84.8±4.11%, F1=57.6±2.34%. PLIP + FR-MIL achieved Acc=84.6±0.99%, AUC=88.2±3.33%, F1=61.7±5.41%. CONCH + CLAM-MB achieved Acc=88.0±1.95%, AUC=91.1±5.02%, F1=65.1±2.62%, Recall=66.6±2.78%, Precision=66.2±6.34%, Kappa=0.73±0.06; CONCH + AMD-MIL achieved AUC=93.0±3.21%. CONCH-V1.5 + AMD-MIL achieved Acc=85.8±2.93%, AUC=90.7±2.55%, F1=63.9±6.76%. CTransPath + CLAM-MB achieved Acc=87.4±1.38%, AUC=89.6±3.84%, F1=65.6±5.08%. The paper emphasizes that Camelyon+ is long-tailed with an imbalance ratio of about 16.1, making macro/micro/ITC size-based four-class classification harder than standard binary cancer detection.
